Total = 60 + 4.5π. 60 + 9π uses a full circle, 60 + 18π uses a radius of 6 for a semicircle, 60 + 3π uses the semicircle's arc length, and 60 + 12.5π uses the 10-unit side as the diameter.

questions.stem: In a circle of radius 13, a chord is 5 units from the center. How long is the chord?
questions.explain: The perpendicular from the center bisects the chord, forming a right triangle with hypotenuse 13 and leg 5. The other leg is √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12, so the chord is 2 × 12 = 24. 12 forgets to double, 8 subtracts 13 − 5, 26 is the diameter, and 18 adds 13 and 5.

questions.stem: A sector of a circle with radius 6 has a central angle of 120°. What is its area?
questions.explain: A 120° sector is 120/360 = 1/3 of the circle, so its area is (1/3)π(6²) = 12π. 4π is the arc length, 36π is the whole circle, 24π takes 2/3 of the circle, and 6π takes 1/6 of it.

questions.stem: A right circular cone has a radius of 3 and a height of 4. What is its volume?
questions.explain: V = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π(9)(4) = 12π. 36π forgets the 1/3 (that is the cylinder), 4π uses r instead of r², 15π is the lateral surface area (πrl with slant height 5), and 48π uses a cylinder of radius 4 and height 3.

questions.stem: A cylinder's radius is doubled and its height is halved. Its volume is
questions.explain: V = πr²h. Doubling r multiplies r² by 4, and halving h multiplies by 1/2, so the volume is multiplied by 4 × 1/2 = 2. Unchanged treats the radius as linear (2 × 1/2), × 4 ignores the height change, halved ignores the radius change, and × 8 cubes the 2.

questions.stem: In a right triangle, cos θ = 0.6 and the hypotenuse is 15. What is the length of the side opposite θ?
questions.explain: cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, so the adjacent side is 0.6 × 15 = 9. The opposite side is √(15² − 9²) = √(225 − 81) = √144 = 12. Check: sin θ = 12/15 = 0.8, and 0.6² + 0.8² = 1. 9 is the adjacent side, 25 divides 15 by 0.6, 16 subtracts 9 from that 25, and 6 subtracts 15 − 9.

questions.stem: sin 30° + cos 60° + tan 45° is equal to
questions.explain: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 60° = 1/2 and tan 45° = 1, so the sum is 1/2 + 1/2 + 1 = 2. 1 drops tan 45° or takes it as 0, 3/2 counts only one of the 1/2 terms, (3 + √3)/2 uses cos 30° in place of cos 60°, and 1 + √3 uses tan 60° in place of tan 45°.

questions.stem: For sin θ ≠ 0, (1 − cos²θ) ÷ sin θ simplifies to
questions.explain: Since sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, the numerator 1 − cos²θ = sin²θ, and sin²θ ÷ sin θ = sin θ. cos θ mixes up the identity, 1 cancels the whole numerator, tan θ divides sin θ by cos θ as well, and sin²θ forgets to divide.

questions.stem: How many positive divisors does 72 have?
questions.explain: 72 = 2³ × 3². A divisor uses 2 to a power from 0 to 3 (4 choices) and 3 to a power from 0 to 2 (3 choices), so there are 4 × 3 = 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 18, 24, 36, 72. 6 multiplies the exponents (3 × 2), 8 adds 1 to only one exponent ((3 + 1) × 2), 10 drops 1 and 72, and 9 uses (3 + 0)(2 + 1).

questions.stem: When a positive integer n is divided by 6, the remainder is 4. What is the remainder when 3n is divided by 6?
questions.explain: Write n = 6k + 4. Then 3n = 18k + 12 = 6(3k + 2), a multiple of 6, so the remainder is 0. Check with n = 10: 30 ÷ 6 = 5 remainder 0. 4 assumes the remainder doesn't change, 12 triples the remainder without reducing it, 2 is the quotient 12 ÷ 6 rather than the remainder, and 3 is just the multiplier.

questions.stem: Two positive integers have a greatest common factor of 6 and a least common multiple of 180. One of them is 36. What is the other?
questions.explain: For any two positive integers, GCF × LCM = the product of the numbers: 6 × 180 = 1,080 = 36 × n, so n = 30. Check: GCF(36, 30) = 6 and LCM(36, 30) = 180. 5 is 180/36, 18 is a factor of 36 whose LCM with it is 36, 60 has GCF 12 with 36, and 180 is the LCM itself.

questions.stem: If −1 < x < 0, which of the following has the greatest value?
questions.explain: Try x = −1/2: −x = 1/2, x² = 1/4, x³ = −1/8, 1/x = −2 and x = −1/2. For any x between −1 and 0, −x is positive and x² = (−x)(−x) is smaller than −x, because −x is less than 1. x² is positive but smaller, x³ and x are negative, and 1/x is less than −1.

questions.stem: The solution set of |x − 4| = 2x + 1 is
questions.explain: Case 1: x − 4 = 2x + 1 gives x = −5, but then 2x + 1 = −9, and an absolute value can't equal a negative number, so −5 is rejected. Case 2: −(x − 4) = 2x + 1 gives 3 = 3x, x = 1, and |1 − 4| = 3 = 2(1) + 1. Keeping both skips the check, −5 only keeps the rejected root, −5/3 comes from writing −(x − 4) as −x − 4, and no solution rejects the valid root.

questions.stem: If 2 log x = log 36 − log 4, then x =
questions.explain: The right side is log(36/4) = log 9, and 2 log x = log x², so x² = 9. Logarithms need x > 0, so x = 3. 9 forgets the 2 in front of log x, 4.5 treats 2 log x as log 2x, 4√2 subtracts 36 − 4 = 32 inside the log, and −3 or 3 keeps a value that is not in the domain of log x.

Divide the numbers and subtract the exponents: 4.8/1.6 = 3.0, and 10⁵ ÷ 10⁻³ = 10⁵⁻⁽⁻³⁾ = 10⁸. 3.0 × 10² subtracts 3 instead of −3, 3.0 × 10⁻⁸ subtracts in the wrong order, 7.68 × 10² multiplies instead of dividing, and 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ multiplies the exponents.

questions.stem: x³ − 27 factors as
questions.explain: A difference of cubes factors as a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²), so x³ − 27 = (x − 3)(x² + 3x + 9). Check by expanding: x³ + 3x² + 9x − 3x² − 9x − 27 = x³ − 27. (x² − 3x + 9) uses the sign pattern for a sum of cubes, (x − 3)³ adds −9x² + 27x terms, (x² + 9) drops the middle term, and (x + 3)(x² − 3x + 9) is x³ + 27.

questions.stem: If x + 1/x = 5, then x² + 1/x² =
questions.explain: Square both sides: (x + 1/x)² = x² + 2 + 1/x² = 25, so x² + 1/x² = 25 − 2 = 23. 25 forgets the middle term 2(x)(1/x) = 2, 27 adds the 2 instead of subtracting, 24 subtracts only 1, and 10 doubles 5 instead of squaring.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Doppler radar reveals air motion from frequency shifts, but it senses only motion along its beam.
Doppler radar has replaced reflectivity radar because it measures rainfall amounts far more accurately.
Rotation inside a thunderstorm can be detected before a funnel cloud becomes visible.
Accurate weather forecasting depends on networks of radars operated from many sites.
Wind blowing across a radar beam is usually much weaker than wind blowing along it.
questions.passage:
Conventional weather radar answers a single question: how much energy bounces back from precipitation at a given range and bearing. Strong returns suggest heavy rain or hail, but a reflectivity picture alone says little about how the air is moving. Doppler radar adds that missing dimension by comparing the frequency of each returned pulse with the frequency that was transmitted. Droplets drifting toward the antenna return a slightly higher frequency; droplets moving away return a slightly lower one. By mapping these shifts, forecasters can see rotation inside a thunderstorm, often as a tight pair of inbound and outbound velocities lying side by side, well before a funnel cloud becomes visible.

The technique has a built-in blind spot, however. A single radar measures only the component of motion along its own beam. Wind blowing exactly across the beam produces no shift at all and appears calm, however fast it is actually moving. For this reason, meteorologists interpret velocity data with the radar's position constantly in mind, and they value overlapping coverage from neighboring sites, which view the same storm from different angles.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the second paragraph is to
options: show how a uniform, disciplined system fixed the problems described earlier
argue that individual heroism was the main reason the airlift eventually succeeded
explain the political reasons the Soviet blockade was eventually lifted
compare air transport unfavorably with the railways that served the city
describe the hardships endured by Berlin's residents during the blockade
questions.passage:
When Soviet authorities cut road, rail and canal access to West Berlin in June 1948, few planners believed the city's two million residents could be supplied by air for long. The early weeks seemed to confirm the doubt. Aircraft of different types flew at different speeds, crews improvised their own approaches, and on one overcast day in August so many planes stacked up over Tempelhof airfield that controllers ordered most of them back to their bases, loads undelivered.

Major General William Tunner, who had taken command of the operation weeks earlier, treated the problem less as a test of heroism than as a production line. He insisted that aircraft fly at the same speed and altitude in a fixed sequence, and that a pilot who missed a landing return home rather than circle and try again. Crews were forbidden to leave their aircraft during unloading; snacks and weather briefings were brought to them on the ramp. The aim was a steady, predictable beat of arrivals rather than bursts of effort. On its best day, in April 1949, the airlift delivered more tonnage than the railways had typically carried into the city before the blockade.
questions.explain: The first paragraph lists mixed speeds, improvised approaches and a pile-up over Tempelhof; the second shows Tunner fixing them with same speeds, a fixed sequence and "a steady, predictable beat of arrivals." The passage says he treated it as "less a test of heroism" (reversed), never discusses why the blockade ended or residents' hardships, and its last sentence favors the airlift over rail, not the reverse.

discourage crews whose flying skills fell below the required standard
reserve the runways at Tempelhof for the heaviest and most urgent loads
give crews more rest between flights during the busiest months of the airlift
reduce the number of different aircraft types flying the route into Berlin

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does a GPS receiver need signals from a fourth satellite?
options: To solve for the error in the receiver's own inexpensive clock
To correct for timing errors in the satellites' atomic clocks
To confirm the speed at which the radio signals are traveling
To choose between two widely separated points where spheres meet
To allow the receiver to transmit its position back to the system
questions.passage:
A GPS receiver does not send anything to the satellites overhead; it only listens. Each satellite continuously broadcasts its own position and the precise time at which its signal left the spacecraft. Because radio waves travel at a known speed, the receiver can convert the delay between transmission and reception into a distance. A distance from one satellite places the receiver somewhere on a vast imaginary sphere; distances from three satellites narrow the possibilities to a single point near the earth's surface.

In practice a fourth satellite is required, and the reason lies in the receiver's clock. The satellites carry atomic clocks accurate to billionths of a second, but a typical handheld unit carries an inexpensive quartz clock. An error of just one millionth of a second would shift each computed distance by roughly 300 meters. Rather than demand a costly clock in every receiver, the system treats the receiver's clock error as one more unknown to be solved. With four distances, the receiver can calculate its three position coordinates and the correction to its own clock at the same time, which is why a unit that can see only three satellites produces unreliable fixes.
questions.explain: The second paragraph says the fourth satellite is needed because of "the receiver's clock," whose error is treated "as one more unknown to be solved." The satellites' atomic clocks are the accurate ones (reversed), the speed of radio waves is described as known, the passage says three spheres already narrow things to a single point, and receivers do not transmit at all.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Since the inner ear can misreport a held turn, pilots must trust instruments over sensation.
Spatial disorientation comes mainly from poor training and can be eliminated through practice.
The semicircular canals are the most reliable of the three senses the body uses for orientation.
Pulling back on the stick is the correct way to stop a descent when the altimeter is unwinding.
Pilots flying without a visible horizon should avoid banking the aircraft whenever possible.
questions.passage:
On the ground, the body judges its orientation by combining three streams of information: what the eyes see, what the muscles and joints feel, and what the vestibular organs of the inner ear sense. In flight without a visible horizon, the eyes lose their reference, and the remaining senses can be badly misled. The fluid-filled semicircular canals detect changes in rotation, not steady rotation. If an aircraft slips gradually into a bank and holds it, the fluid soon catches up with the canal walls and the sensation of turning fades. The pilot feels level while still turning.

The danger grows when the pilot notices the altimeter unwinding. Feeling level, the pilot pulls back on the stick to stop the descent, but in a banked aircraft this tightens the turn and steepens the descent. If the pilot then rolls out correctly, the canals may register the roll as a turn in the opposite direction, tempting the pilot to re-enter the original bank. Training cannot remove these illusions, which are normal physiology rather than signs of weakness. What training can do is teach pilots to recognize the conflict and to believe the instruments over the body's insistent signals.
questions.explain: The passage explains how the canals stop sensing a held bank and then concludes that training should "teach pilots to recognize the conflict and to believe the instruments." It states that "Training cannot remove these illusions" (reversed), shows the canals misleading the pilot, describes pulling back as the move that "tightens the turn," and never advises against banking.

options: A clear, visible horizon outside the cockpit

A higher cruising altitude above the ground

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does an engine with a narrow, very fast exhaust jet waste fuel?
options: Its exhaust keeps kinetic energy that grows with the square of exhaust speed.
It accelerates too large a mass of air for the amount of thrust it produces.
It produces less total thrust than a broad, slow stream of air would provide.
Its wide nacelle adds frontal area and drag at every speed it flies.
It sends most of its air around the core instead of through the core.
questions.passage:
A jet engine produces thrust by accelerating air rearward, and there are two ways to obtain a given amount of thrust: accelerate a small mass of air to a very high speed, or a large mass of air to a modest speed. Both can deliver the same push, but they differ sharply in efficiency. The kinetic energy left behind in the exhaust is wasted, and that energy rises with the square of the exhaust velocity. An engine that blasts a narrow jet far faster than the aircraft is flying therefore throws away much of the fuel it burns.

The high-bypass turbofan exploits this principle. A large fan at the front drives most of its air around the engine core rather than through it, so that the bulk of the thrust comes from a broad, relatively slow stream. Modern airliner engines may bypass ten or more pounds of air for every pound that passes through the core. The tradeoff is size and drag: a large fan needs a wide nacelle, and at supersonic speeds that frontal area becomes a heavy penalty. That is why fighters, which must dash past the speed of sound, use low-bypass engines with narrow, fast exhausts.
questions.explain: The first paragraph says the energy left in the exhaust "is wasted, and that energy rises with the square of the exhaust velocity," so a very fast jet throws much of it away. A fast narrow jet moves a small mass of air, not a large one; the passage says both methods "can deliver the same push"; the wide nacelle and the bypass flow belong to the high-bypass turbofan.

low-bypass engines, because narrow exhausts give more thrust per pound of fuel
engines with the narrowest possible nacelles to cut frontal area at all costs

whichever engine design produces the highest possible exhaust velocity

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the central point of the passage?
options: Stating purpose and end state lets subordinates adapt when detailed plans no longer fit, but it depends on trust.
Detailed orders should be abandoned entirely because they make it difficult to judge a subordinate's performance.
Commanders should give subordinates as little guidance as possible so that they can act independently.
Plans become outdated because enemy forces change their positions faster than friendly forces do.
Military success depends mainly on the personal skill and experience of the commanding officer.
questions.passage:
Orders written in exhaustive detail have an obvious appeal. They seem to leave nothing to chance, and they make it easy to judge afterward whether a subordinate did what was asked. Yet detailed orders age quickly. A plan is written against a picture of the enemy, the weather and one's own forces that begins to go stale the moment it is published, and a subordinate bound to the letter of the instructions may find, at the critical hour, that they no longer fit the situation in front of them.

The alternative is not vagueness. A commander who expresses intent explains the purpose behind a task and the end state that would count as success, while leaving the method to those closer to the action. This places real demands on both sides. The commander must think hard enough about the purpose to state it in a sentence or two, and must tolerate subordinates sometimes choosing methods the commander would not have chosen. Subordinates, for their part, must understand the purpose well enough to act on it when no one is available to ask. Intent is less a way of writing orders than a relationship of trust that has to be built before it is needed.
questions.explain: The passage argues that detailed orders "age quickly," offers commander's intent as the alternative, and ends by calling intent "a relationship of trust that has to be built before it is needed." It says detailed orders make judging subordinates easy (reversed), states "The alternative is not vagueness," never compares the pace of enemy and friendly change, and stresses demands on both sides rather than the commander alone.

questions.stem: The author compares a pilot to a ship's captain following lighthouses in order to
options: clarify how pilots navigated by moving from one visible light to the next
suggest that most of the early airmail pilots had first trained as ship's officers
argue that travel by sea was safer than travel by air at night
emphasize how dangerous night flying became in fog and low cloud
show that the beacon towers were built and run by coastal agencies
questions.passage:
In the early 1920s, airmail could beat the railroads only by day. At dusk, pilots landed and handed their sacks to trains, which carried the mail through the night while the planes sat idle, and much of the advantage of flight was lost in the dark. The solution was not a better airplane but a lighted path across the country. Beginning in 1923, crews erected rotating beacons on towers spaced roughly every ten to fifteen miles along the route, many standing beside enormous concrete arrows that pointed toward the next beacon and were painted bright yellow.

A pilot on a clear night could fly from flash to flash, much as a ship's captain follows lighthouses down a coast. The system had obvious weaknesses. Low clouds or fog hid the beacons entirely, and pilots who pressed on into bad weather were sometimes killed. Within two decades, radio navigation aids had made the towers largely obsolete. Yet for a time the beacons turned the airplane from a daytime novelty into a round-the-clock carrier, and the routes they marked helped shape the airway system that followed.
questions.explain: The comparison immediately follows "A pilot on a clear night could fly from flash to flash," so it explains the method of navigation by a familiar image. Nothing is said about pilots' backgrounds, sea safety or who built the towers, and the danger of fog is raised in the next sentences as a separate point about the system's weaknesses.

questions.stem: The detail that the concrete arrows were painted bright yellow most strongly suggests that
options: the route markings were meant to guide pilots by day as well as by night
the beacons alone were bright enough to guide pilots through fog

questions.passage:
In the early 1920s, airmail could beat the railroads only by day. At dusk, pilots landed and handed their sacks to trains, which carried the mail through the night while the planes sat idle, and much of the advantage of flight was lost in the dark. The solution was not a better airplane but a lighted path across the country. Beginning in 1923, crews erected rotating beacons on towers spaced roughly every ten to fifteen miles along the route, many standing beside enormous concrete arrows that pointed toward the next beacon and were painted bright yellow.

A pilot on a clear night could fly from flash to flash, much as a ship's captain follows lighthouses down a coast. The system had obvious weaknesses. Low clouds or fog hid the beacons entirely, and pilots who pressed on into bad weather were sometimes killed. Within two decades, radio navigation aids had made the towers largely obsolete. Yet for a time the beacons turned the airplane from a daytime novelty into a round-the-clock carrier, and the routes they marked helped shape the airway system that followed.
questions.explain: At night the rotating beacons did the guiding; bright paint helps only when there is daylight to see it by, so the arrows were meant to serve daytime flights too. The passage says fog "hid the beacons entirely," a painted arrow would be useless on a dark night, radio aids came later and replaced the towers, and the whole point of the system was night flying, so "chiefly for daylight" overstates.

questions.passage:
Low earth orbit is not crowded in the way a highway is crowded; the volume of space is enormous, and the objects in it are small. The hazard lies instead in speed. At typical orbital velocities, two objects in crossing orbits can meet at ten kilometers per second or more, and at such speeds even a fragment the size of a marble carries the energy of a small explosive charge. Shielding can protect a spacecraft against the tiniest particles, but objects a few centimeters across can be lethal and are too small to be tracked reliably from the ground.

The outcome that most concerns planners is a chain reaction. Every collision between large objects produces thousands of new fragments, each of which raises the odds of further collisions. Beyond some density, debris could multiply on its own even if no new satellites were launched, rendering certain orbital altitudes too risky to use for generations. Debris at lower altitudes eventually falls back as the thin upper atmosphere drags it down, but at higher altitudes it can remain for centuries. For this reason, tracking agencies watch the population closely, and newer satellites are increasingly designed to lower themselves out of orbit when their missions end.
questions.explain: Debris multiplying on its own would make certain altitudes "too risky to use," so "rendering" means causing something to become a certain way. "Drawing" (an artist's rendering), "surrendering" (render up), "melting" (rendering fat) and "translating" are other senses of the word that make no sense with "too risky to use."

questions.stem: The author's main point about the Wrights' wind tunnel work is that
options: its significance lay in their readiness to test accepted data, not in the tunnel's novelty
the Wrights invented the wind tunnel in order to test Lilienthal's original glider designs
Lilienthal's tables were the chief cause of failure throughout early aviation
simple homemade instruments always give better results than precision equipment
the 1902 glider proved that larger wings were the solution to the lift shortfall
questions.passage:
By 1901 the Wright brothers faced a problem their gliders could not explain away. Their machines produced far less lift than the published tables, built largely on the work of the German glider pioneer Otto Lilienthal, said they should. The brothers might have concluded that their own construction was at fault, or simply built bigger wings and hoped. Instead they built a small wind tunnel in their Dayton bicycle shop and began measuring for themselves.

Over a few months in late 1901 they tested some two hundred miniature wing shapes, using balances made from bicycle spokes and hacksaw blades to compare lift and drag. The results showed that a coefficient used in the standard lift equation, a figure dating back more than a century, was too high, which helped account for the shortfall, and they revealed which wing shapes performed best. What distinguishes the episode is less the tunnel itself, since others had built wind tunnels before, than the brothers' willingness to doubt accepted figures and replace them with data they could check. The glider they flew in 1902, designed from their own tables, finally performed as predicted.
questions.explain: The author says the episode is distinguished "less the tunnel itself, since others had built wind tunnels before, than the brothers' willingness to doubt accepted figures." That same sentence rules out the claim that they invented the tunnel; the passage blames one old coefficient rather than all of early aviation, never says homemade tools are always better, and presents bigger wings as the option they rejected.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, Boyd would most likely consider which information the most useful to a pilot before engaging an enemy fighter?
options: Where in the envelope the pilot's aircraft gains energy faster than the enemy's
Which of the two aircraft can reach the higher maximum speed in level flight
How much fuel each aircraft carries at the start of the engagement
Which of the two aircraft types entered operational service more recently
Which pilot has logged more total flying hours in high-performance fighter aircraft
questions.passage:
Before the 1960s, fighter performance was often judged by a few headline figures, above all top speed. John Boyd, an Air Force fighter pilot, argued that such figures said little about who would win a turning fight. What mattered was the aircraft's total energy, made up of altitude and speed, either of which could be traded for the other: height for speed in a dive, speed for height in a climb. Every hard turn bleeds energy away through drag, and the engine restores it. A fighter's real advantage, Boyd reasoned, lay in how quickly it could gain or regain energy at a given speed and altitude, a quantity he called specific excess power.

Working with the civilian mathematician Thomas Christie, who helped him obtain computer time to run the calculations, Boyd plotted these values across the whole flight envelope. The charts showed, region by region, where one aircraft could out-turn or out-climb another and where it should decline to fight. Pilots gained a tactical map; designers gained a new standard. The approach shaped the requirements for the lightweight, highly maneuverable fighters of the following decade, aircraft that gave up some top speed for superior energy performance.
questions.explain: Boyd's charts showed "region by region, where one aircraft could out-turn or out-climb another and where it should decline to fight," based on how quickly each gains energy at a given speed and altitude. He argued top speed "said little about who would win a turning fight" (reversed), and fuel, service dates and pilot hours are never part of his theory.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Geostationary and low orbits each carry unavoidable costs, so the right choice depends on the mission.
Low orbits have replaced geostationary orbits because they eliminate the delay in satellite signals.
Geostationary satellites are the better choice because they require no tracking antennas on the ground.
Signal delay is the most serious engineering problem facing the designers of communications satellites.
Three geostationary satellites are enough to provide communications to nearly the whole inhabited world.
questions.passage:
A satellite placed about 22,000 miles above the equator circles the earth once a day, exactly matching the planet's rotation. Seen from the ground it hangs motionless, so a fixed dish can stay pointed at it without tracking, and three such satellites spaced around the equator can see nearly the whole inhabited world. For decades this geostationary orbit was the natural home of communications satellites.

The arrangement carries a cost that no engineering can eliminate: distance. A radio signal needs roughly a quarter of a second to travel up to a geostationary satellite and back down, a delay that callers notice as awkward pauses and that slows interactive data links. Satellites in low orbit, a few hundred miles up, cut that delay to a few hundredths of a second. But a low satellite races across the sky in minutes and sees only a small patch of the earth at a time, so continuous service requires hundreds or thousands of them, linked together, along with ground antennas that can follow them. The choice between the two is therefore not a matter of which orbit is better, but of which compromise a particular mission can best accept.
questions.explain: The passage closes by saying the choice "is therefore not a matter of which orbit is better, but of which compromise a particular mission can best accept," after listing the costs of each orbit. Low orbits only reduce delay and are never said to have replaced geostationary ones; calling either orbit simply better contradicts the conclusion; and the three-satellite point is a single detail (too narrow).

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which crew member is likely to be the LEAST alert?
options: One who has been awake for 18 hours and is working at 3:00 a.m.
One who has been awake for 3 hours and is working at 4:00 a.m.
One who has been awake for 12 hours and is working at 7:00 in the evening
One who has been awake for 8 hours and is working at 3:00 p.m.
One who has been awake for 3 hours and is working at 10:00 a.m.
questions.passage:
Fatigue is often treated as a simple matter of hours awake, but the body keeps a second account. Alongside the pressure for sleep that builds steadily the longer a person stays up, an internal clock of roughly twenty-four hours raises and lowers alertness on its own schedule. For most people, that clock produces a deep trough in the early morning hours, typically between about two and six, and a smaller dip in mid-afternoon. A crew member who has been awake only a few hours but is working at four in the morning may therefore be less alert than one who has been awake twelve hours in the early evening.

This has practical consequences for scheduling. Simply limiting the length of a duty period does not guarantee an alert crew if the period falls across the early-morning low. Nor can the internal clock be reset overnight: after an abrupt shift to night work or a flight across several time zones, it adjusts by only about an hour per day. Planners who understand both processes can place the most demanding tasks, such as an approach and landing, away from the trough where possible, and treat the hours that fall within it with special caution.
questions.explain: The passage describes two separate processes: sleep pressure that "builds steadily the longer a person stays up" and a clock trough "between about two and six" in the morning. Only the 18-hour, 3:00 a.m. crew member suffers heavily from both at once. The 3-hours-at-4:00 a.m. case has the trough but little sleep pressure, the afternoon case has only the "smaller dip," and the others fall outside the low points.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Checklists guard skilled crews of complex systems against forgetting simple, critical steps.
The Model 299 was too complicated for even an experienced crew to fly safely.
More thorough training is the most effective way to prevent aircraft accidents.
The B-17 went on to become one of the most successful bombers of its era.
Inexperienced crews are responsible for most of the accidents that occur in complex aircraft.
questions.passage:
In October 1935 Army Air Corps officials gathered at Wright Field to watch a demonstration flight of Boeing's Model 299, the prototype of what would become the B-17. The big four-engine bomber climbed steeply, stalled and crashed, and two of the crew later died. Investigators found no mechanical failure. The highly experienced crew had simply forgotten to release a lock that held the control surfaces fixed while the aircraft sat on the ground. Some newspapers concluded that the airplane was too complicated for anyone to fly.

The response that followed was modest in form and lasting in effect. Rather than demand more training or blame the crew, test pilots wrote a short list of items to be checked before takeoff, landing and other critical phases. The checklist did not teach anyone to fly; it assumed expert pilots and guarded against the lapses that expertise does not prevent, especially in routine moments when attention drifts. Its lesson has outlived the aircraft. Complex systems fail less often from ignorance than from the omission of a simple step that everyone knows and someone, on one particular day, forgets.
questions.explain: The passage uses the crash to show that the checklist "assumed expert pilots and guarded against the lapses that expertise does not prevent," ending with the general lesson about omitted simple steps. "Too complicated" is the newspapers' view, which the response refutes; the test pilots chose a checklist "Rather than demand more training"; the B-17's later record is true but not discussed; and the crew was "highly experienced."

In October 1935 Army Air Corps officials gathered at Wright Field to watch a demonstration flight of Boeing's Model 299, the prototype of what would become the B-17. The big four-engine bomber climbed steeply, stalled and crashed, and two of the crew later died. Investigators found no mechanical failure. The highly experienced crew had simply forgotten to release a lock that held the control surfaces fixed while the aircraft sat on the ground. Some newspapers concluded that the airplane was too complicated for anyone to fly.

The response that followed was modest in form and lasting in effect. Rather than demand more training or blame the crew, test pilots wrote a short list of items to be checked before takeoff, landing and other critical phases. The checklist did not teach anyone to fly; it assumed expert pilots and guarded against the lapses that expertise does not prevent, especially in routine moments when attention drifts. Its lesson has outlived the aircraft. Complex systems fail less often from ignorance than from the omission of a simple step that everyone knows and someone, on one particular day, forgets.
questions.explain: The author says the checklist "assumed expert pilots" and guarded against lapses "especially in routine moments when attention drifts." questions.stem: According to the passage, an aircraft's airspeed collapses during a microburst encounter when the aircraft
options: reaches the tailwind on the far side of the outflow
first meets the headwind at the edge of the outflow
balloons above the glide path on entering the outflow
climbs at maximum power after the encounter is confirmed
is still several miles from the thunderstorm itself
questions.passage:
A microburst is a column of sinking air, often less than two and a half miles across, that strikes the ground beneath a thunderstorm and spreads outward in all directions. For an aircraft on final approach, the encounter typically unfolds in a deceptive sequence. Entering the outflow, the aircraft first meets a strong headwind. Airspeed jumps, the aircraft balloons above the glide path, and the pilot's natural response is to reduce power and lower the nose. Moments later the aircraft passes through the core, where the air is pouring downward, and then into the far side of the outflow, where the headwind has become a tailwind. Airspeed collapses just as the aircraft is low, slow and configured for landing, with power already reduced.

Because the first sign of trouble seems to be an improvement in performance, crews were for years caught off guard. Modern training reverses the instinct. An unexpected gain in airspeed on approach near a thunderstorm is treated as a possible warning, and the recommended response to a confirmed encounter is maximum power and a climb, not a correction back down toward the glide path.
questions.explain: The passage says the aircraft passes into "the far side of the outflow, where the headwind has become a tailwind. Airspeed collapses." The headwind and ballooning come first and make airspeed jump, maximum power and a climb are the recommended recovery, and a microburst is described as often less than two and a half miles across, beneath the storm.

questions.stem: A radar can detect a certain aircraft at 80 miles. According to the relationship described in the passage, at about what range could the same radar detect the aircraft if its radar cross section were cut to one-sixteenth of its former value?
questions.passage:
A radar detects a target by catching the faint echo of its own pulse, and that echo weakens dramatically with distance. The pulse spreads out on its way to the target, and the reflected energy spreads out again on its way back, so the returned signal falls with the fourth power of range. Double the distance, and the echo becomes sixteen times weaker. One consequence surprises many people: shrinking an aircraft's radar cross section, its apparent size to a radar, reduces detection range far less than the raw numbers suggest. Cutting the cross section to one-sixteenth of its former value only halves the range at which a given radar can detect it.

Designers of stealth aircraft accept this arithmetic and therefore pursue reductions of a thousandfold or more rather than modest gains. Shaping does most of the work: flat panels and aligned edges steer reflections away from the radar rather than back toward it, and internal weapons bays keep bombs and missiles from adding reflective surfaces. Radar-absorbent coatings soak up some of what remains. Even so, stealth is a matter of degree. It shortens the distance at which a defender can see and engage the aircraft, buying time and freedom of action, rather than making the aircraft invisible.
questions.explain: The passage states that "Cutting the cross section to one-sixteenth of its former value only halves the range," so 80 miles becomes 80 / 2 = 40 miles. Dividing by 16 (5 miles) treats range as falling in step with cross section, 20 miles divides by 4 (a square-root rule), 10 miles divides by 8, and 60 miles is an unsupported guess.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Radar mattered in 1940 because a reporting and control system turned its imperfect data into decisions.
British radar in 1940 was more advanced than any other military technology in use during the period.
Ground observers, rather than radar, were the true reason that the Royal Air Force won the battle.
Standing patrols were the most effective way for the Royal Air Force to defend against raids.
Popular accounts of the Second World War are generally unreliable and should be avoided.
questions.passage:
Popular accounts of the Battle of Britain often credit radar with the British victory in 1940, as though the sets along the coast had simply revealed the enemy and the fighters had done the rest. The radar of the day was in fact crude. It could misjudge an incoming formation's height and size, it looked out to sea and could not follow aircraft once they had crossed the coast, and its reports arrived as a flood of raw, sometimes contradictory plots.

What made radar decisive was the system built around it. Reports from the coastal stations and from thousands of ground observers flowed to filter rooms, where staff reconciled conflicting plots into a single picture. That picture passed to operations rooms, where controllers decided which squadrons to launch and directed them by radio toward the raiders. Because fighters could be held on the ground until a raid was confirmed, the Royal Air Force avoided wearing out pilots and aircraft on standing patrols. The system's great achievement was not detection alone but the rapid conversion of uncertain information into decisions.
questions.explain: The passage calls the radar "crude" but says "What made radar decisive was the system built around it," ending with "the rapid conversion of uncertain information into decisions." The word "crude" rules out "most advanced"; observers were one input to the system, not a replacement for radar; standing patrols were what the system let the RAF avoid; and one corrected story does not make all popular accounts unreliable (too broad).

questions.stem: In the sentence beginning "It adheres strongly," the word "clear" most nearly means
questions.passage:
Water in clouds does not necessarily freeze at 32 degrees Fahrenheit. Tiny droplets, free of the dust or ice crystals that would give freezing a starting point, can remain liquid well below that temperature. These supercooled droplets are stable only until something disturbs them, and an aircraft wing passing through the cloud is exactly such a disturbance. On contact the droplets freeze, and the way they freeze determines the kind of ice that forms.

Very small droplets at colder temperatures tend to freeze almost instantly where they strike, trapping air between them and building rough, milky rime ice on the leading edges. Larger droplets at temperatures nearer freezing do not solidify all at once; part of each drop flows back across the surface before it freezes, producing clear ice, which is glassy, dense and hard to see. Clear ice is generally regarded as the more hazardous of the two. It adheres strongly, can spread beyond the areas that ice protection equipment is built to clear, and can form irregular ridges that disrupt the airflow over the wing. Even a thin, rough coating of either kind, however, can sharply reduce lift and raise the speed at which the wing stalls.
questions.explain: Clear ice can spread beyond the areas that ice protection equipment is built to clear, meaning the areas the equipment is designed to rid of ice. Make transparent borrows the sense of clear in "clear ice" earlier in the same paragraph, authorize for use is the "cleared for takeoff" sense, and pass safely over is the sense of clearing an obstacle. Heat evenly describes how some equipment works, not what the word means here.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the aircrew debrief is best described as
options: approving, while warning of two opposite ways it can be misapplied
skeptical, regarding it as a poor use of time after demanding flights
uncritically enthusiastic about excusing every error crews make
nostalgic for an era in which rank was more strictly respected
indifferent to whether other organizations practice it correctly
questions.passage:
Among aircrews, the debrief that follows a sortie is often more demanding than the flight itself. Its purpose is not to assign a grade but to find out what happened and why, and that requires a peculiar kind of honesty. Rank is set aside: a lieutenant may point out a flight lead's error, and the flight lead is expected to own it without defensiveness. The most respected participants are frequently those quickest to name their own mistakes, because doing so makes it safe for others to do the same.

Organizations that borrow this habit sometimes misunderstand it. A debrief that turns into a search for someone to blame quickly teaches people to stay silent, and the errors that matter most, the near misses no one else saw, are the first to go unreported. Yet the opposite mistake is just as damaging. A culture that excuses everything learns nothing, because lessons without accountability are not taken seriously. The aim is a narrow path between the two: errors are discussed openly and without punishment, while reckless or deliberate violations are still treated as the serious matters they are.
questions.explain: The author praises the debrief's honesty and its most respected participants, then warns against both a blame-seeking debrief and "A culture that excuses everything," calling for "a narrow path between the two." Nothing suggests the author thinks it wastes time, the author rejects excusing everything, setting rank aside is approved rather than mourned, and the warnings show the author cares how it is practiced.

questions.stem: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred about the tests that "hinted at the problem"?
options: Taking them more seriously might have revealed the flaw before launch.
They were the source of the error in the shape of the primary mirror.
They were carried out only after the telescope had reached orbit.
They were known to be more accurate than the primary test at the time.
They showed that the mirror's surface had been polished unevenly.
questions.passage:
When the Hubble Space Telescope returned its first images in 1990, astronomers expected unprecedented sharpness. Instead, stars appeared surrounded by a faint haze. The cause was traced to the primary mirror, which had been polished with extraordinary smoothness to the wrong shape: near its edge it was too flat by roughly two micrometers, about one-fiftieth the width of a human hair. The error came from a testing instrument that had been assembled with one element slightly out of position. The mirror had been made precisely to a flawed standard, and other tests that hinted at the problem had been discounted because they were considered less accurate than the primary one.

The flaw could not be polished away in orbit, but because it had been made so precisely, it could also be measured precisely. Engineers designed corrective optics that introduced an equal and opposite error, much as eyeglasses correct a person's vision. Astronauts installed them during a servicing mission in December 1993, and the telescope went on to deliver the images its builders had promised. The episode is remembered both as an embarrassment and as an unusual case in which the very precision of a mistake made it curable.
questions.explain: These tests pointed to the problem but "had been discounted," so taking them seriously could have exposed the flaw while the mirror was still on the ground. The error came from the misassembled primary instrument, the hints came before the 1990 images, the passage says they "were considered less accurate," and the mirror was polished "with extraordinary smoothness," just to the wrong shape.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the phrase "lost their bite" most nearly means
questions.passage:
In the mid-1940s, the "sound barrier" was less a wall than a region of trouble. As aircraft approached the speed of sound, shock waves formed on the wings and tail, airflow separated behind them, and controls that had worked well at lower speeds lost their bite. Some pilots who dove toward Mach 1 found that pulling back on the stick did almost nothing, because the shock wave on the horizontal tail had made the elevator nearly useless.

The rocket-powered Bell X-1 carried a partial answer. Its entire horizontal stabilizer could be adjusted in flight, rather than relying only on the hinged elevator at its trailing edge. questions.stem: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred about the German forecasters' error?
options: They missed the brief improvement because they had fewer Atlantic observations.
They failed to detect the storm that forced Eisenhower to postpone the landings.
They foresaw the brief improvement but judged it too short for a landing.
They relied on the same forecasting teams as Stagg but read the data differently.
They expected the later June window to bring better weather than early June.
questions.passage:
In the first days of June 1944, the fate of the Normandy invasion rested partly on a weather map. The landings required a rare combination of conditions: a late-rising moon for the airborne drops, a low tide shortly after dawn so that beach obstacles would be exposed, winds calm enough for landing craft, and cloud high enough for bombers to see their targets. Only a few days each month met the tidal and lunar requirements, and the first such window began on June 5.

Group Captain James Stagg, the chief meteorologist advising General Eisenhower, had no satellites and no computer models. He relied on reports from ships, aircraft and weather stations scattered across the North Atlantic, and on the judgment of three forecasting teams that did not always agree. On June 4 he advised that a storm would make a June 5 landing hazardous, and Eisenhower postponed the operation. That evening Stagg reported something subtler: a brief interval of improving weather, likely to arrive behind the storm on June 6, before conditions deteriorated again. The break would be marginal, not ideal. Eisenhower chose to go.

German forecasters, working from far fewer Atlantic observations, saw the storm but not the interval behind it. Confident that no invasion could come in such weather, several senior commanders left their posts; Field Marshal Erwin Rommel traveled home to Germany. The next suitable tidal window, later in June, brought one of the worst Channel storms in decades.

Stagg's achievement is often described as a lucky call. It is more accurately seen as a judgment made under uncertainty, in which the value of the forecast lay less in its precision than in its timing and in the fact that the other side lacked it.
questions.explain: The passage says the German forecasters, "working from far fewer Atlantic observations, saw the storm but not the interval behind it," linking the error to their lack of data. They did see the storm, so the first wrong option contradicts the passage. Nothing says they spotted the interval and dismissed it, that they used Stagg's teams, or that they made any forecast about the later window.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Each refueling system trades some advantages for others, and their coexistence complicates joint operations.
The boom's higher transfer rate has made it the better choice for most air forces, despite its complexity.
The drogue asks more of the receiving pilot, but its simplicity has made adapters unnecessary in coalitions.
Air refueling has extended the range of both large and small military aircraft since the 1950s.
The Air Force chose the boom for its bombers, while the Navy chose the drogue for its helicopters.
questions.passage:
Two methods of passing fuel between aircraft in flight have survived since the 1950s, and each reflects a different answer to the question of who should do the hardest flying.

In the flying boom system, a rigid telescoping tube hangs beneath the tanker's tail. An operator aboard the tanker steers the boom with small control surfaces and extends it into a receptacle on the receiving aircraft, whose pilot need only hold a steady position in formation. Because the boom is rigid and wide, it can pass fuel at a very high rate, which matters to large bombers and transports that may take on tens of thousands of pounds in a single contact.

In the probe-and-drogue system, the tanker trails a flexible hose ending in a funnel-shaped basket, the drogue. The receiving pilot must fly a fixed probe into the basket, a task made harder by the basket's tendency to bob in turbulent air. Transfer rates are lower. In exchange, the equipment is simpler and lighter, hoses can be mounted in pods under each wing so that two receivers can refuel at once, and small aircraft, including helicopters, can be fitted with probes far more easily than with receptacles.

Neither system is simply better. The U.S. Air Force, whose fleet was built around long-range bombers, standardized on the boom; the Navy and most allied air forces chose the drogue. The result is a persistent compatibility problem in coalition operations, which is why Air Force tankers are often fitted with an adapter that converts the boom into a short hose and basket before a mission with Navy or allied receivers. The adapter solves the immediate problem, but a tanker so fitted cannot refuel boom-equipped aircraft until it lands and is reconfigured.
questions.explain: The passage weighs the boom's high transfer rate against the drogue's simplicity and flexibility, states that "Neither system is simply better," and ends on the compatibility problem the split creates. The first wrong option contradicts "Neither system is simply better" and the fact that most allied air forces chose the drogue. The second contradicts the passage's account of tankers being fitted with adapters. The range point is too broad, and the last option gives the Navy a reason the passage never states while leaving out the compatibility problem.

questions.stem: A single Air Force tanker fitted with the adapter must refuel Navy fighters and then, later on the same flight, Air Force bombers that carry receptacles. Based on the passage, what problem would arise?
options: The tanker could not refuel the bombers without first landing to remove the adapter.
The bombers would have to fly probes into the basket in turbulent air.
The fighters would take on fuel faster than the bombers could.
The boom operator would have to steer the drogue into each fighter's receptacle.
The fighters would need receptacles fitted before the mission could begin.

options: it can be fitted to small aircraft such as helicopters
it lets the tanker crew do the most precise flying
it passes fuel at a higher rate than the flying boom
its basket stays steady even in turbulent air

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's view that the 1943 losses exposed a flaw in the self-defending bomber theory rather than bad luck on two missions?
options: Unescorted formations on other deep raids that autumn also suffered heavy losses.
Cloud over Schweinfurt in October made accurate bombing unusually difficult.
The ball-bearing factories were back in production within weeks of each raid.
German fighter strength near Schweinfurt was unusually concentrated on both days.
Some escorted raids in 1944 also lost a substantial number of bombers.
questions.passage:
Before the Second World War, many American air planners believed that a tight formation of heavily armed bombers could fight its way to a target in daylight without fighter escort. The idea was not careless. Escort fighters of the 1930s lacked the range to accompany bombers deep into enemy territory, and the bombers' massed machine guns appeared, on paper, to create a lethal zone around the formation. If the self-defending bomber was a fact, long-range escorts were an expensive luxury.

The air war over Germany in 1943 tested the idea directly. In two deep raids, one in August against Schweinfurt and Regensburg together and one in October against the ball-bearing factories at Schweinfurt alone, the Eighth Air Force lost about sixty bombers each time, and October's losses, roughly a fifth of the force dispatched, could not be sustained. German fighters had learned to attack from head-on, where the bombers' defensive fire was weakest, and to wait until the escorts turned back at the limit of their range. Deep raids were largely suspended for several months.

The remedy combined new equipment with new orders. Drop tanks extended the reach of existing fighters, and the P-51 Mustang, re-engined with the Rolls-Royce Merlin, could fly to Berlin and back. Early in 1944, commanders also loosened the rule that tied escorts closely to the bombers, allowing fighters to range ahead and hunt German interceptors. The bombers became, in effect, bait that drew the Luftwaffe into battles it could not afford to lose.

The lesson was not that the prewar planners lacked intelligence. It was that a theory that could not be tested in peacetime had been treated as settled, and that the cost of discovering its flaws was paid by aircrews.
questions.explain: If unescorted bombers suffered similar losses on other deep raids, the problem was general to the theory, not peculiar to two missions. Bombing accuracy and factory repairs say nothing about bomber losses. Unusually concentrated German fighters would suggest special circumstances, which weakens the author's view, and losses on escorted raids would cast doubt on escorts as the remedy rather than support the claim.

options: the bombers drew enemy fighters into combat with the escorts
the bombers were sent against targets of little real value
commanders no longer cared whether the bombers hit their targets

the bombers carried fewer guns so that they would look vulnerable

questions.stem: Based on the final paragraph, the author would most likely agree with which statement?
options: An untested doctrine should be treated as provisional, however sound it seems.
Prewar planners erred chiefly by underestimating the skill of German pilots.

Heavy losses are an unavoidable price of testing any new air doctrine.

questions.stem: The author's view that CRM improves safety without weakening command depends on which assumption?
options: Captains given plainly stated concerns will tend to act on them.
Junior officers usually understand fuel better than captains do.
Most accidents begin with a faulty landing gear indication.
Crews should vote on major decisions during an emergency.
Military command structures are identical to airline ones.
questions.passage:
On a December evening in 1978, a DC-8 airliner approaching Portland, Oregon, reported a problem with its landing gear. The indicator lights suggested the gear might not be locked down, and the captain entered a holding pattern to work through the problem and prepare the cabin for a possible emergency landing. For about an hour the crew focused on the gear. During that time the flight engineer and the first officer both mentioned the dwindling fuel, but their remarks were tentative, phrased as observations rather than as warnings, and the captain did not act on them. The aircraft ran out of fuel and crashed several miles short of the runway. Ten people died. The gear, investigators found, had been down and locked.

The accident was not caused by a lack of skill or knowledge. Every member of the crew could have calculated the fuel remaining. What failed was the way information moved among them. The National Transportation Safety Board recommended training that would teach captains to invite input and teach other crew members to state concerns plainly, and in the years that followed, airlines adopted what became known as crew resource management.

CRM is sometimes misunderstood as an attempt to replace command with consensus. It is nothing of the kind. The captain still decides. What changes is the quality of the information on which the decision rests. A first officer who says, "We have fifteen minutes of fuel, and we need to land now," is not usurping authority; that officer is giving the captain what the captain needs to exercise it. The military services, which found the same pattern in their own mishap reports, built similar programs, adapting the language to their own command structures.
questions.explain: CRM, as described, changes only "the quality of the information on which the decision rests," while "The captain still decides." That improves safety only if better information leads captains to better decisions. The passage says every crew member could calculate fuel, so junior officers need not know more. One accident does not show most accidents start with gear problems, voting is the "consensus" model the author rejects, and the military adapted CRM to its own command structures, so they are not identical.

options: were not stated forcefully enough to prompt action

argue that the closure commission holds too much power over defense

questions.passage:
For most of the 1980s, closing an unneeded military base in the United States was nearly impossible. Each installation supported jobs and businesses in a particular congressional district, and the member who represented that district had every reason to block the closure, while colleagues whose districts were unaffected had little reason to resist. Procedural requirements adopted in the 1970s gave opponents further tools for delay. The armed forces were left maintaining facilities they did not need, at a cost that came out of training, maintenance and equipment budgets.

The solution Congress devised was, in effect, a way to bind its own hands. Under the base realignment and closure process, in the form used since 1991, the Department of Defense proposes a list of installations to close or reduce. An independent commission reviews the list, may add or remove bases, and sends its recommendations to the President, who must accept or reject them as a whole. Congress then has a fixed period in which it may disapprove the entire package; it cannot amend the package or remove individual bases. If Congress does nothing, the closures proceed.

The design works by changing the question each legislator must answer. No member votes to close a particular base. Instead, members face a single choice about a nationwide package in which the savings are broad and the losses are scattered, and a member who opposes one closure must reject all the others to stop it. Several rounds since 1988 have closed or reshaped hundreds of installations.

Critics note that the process transfers real power to an unelected commission and that projected savings have sometimes been overstated. Supporters reply that the alternative was never careful case-by-case review, but no closures at all.
questions.explain: The passage describes the political obstacle (each member defends a local base), then explains how the package vote "works by changing the question each legislator must answer." The commission's power and overstated savings appear only as critics' points in the last paragraph. Local economic harm is the reason for the obstacle, not the subject, and the rounds are never compared.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a blunt shape reduces the heat that reaches the vehicle because it
options: holds the shock wave some distance away from the surface
produces less drag than a slender, pointed nose
prevents the air ahead of the vehicle from compressing
keeps the vehicle at high speed lower in the atmosphere
conducts the heat rapidly into the vehicle's structure
questions.passage:
Engineers designing the first ballistic missile warheads in the early 1950s faced a problem that intuition handled badly. A warhead returning from space arrives at several miles per second, and nearly all of its enormous kinetic energy must be shed in the atmosphere, much of it as heat. The obvious design was a slender, pointed body that would slice through the air with little drag, as a bullet does. Calculations showed that such a shape would be destroyed.

The difficulty lay in where the heat went. At these speeds the air ahead of the vehicle is compressed into a shock wave and heated to thousands of degrees. Around a sharp, pointed nose, the shock clings close to the surface, and a large share of the heat passes directly into the vehicle. H. Julian Allen, an aerodynamicist at the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, argued that the solution was to give up the goal of low drag altogether. A broad, blunt face pushes the shock wave forward, so that it stands some distance ahead of the vehicle. Most of the heat is then generated in the air between the shock and the body and is swept away around the sides rather than conducted into the structure. The blunt body also slows down higher, in the thin upper atmosphere, spreading the deceleration over a longer period.

The idea seemed perverse to many at first, but it shaped every crewed capsule from Mercury onward. Combined with ablative shields, which char and erode in a controlled way and carry heat off as they do, the blunt body made returning from orbit survivable. Its lesson for engineers was that a design objective that serves well in one regime can become the source of failure in another.
questions.explain: The passage says a blunt face "pushes the shock wave forward, so that it stands some distance ahead of the vehicle," and the heat is swept away around the sides. Allen's idea was to give up low drag, so the blunt body has more drag, not less. The air is still compressed into a shock wave. The blunt body slows down higher, not lower, and the point is that heat is not conducted into the structure.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Repeated success can lead an organization to accept growing risk without anyone deciding to.
Challenger was lost because managers deliberately ignored engineers' warnings about the O-rings.
Engineers should never clear a vehicle that has shown any damage at all on earlier flights.
Problems with rubber seals caused most of the difficulties of the space shuttle program.
Hospitals and factories face greater risks from deviance than military flying units do.
questions.passage:
Sociologist Diane Vaughan, studying the loss of the space shuttle Challenger in 1986, coined a phrase for a pattern that has since been recognized in hospitals, factories and flying units: the normalization of deviance. The term describes how an organization comes to accept, step by step, conditions that it once would have treated as unacceptable.

The pattern begins with an anomaly. In Challenger's case, engineers found that the rubber O-rings sealing joints in the solid rocket boosters had been partly eroded by hot gas on earlier flights. The design did not allow for any erosion at all. But each time, the shuttle returned safely, and each time, the engineers analyzed the damage, concluded that it stayed within a margin they could justify, and cleared the next flight. The erosion was never ignored; it was studied, explained and documented. That was precisely the problem. Every successful flight became evidence that the erosion was acceptable, and the boundary of what counted as acceptable moved outward without any single decision to move it.

Vaughan's most unsettling conclusion was that no one had to break the rules for this to happen. The managers who approved the final launch were following procedures, not defying them. The danger lay in a gradual shift in the standard against which those procedures measured risk.

For military aviators, the lesson is uncomfortable because it runs against a natural habit of mind. A shortcut that has worked a dozen times feels proven. Vaughan's work suggests the opposite reading: a deviation that has caused no harm so far has not been shown to be safe. It has only been shown not to have failed yet.
questions.explain: The passage defines the normalization of deviance and shows how, with each safe flight, "the boundary of what counted as acceptable moved outward without any single decision to move it." It says the erosion "was never ignored" and that managers were "following procedures," which contradicts the first wrong option. The passage does not set a zero-damage rule, discusses only one seal problem, and does not rank hospitals and factories against flying units.

the engineers spent so long on paperwork that they missed other faults
the documents were kept from the managers who approved the launches

questions.stem: The analysts' test of the "AF" designator could succeed only if which of the following was true?
options: The Japanese would take the water report as genuine and pass it on.
Midway's water distillation plant had actually broken down.
Officers in Washington had already agreed that AF meant Midway.
The Japanese could read the cable messages sent to Midway.
Nimitz had more carriers available than the Japanese expected.
questions.passage:
In May 1942, American naval codebreakers at Pearl Harbor knew that Japan was preparing a major operation in the central Pacific, and they could read enough of the Japanese navy's coded messages to follow its outline. What they could not read with certainty was the target. Intercepted messages referred to it by a two-letter designator, "AF." Commander Joseph Rochefort and his analysts believed AF was Midway, the small atoll at the western end of the Hawaiian chain. Some officers in Washington suspected other targets, including Hawaii itself or the Aleutian Islands.

The disagreement mattered. Admiral Chester Nimitz, commanding the Pacific Fleet, had only three carriers available, and committing them to the wrong place could leave the true target undefended. To settle the question, the analysts devised a test. Midway was instructed, through the secure undersea cable, to send an uncoded radio message reporting that its water distillation plant had broken down. Soon afterward, an intercepted Japanese message reported that AF was short of water.

The result did more than identify a target. It gave Nimitz enough confidence to position his carriers northeast of Midway before the Japanese fleet arrived, where they could strike the enemy carriers by surprise. On June 4, aircraft from those carriers fatally damaged four Japanese fleet carriers, a loss from which the Japanese navy never fully recovered.

Intelligence alone did not win the battle; it was decided by the courage of aircrews and by moments of luck on both sides. But without the codebreakers' work, there would have been no American carriers waiting in that stretch of ocean when the Japanese arrived.
questions.explain: The test worked only if the Japanese believed the false report and relayed it under their own designator. The plant did not need to be broken, since the report was invented. Washington's doubts were what the test was meant to settle. If the Japanese could read the cable, they would have seen the instruction and the ruse would fail, and the number of carriers has nothing to do with the test.

the Japanese were unable to intercept uncoded radio messages

praise the aircrews at the expense of the codebreakers

questions.stem: According to the passage, a contrail that enters air supersaturated with respect to ice
options: grows by taking up water vapor already in the air
evaporates more quickly than it would in dry air
can last only while the aircraft keeps climbing
becomes visible to observers only at night
turns to rain that falls to lower altitudes
questions.passage:
The white trail behind a high-flying jet is a cloud that the aircraft makes. Engine exhaust is hot and contains water vapor from burning fuel. When it mixes with the very cold air at cruising altitude, the vapor condenses on tiny particles and freezes into ice crystals. Whether a contrail forms at all depends mainly on the temperature and humidity of the surrounding air and on the characteristics of the engine.

Whether it lasts is a different question, and it depends almost entirely on the atmosphere. In dry air, the ice crystals turn quickly back into vapor and the trail vanishes within seconds or minutes. But air at these altitudes is sometimes supersaturated with respect to ice: it holds more water vapor than can remain in balance with ice, yet not enough for a cloud to form on its own. A contrail entering such air does not evaporate. Instead its crystals draw in the excess vapor and grow, and the trail can spread over hours into a sheet of cirrus covering thousands of square miles.

These spreading contrails matter because of what they do to the earth's heat balance. By day they reflect some sunlight back to space, which cools, but they also trap heat radiating from the surface, which warms. At night only the warming effect operates. Studies suggest that, taken together, contrail cirrus adds to warming, and some estimates rank its effect alongside that of aviation's carbon dioxide.

Because ice-supersaturated layers are often only a few thousand feet thick, researchers have proposed small changes of altitude to avoid them. The obstacle is forecasting: current weather models predict humidity at cruising altitude poorly, and a diversion that misses the layer burns extra fuel for no benefit.
questions.explain: The passage says such a contrail "does not evaporate. Instead its crystals draw in the excess vapor and grow." It is dry air, not supersaturated air, that makes trails vanish quickly. The aircraft's climb, visibility at night and rain are not mentioned; night appears only in the discussion of warming.

options: One formed at night in ice-supersaturated air

options: preparing forces that combatant commanders would employ

giving the President his principal military advice
approving the joint assignments of their officers
deciding which officers were promoted to general
questions.passage:
By the early 1980s, critics inside and outside the Pentagon argued that the American armed forces were organized to compete with one another more than to fight together. The failed attempt to rescue the hostages in Iran in 1980, which combined aircraft and personnel from several services that had rarely trained together, and the coordination problems of the 1983 invasion of Grenada seemed to confirm the charge. The Joint Chiefs of Staff, who were expected to give unified military advice, usually produced compromises that each service could accept rather than the best advice available.

The Goldwater-Nichols Act of 1986 attacked the problem through structure rather than exhortation. It made the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, rather than the chiefs as a body, the principal military adviser to the President and the Secretary of Defense. It ran the operational chain of command from the President through the Secretary directly to the commanders of the unified combatant commands, leaving the service chiefs responsible for organizing, training and equipping forces rather than directing them in combat. And it required officers to serve in joint assignments before they could be promoted to general or admiral.

The last provision was perhaps the most consequential, because it worked on incentives. An ambitious officer could no longer reach the top while spending an entire career inside a single service. Joint staff work, once regarded as a detour, became a necessary step.

The services resisted the law strongly. Yet within five years, the unified command arrangements under which the 1991 Gulf War was fought were widely held up as evidence that it had worked.
questions.explain: The Act left "the service chiefs responsible for organizing, training and equipping forces rather than directing them in combat," while the chain of command ran to the combatant commanders. Directing forces in combat is exactly what they lost. The Chairman, not the chiefs, became the principal military adviser, and the passage does not give the chiefs control over joint assignments or promotions.

joint staff work is more demanding than work within a single service
the Chairman's new advisory role had little effect on military advice
the services would eventually stop resisting the new law entirely

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Stalls depend on angle of attack, so airspeed is only an indirect guide to them.
Student pilots should practice stalls in steep turns rather than in level flight.
The stall speeds printed in flight manuals are usually calculated incorrectly.
Lowering the nose near the ground is more dangerous than allowing a stall.
Modern military aircraft no longer need to display airspeed to their pilots.
questions.passage:
Ask a student pilot what causes a stall, and the answer is often "flying too slowly." It is an understandable belief, because in the most common training exercise the aircraft is slowed in level flight until the wing quits. But the belief is wrong in a way that has killed experienced pilots.

A wing stalls when its angle of attack, the angle between the wing and the oncoming air, exceeds a critical value, roughly 15 to 18 degrees for many light-aircraft wings. Beyond that angle the airflow can no longer follow the curved upper surface; it separates, and lift drops sharply. Speed enters the story only indirectly. To support the aircraft's weight at low speed, the wing must meet the air at a high angle, so slow flight and stalls tend to go together. They need not. In a steep turn or an abrupt pull-up, the wing must produce much more lift than the aircraft weighs, and it can reach the critical angle at a speed well above the published stall speed. Conversely, an aircraft pointed steeply down at low speed may be far from stalling if the wing is meeting the air at a small angle.

For this reason, the stall speeds printed in a flight manual are conditional statements, valid only for a particular weight and for level, unaccelerated flight. The only reliable cure for a stall is to reduce the angle of attack, usually by lowering the nose, even when the ground is close and every instinct urges the pilot to pull back. Many military aircraft display angle of attack directly, precisely because airspeed alone can mislead.
questions.explain: The passage argues that a wing stalls when it "exceeds a critical value" of angle of attack and that "Speed enters the story only indirectly." It never prescribes how stalls should be trained. It calls manual stall speeds "conditional statements," not wrong ones. It says to lower the nose even near the ground, the opposite of the third wrong option, and it says airspeed alone can mislead, not that it is unnecessary.

will stall only if the aircraft is heavier than normal
is protected from a stall because it began in a dive
will stall only after airspeed falls to the stall speed

become less accurate as the aircraft climbs to high altitude
are minimums to which pilots should add a safety margin
apply only to the light aircraft used in pilot training
