questions.explain: Pascal's principle says the pressure is transmitted equally: 20 lb / 2 in² = 10 psi, and 10 psi x 50 in² = 500 lb. 20 lb assumes force rather than pressure is passed along, 40 lb multiplies by the small area, 0.8 lb inverts the area ratio, and 1,000 lb multiplies the force by the large area without first finding the pressure.

questions.stem: Air flows steadily through a horizontal tube that narrows from a cross-sectional area of 6 cm² to 2 cm². Treating the air as incompressible, compared with the wide section the air in the narrow section moves
options: three times as fast, at lower pressure
three times as fast, at higher pressure
one-third as fast, at higher pressure
nine times as fast, at lower pressure
at the same speed, at lower pressure
questions.explain: For steady flow the same volume of air must pass every section each second (continuity), so speed times area stays constant: the area falls to one-third, so the speed triples. By Bernoulli's principle, where a fluid moves faster its pressure is lower, which is how a venturi works. Higher pressure reverses Bernoulli's principle, one-third as fast inverts the area ratio, nine times squares the area ratio, and the same speed ignores continuity.

questions.stem: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 200 g of water from 20°C to 35°C? (Specific heat of water = 1 cal/g·°C)
questions.explain: Use Q = mcΔT with the temperature change, not a temperature reading: ΔT = 35 − 20 = 15°C, so Q = 200 x 1 x 15 = 3,000 cal. 7,000 cal uses the final temperature, 4,000 cal uses the starting temperature, 13.3 cal divides mass by the temperature change, and 12,600 is the answer converted to joules but still labeled calories.

questions.stem: A pan of crushed ice at 0°C is heated steadily. While the ice is melting, the thermometer stays at 0°C. Where is the added energy going?
options: Into breaking the bonds that hold the solid together
Into raising the average kinetic energy of the molecules
Nowhere; it is lost because the temperature is unchanged
Into lowering the specific heat of the melting water
Into the thermometer and the pan rather than the ice
questions.explain: During a phase change the added heat (the latent heat of fusion) goes into potential energy, pulling molecules out of the rigid crystal, so the temperature stays put until all the ice has melted. Raising average kinetic energy would raise the temperature, energy is conserved rather than lost, the heat does not change specific heat, and the ice really is absorbing the energy, which is why it melts.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 6 L at a pressure of 2 atm. At constant temperature, it is compressed to 3 L. What is its new pressure?
questions.explain: Boyle's law: at constant temperature P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so 2 x 6 = P₂ x 3 and P₂ = 4 atm. Halving the volume doubles the pressure. 1 atm treats pressure as directly proportional to volume, 3 atm divides 6 by 2, 9 atm adds the two volumes, and 12 atm is the P x V product itself.

questions.stem: A balloon holds 4.0 L of gas at 27°C. At constant pressure, the gas is heated to 327°C. What is the new volume?
questions.explain: Charles's law needs absolute temperatures: 27°C = 300 K and 327°C = 600 K, so the Kelvin temperature doubles and the volume doubles from 4.0 L to 8.0 L. 48 L uses the Celsius ratio (about 12 times), 2.0 L inverts the relationship, 4.0 L assumes volume does not change with temperature, and 16 L squares the factor.

questions.stem: Sweat evaporating from the skin cools the body because
options: the fastest molecules escape, so the water left behind cools
evaporation gives off heat, which the skin then loses to the air
water drops below 0°C at the moment it turns to vapor
the vapor forms a layer that reflects body heat away
liquid water has a lower specific heat than skin
questions.explain: Temperature reflects the average kinetic energy of molecules. The molecules that escape as vapor are the most energetic ones, and they carry away latent heat, so the remaining liquid and the skin it touches cool down. Evaporation absorbs heat rather than giving it off, water does not freeze as it evaporates, vapor does not reflect heat, and water actually has a high specific heat.

questions.stem: Sound travels at 340 m/s in air. What is the wavelength of a 680 Hz tone?
questions.explain: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength (v = fλ), so λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.5 m. 2 m divides frequency by speed, 231,200 m multiplies speed and frequency, 1,020 m adds them, and 0.25 m halves the correct answer, as if it were a round trip.

questions.stem: A sound wave passes from air into water, where sound travels about four times faster. What happens to the wave's frequency and wavelength?
options: Frequency stays the same; wavelength increases
Frequency increases; wavelength stays the same
Frequency stays the same; wavelength decreases
questions.explain: Frequency is set by the source, so it does not change when a wave enters a new medium. Since v = fλ and the speed rises while f stays fixed, the wavelength must rise by the same factor (about 4 times). Any option that changes the frequency is wrong, and a shorter wavelength would mean the wave had slowed down.

questions.stem: An ambulance siren emits a steady 700 Hz tone. The ambulance drives at constant speed toward a stationary listener, passes, and drives away. The listener hears
options: a constant pitch above 700 Hz, then a constant pitch below it
a constant pitch below 700 Hz, then a constant pitch above it
a steady 700 Hz tone that grows louder, then quieter
a pitch that rises steadily as it nears, peaking as it passes
a pitch above 700 Hz both as it nears and as it drives away
questions.explain: In the Doppler effect an approaching source squeezes the waves together, giving a higher frequency, and a receding source stretches them out, giving a lower one; at constant speed each shifted pitch stays constant, with the drop at the moment it passes. The reversed order is backward, the pitch does change (not just loudness), a steadily rising pitch confuses pitch with loudness, and a receding source always sounds lower.

questions.stem: A ray of light passes at an angle from air into a block of glass. Compared with the ray in air, the ray in the glass
options: slows down and bends toward the normal
slows down and bends away from the normal
speeds up and bends toward the normal
speeds up and bends away from the normal
keeps the same speed but changes frequency
questions.explain: Glass has a higher index of refraction than air, so light travels more slowly in it, and a ray entering a slower medium bends toward the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface). Bending away happens when light enters a faster medium such as glass to air, light does not speed up in glass, and frequency never changes on crossing a boundary; the speed and wavelength do.

questions.stem: What is the shortest flat wall mirror in which a 6 ft tall person can see their entire body, head to toe?
options: 3 ft, at any distance from the mirror
6 ft, at any distance from the mirror
3 ft, but only when standing close to it
2 ft, if the person stands far enough back
questions.explain: By the law of reflection, light from your feet reaches your eyes by hitting the mirror halfway between them, and the same is true for the top of your head, so the mirror needs only half your height: 3 ft. Moving back makes your image farther away as well, so the required size does not change with distance. 6 ft assumes the mirror must match your height, the distance conditions are wrong because distance cancels, and 12 ft doubles instead of halving.

questions.stem: A shirt looks red in white light. In a dark room lit only by pure blue light, the shirt appears
questions.explain: An object's color is the light it reflects: red dye reflects red and absorbs the other colors. Under pure blue light there is no red to reflect, and the blue is absorbed, so almost no light comes off the shirt and it looks black. Purple assumes the colors mix like paint, red assumes the color belongs to the shirt regardless of the light, blue assumes it reflects whatever falls on it, and white would require reflecting all colors.

questions.stem: Which of the following has the highest frequency, and therefore the most energy per photon?
questions.explain: In order of increasing frequency the spectrum runs radio, microwave, infrared, visible (red to violet), ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. Ultraviolet lies just beyond violet, so it has a higher frequency and photon energy (E = hf) than violet light. Violet is the highest-frequency visible color but still below UV, and infrared, microwaves and radio are all lower frequencies with longer wavelengths.

questions.stem: A 12 V battery is connected across a 4 Ω resistor. How much power does the resistor dissipate?
questions.explain: Ohm's law gives I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A, and power is P = VI = 12 x 3 = 36 W (the same as V²/R = 144/4). 3 W is the current, not the power; 48 W multiplies voltage by resistance; 9 W squares the current but forgets to multiply by R; and 144 W is V² without dividing by R.

questions.stem: A 6 Ω resistor and a 3 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across an 18 V source. What total current does the source supply?
questions.explain: In parallel each resistor gets the full 18 V: the 6 Ω branch draws 3 A and the 3 Ω branch draws 6 A, so the total is 9 A (equivalently, the combined resistance is 6 x 3 / (6 + 3) = 2 Ω and 18/2 = 9 A). 2 A treats the resistors as in series (9 Ω), 3 A and 6 A are single branches only, and 4 A uses the average resistance of 4.5 Ω.

questions.stem: Two identical bulbs are wired in parallel to a battery with negligible internal resistance. A third identical bulb is then added in parallel. What happens?
options: Battery current increases; the original bulbs stay equally bright
Battery current increases; the original bulbs get dimmer
Battery current stays the same; all three bulbs get dimmer
Battery current decreases; the original bulbs get brighter
Battery current decreases; the original bulbs stay equally bright
questions.explain: Each parallel branch has the full battery voltage across it, so each original bulb carries the same current as before and keeps its brightness. Adding a branch lowers the total resistance, so the battery supplies more total current (now three bulbs' worth). Dimming is what happens when bulbs are added in series, the battery current cannot stay fixed while a new branch draws current, and adding a parallel path never lowers the total current.

questions.stem: A 1,500 W space heater runs for 4 hours. If electricity costs 15 cents per kilowatt-hour, how much does this cost?
questions.explain: Energy = power x time = 1.5 kW x 4 h = 6 kWh, and 6 kWh x $0.15 = $0.90. $9.00 and $0.09 are decimal slips, $900 uses watts instead of kilowatts (6,000 Wh), and $0.60 multiplies the hours by the price and leaves out the heater's power.

questions.stem: One ampere is equivalent to one
questions.explain: Current is the rate at which charge flows, so 1 ampere = 1 coulomb of charge passing a point each second. A joule per second is a watt (power), a joule per coulomb is a volt (potential difference), a coulomb per volt is a farad (capacitance), and a newton per coulomb is a unit of electric field strength.

questions.stem: A bar magnet is cut in half across its middle, between its north and south poles. What results?
options: Two smaller magnets, each with its own north and south pole
One isolated north pole and one isolated south pole
Two nonmagnetic pieces, since the poles have been separated
One magnet and one piece of plain, nonmagnetic metal
Two pieces that each have a single, weaker pole
questions.explain: Magnetism comes from the alignment of countless tiny atomic magnets throughout the bar, each with its own north and south, so every piece is a complete magnet and new poles appear at the cut. Isolated single poles (monopoles) have never been observed, the alignment is not destroyed by cutting, and both halves keep the same arrangement, so neither becomes nonmagnetic.

questions.stem: A bar magnet is held motionless inside a coil of wire connected to a sensitive ammeter. What does the ammeter show?
options: No current, because the magnetic flux through the coil is not changing
A steady current, because the coil sits in a strong magnetic field
A current that keeps growing the longer the magnet stays inside
An alternating current at the magnet's natural frequency
A current, but only if the coil is wound around an iron core
questions.explain: Faraday's law of induction says a current is induced only when the magnetic flux through the coil changes, for example while the magnet is moving in or out. A motionless magnet gives a constant flux, so the current is zero. A strong but steady field induces nothing, the current does not build up over time, a still magnet has no oscillation to drive an alternating current, and an iron core would only strengthen a changing flux.

questions.stem: 0.045 kilograms is equal to how many milligrams?
questions.explain: 1 kg = 1,000 g and 1 g = 1,000 mg, so 1 kg = 1,000,000 mg, and 0.045 x 1,000,000 = 45,000 mg. 45 mg converts kilograms to grams but stops there, 450 mg and 4,500 mg misplace the decimal, and 450,000 mg shifts one place too far.

questions.stem: Which combination of SI base units is equivalent to a watt?
questions.explain: A newton is kg·m/s², a joule is a newton times a meter (kg·m²/s²), and a watt is a joule per second, which gives kg·m²/s³. kg·m²/s² is the joule (energy, not power), kg·m/s² is the newton (force), kg·m/s is the unit of momentum, and kg/(m·s²) is the pascal (pressure).

questions.stem: Chlorine has atomic number 17. A chloride ion with mass number 37 (³⁷Cl⁻) contains
questions.explain: The atomic number fixes the protons at 17; neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 37 − 17 = 20; and the 1− charge means one electron more than the protons, so 18 electrons. 16 electrons treats the minus sign as a lost electron, 18 protons would make it argon, 37 neutrons uses the mass number as the neutron count, and 17 electrons describes the neutral atom.

questions.stem: Moving from left to right across a period of the periodic table, atomic radius generally
options: decreases, as rising nuclear charge pulls the same shell inward
increases, because each element has more electrons
increases, because each element adds a new electron shell
decreases, because each element has fewer neutrons
stays the same, because the shell number is constant
questions.explain: Across a period, each element adds a proton to the nucleus while its new electron goes into the same outer shell, so the stronger nuclear charge pulls that shell closer and the atom shrinks. More electrons in the same shell does not make the atom larger, new shells are added going down a group rather than across a period, neutron number does not set atomic size (and generally rises), and the radius does change.

questions.stem: Which element most strongly attracts the shared electrons in a chemical bond (has the highest electronegativity)?
questions.explain: Electronegativity increases toward the upper right of the periodic table (excluding the noble gases), and fluorine, a small atom with a high nuclear charge pulling on its outer shell, is the most electronegative element. Oxygen is second and nitrogen is lower, both being to the left of fluorine; chlorine is below fluorine in the same group, so it is larger; and cesium, at the lower left, is among the least electronegative.

questions.stem: Which molecule is nonpolar overall even though its individual bonds are polar?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide is linear (O=C=O), so its two polar C=O bonds point in exactly opposite directions and cancel, leaving no net dipole. Water is bent and ammonia is pyramidal, so their bond dipoles do not cancel; HCl has a single polar bond; and in CH₃Cl the one C–Cl bond is not balanced by the C–H bonds, so all four are polar molecules.

questions.stem: When the equation __C₃H₈ + __O₂ → __CO₂ + __H₂O is balanced with the smallest whole numbers, the coefficient of O₂ is
questions.explain: Balance carbon first (3 CO₂), then hydrogen (8 H gives 4 H₂O). The products now hold 3 x 2 + 4 x 1 = 10 oxygen atoms, which takes 5 O₂ molecules: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. 3 and 4 are the coefficients of CO₂ and H₂O, 7 adds those two together, and 10 counts oxygen atoms rather than O₂ molecules.

questions.stem: How many moles of oxygen gas (O₂) are in 64 g of O₂? (Atomic mass of O = 16)
questions.explain: Oxygen gas is diatomic, so its molar mass is 2 x 16 = 32 g/mol, and 64 g / 32 g/mol = 2 mol. 4 mol uses the atomic mass of 16 as if the gas were single O atoms, 1 mol assumes 64 g is one mole, 0.5 mol divides the molar mass by the sample mass, and 32 is the molar mass in g/mol rather than a number of moles.

questions.stem: Solution A has a pH of 3 and solution B has a pH of 5. Compared with solution B, solution A has
questions.explain: pH is a base-10 logarithmic scale: each unit lower means 10 times more hydrogen ions, so 2 units lower is 10 x 10 = 100 times more. 2 times treats the scale as linear, 1/100 reverses the direction (lower pH is more acidic), 20 times multiplies instead of using powers of 10, and the hydroxide concentration actually drops to 1/100 in the more acidic solution.

questions.stem: How many milliliters of 0.25 M NaOH are needed to exactly neutralize 20 mL of 0.50 M HCl?
questions.explain: HCl and NaOH react 1:1. Moles of HCl = 0.50 mol/L x 0.020 L = 0.010 mol, so 0.010 mol of NaOH is needed, and at 0.25 M that is 0.010 / 0.25 = 0.040 L = 40 mL. Because the base is half as concentrated, it takes twice the volume. 10 mL inverts the concentration ratio, 20 mL assumes equal volumes always neutralize, 80 mL doubles twice, and 5 mL multiplies the volume by the base's molarity.

questions.stem: A sample contains 80 g of a radioactive isotope with a half-life of 5 days. How much of the isotope remains after 20 days?
questions.explain: 20 days is 20/5 = 4 half-lives, and each one halves the amount: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5 g. 20 g divides by the number of half-lives instead of halving each time, 10 g stops after three half-lives, 0 g treats decay as linear (losing 40 g per half-life), and 40 g counts only one half-life.

questions.stem: Carbon-14 (atomic number 6) undergoes beta-minus decay. What nucleus is produced?
questions.explain: In beta-minus decay a neutron changes into a proton and emits an electron, so the atomic number rises by 1 (6 to 7, nitrogen) while the mass number stays at 14. Boron-14 lowers the atomic number, as in positron emission; carbon-13 assumes a neutron is simply lost; nitrogen-15 wrongly raises the mass number; and beryllium-10 is what alpha decay (losing 2 protons and 2 neutrons) would give.

questions.stem: A 200 g stone is lowered into a graduated cylinder, and the water level rises from 50 mL to 130 mL. What is the stone's density?
questions.explain: The stone's volume is the water it displaces: 130 − 50 = 80 mL = 80 cm³, and density = mass/volume = 200/80 = 2.5 g/cm³. 0.4 divides volume by mass, 1.54 uses the final reading of 130 mL as the volume, 4.0 uses the starting reading of 50 mL, and 120 subtracts the volume from the mass instead of dividing.

questions.stem: Why is it summer in the Northern Hemisphere in July?
options: The Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun
Earth is at its closest point to the Sun in July
Earth moves fastest in its orbit during July
The Sun gives off more energy each July
The Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun
questions.explain: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, and in July the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, so sunlight strikes it more directly and days are longer, delivering more energy per square meter. Earth is actually farthest from the Sun in early July and so moves slowest then, the Sun's output does not follow a yearly cycle, and tilting away is what causes the northern winter.

questions.stem: Most coastlines get two high tides a little more than every 24 hours. The main reason is that
options: the Moon's gravity raises bulges on Earth's near and far sides
the Moon and the Sun each raise one bulge, on opposite sides of Earth
the Moon orbits Earth twice during each day
Earth's spin sloshes the oceans back and forth twice a day
the Sun's heat swells the oceans each morning and evening
questions.explain: The Moon pulls the near side of Earth more strongly than its center, and its center more strongly than the far side, so the oceans are stretched into two bulges, one facing the Moon and one opposite. Earth rotates through both bulges each day, and because the Moon moves along its orbit the cycle takes about 24 hours 50 minutes. The Sun's effect only strengthens or weakens these tides (spring and neap), the Moon takes about a month to orbit once, and neither sloshing nor heating causes tides.

questions.stem: The pulley system shown is 80% efficient. What effort F is needed to lift the 600 N load at a steady speed?
questions.explain: Four rope segments support the load, so the ideal mechanical advantage is 4 and an ideal effort would be 600 ÷ 4 = 150 N. At 80% efficiency you need more: 150 ÷ 0.8 = 187.5 N. 150 N ignores friction, 120 N multiplies by 0.8 instead of dividing, 240 N counts only 2.5 ropes' worth, and 480 N is 80% of the load.

questions.stem: Gear A turns clockwise at 300 rpm. What are the speed and direction of gear C?
questions.explain: In a simple train the middle (idler) gear B doesn't change the overall ratio: C's speed = 300 × 12 ÷ 24 = 150 rpm. Each mesh reverses direction, so A clockwise → B counterclockwise → C clockwise. 100 rpm is B's speed (300 × 12 ÷ 36), and 600 rpm inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: What class of lever is shown, and what is true of its mechanical advantage?
options: Third class; mechanical advantage less than 1
Second class; mechanical advantage greater than 1
First class; mechanical advantage less than 1
Third class; mechanical advantage greater than 1
Second class; mechanical advantage less than 1
questions.explain: The effort sits between the fulcrum (at the end) and the load, which makes it a third-class lever, like a forearm or tweezers. The effort arm is shorter than the load arm, so the effort must exceed the load: mechanical advantage is less than 1, traded for more speed and distance at the load. A second-class lever would have the load in the middle.

questions.stem: The bar shown is hinged at the left end. What upward force F at the right end holds the 400 N load level? (Ignore the bar's weight.)
questions.explain: Take moments about the hinge: 400 N × 0.5 m = F × 2.0 m, so F = 200 ÷ 2 = 100 N. 80 N adds the two distances (2.5 m) as the effort arm, 133 N measures the effort arm from the load (1.5 m), 200 N is the moment's value read as a force, and 1,600 N inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: The cam shown turns clockwise. After it completes a quarter turn (90°), the follower will be
options: at the same height as now
falling after passing its highest point
questions.explain: The lobe now points left, so the follower rests on the low base circle. Turning clockwise, the lobe swings from left to straight up in a quarter turn, which pushes the follower to its highest point. Another quarter turn would carry the lobe to the right and the follower back down.

questions.stem: In the circuit shown, what current flows through R1?
questions.explain: R2 and R3 are in parallel: (6 × 12) ÷ (6 + 12) = 4 Ω. That 4 Ω is in series with R1's 4 Ω, giving 8 Ω, so the total current, which all passes through R1, is 24 ÷ 8 = 3 A. 1.1 A wrongly adds all three resistors (22 Ω), 6 A uses R1 alone, 2 A is the current through R2, and 1 A is the current through R3.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off the edge of a table 20 m high at 5 m/s horizontally. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², how far from the base of the table does it land?
questions.explain: The horizontal and vertical motions are independent. The fall time comes from 20 = ½(10)t², so t² = 4 and t = 2 s. In 2 s at a constant 5 m/s horizontally, the ball travels 10 m. 20 m is the height, 5 m uses 1 s, 4 m divides the height by the speed, and 100 m multiplies them.

questions.stem: A car speeds up uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 4 s. How far does it travel during those 4 s?
questions.explain: With uniform acceleration the average velocity is (10 + 30) ÷ 2 = 20 m/s, so the distance is 20 × 4 = 80 m. Check: a = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 m/s², and 10(4) + ½(5)(16) = 40 + 40 = 80 m. 120 m uses the final speed throughout, 40 m uses the starting speed, 60 m adds the 20 m/s change to 40 m, and 160 m doubles the correct answer.

questions.stem: A 50 kg crate slides across a level floor at constant speed. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.3. Using g = 10 m/s², what horizontal pushing force is being applied?
questions.explain: At constant speed the net force is zero, so the push equals friction. Friction = μ × normal force = 0.3 × (50 × 10) = 0.3 × 500 = 150 N. 500 N is the crate's weight, 15 N uses the mass instead of the weight, 350 N subtracts friction from the weight, and 650 N adds them.

questions.stem: A block slides down a frictionless ramp inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Using g = 10 m/s², what is its acceleration along the ramp?
questions.explain: Only the component of gravity along the ramp accelerates the block: a = g sin θ = 10 × sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m/s². 10 m/s² is free fall, 8.7 m/s² uses cos 30°, which is the component pressing into the ramp, 0 m/s² assumes the normal force cancels gravity completely, and 20 m/s² divides by sin 30°.

questions.stem: A car rounds a curve of fixed radius. If its speed doubles, the centripetal force needed to keep it on the curve
questions.explain: Centripetal force F = mv²/r, so force depends on the square of speed: doubling v multiplies F by 2² = 4. This is why taking a curve twice as fast needs four times the grip. Doubling treats F as proportional to v, staying the same ignores speed, halving inverts the relationship, and eight times cubes the speed.

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg ball traveling at 20 m/s hits a wall head-on and bounces straight back at 20 m/s. The ball is in contact with the wall for 0.05 s. What is the average force on the ball?
questions.explain: The change in momentum is from +10 kg·m/s to −10 kg·m/s, a change of 20 kg·m/s, because the direction reverses. Force = change in momentum ÷ time = 20 ÷ 0.05 = 400 N. 200 N counts only the stop and not the rebound, 0 N compares speeds rather than velocities, 1 N multiplies by the time instead of dividing, and 800 N doubles the momentum change again.

questions.stem: A 1,200 kg car traveling at 20 m/s brakes to a stop on a level road. The average braking force is 6,000 N. How far does the car travel while braking?
questions.explain: The brakes must remove all the kinetic energy: KE = ½mv² = ½(1,200)(20²) = 240,000 J. Work = force × distance, so d = 240,000 ÷ 6,000 = 40 m. 80 m forgets the ½, 4 m uses 1,200 × 20 for the energy, 20 m halves again, and 400 m drops a factor of 10 in the force.

questions.stem: An electric winch motor takes in 2,000 W and is 75 percent efficient. It lifts a 300 N load straight up at constant speed. How fast does the load rise?
questions.explain: Useful output power = 0.75 × 2,000 = 1,500 W. For lifting at constant speed, power = force × velocity, so v = 1,500 ÷ 300 = 5 m/s. 6.7 m/s ignores the efficiency (2,000 ÷ 300), 3.75 m/s applies the efficiency twice, 0.2 m/s divides the load by the power, and 1.5 m/s divides the output power by 1,000 instead of by the load.

questions.stem: A spring with a spring constant of 400 N/m is compressed 0.2 m. How much energy is stored in it?
questions.explain: Elastic potential energy = ½kx² = ½ × 400 × 0.2² = ½ × 400 × 0.04 = 8 J. 80 J is the force (kx) in newtons, 16 J forgets the ½, 40 J halves kx instead of squaring x, and 4 J halves the answer again.

questions.stem: A simple pendulum's length is made four times as long. Its period of swing
questions.explain: The period of a simple pendulum is T = 2π√(L/g), so it depends on the square root of the length. Four times the length gives √4 = 2 times the period. Four times treats T as proportional to L, staying the same confuses length with mass or amplitude (which don't matter), halving inverts the relationship, and sixteen times squares the factor instead of taking its root.

questions.stem: A 1,200 N crate rests on a face that measures 0.4 m by 0.5 m. What pressure does it exert on the floor?
questions.explain: Pressure = force ÷ area. The area is 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 m², so pressure = 1,200 ÷ 0.2 = 6,000 Pa (N/m²). 600 Pa multiplies the force by 0.5, 2,400 Pa divides by 0.5 only, 3,000 Pa divides by 0.4 only, and 480 Pa multiplies by 0.4.

questions.stem: A metal part weighs 30 N in air and 20 N when fully submerged in water (density 1.0 g/cm³). What is the density of the metal?
questions.explain: The apparent loss of weight, 30 − 20 = 10 N, is the buoyant force, which equals the weight of water displaced. The part therefore weighs 30 ÷ 10 = 3 times as much as an equal volume of water, so its density is 3.0 g/cm³. 1.5 divides 30 by 20, 0.67 inverts that, 2.0 divides 20 by 10, and 10 gives the buoyant force in newtons.

questions.stem: On a sunny afternoon at the coast, a breeze blows from the sea toward the land. The main reason is that
options: the land heats faster, so air rises over it and cooler sea air flows in
the sea heats faster, so its warm air spreads out over the cooler land
Earth's rotation pushes coastal air toward the land each afternoon
high pressure forms over the land as it warms, pushing air inland
evaporation from the sea creates a current of moist air toward land
questions.explain: Land has a much lower specific heat than water, so it warms quickly in sunshine. Air over the land warms, expands and rises, lowering the surface pressure there, and cooler, denser air over the sea flows in to replace it. At night the pattern reverses into a land breeze. Water heats more slowly than land, not faster, the Coriolis effect doesn't produce a daily onshore wind, warming land creates low pressure rather than high, and evaporation doesn't drive the breeze.

questions.stem: 100 g of water at 80°C is mixed with 300 g of water at 20°C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?
questions.explain: Heat lost by the hot water equals heat gained by the cold water: 100(80 − T) = 300(T − 20), so 8,000 − 100T = 300T − 6,000, 14,000 = 400T and T = 35°C. Check: the hot water drops 45°C and the cold water, three times the mass, rises 15°C. 50°C averages the temperatures without weighting by mass, 65°C weights them the wrong way round, 15°C is the cold water's temperature rise, and 45°C is the hot water's temperature drop.

questions.stem: How much heat is needed to melt 50 g of ice at 0°C and then warm the water to 20°C? (Latent heat of fusion of ice = 80 cal/g; specific heat of water = 1 cal/g·°C.)
questions.explain: Melting: 50 × 80 = 4,000 cal, with no temperature change. Warming: 50 × 1 × 20 = 1,000 cal. Total = 5,000 cal. 1,000 cal forgets the melting, 4,000 cal forgets the warming, 3,000 cal subtracts 20 from 80 before multiplying by 50, and 6,000 cal uses 100 cal/g, the boiling-point temperature, as the latent heat.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 6.0 L at 2.0 atm and 300 K. It is heated to 450 K and its pressure is raised to 3.0 atm. What is its new volume?
questions.explain: Use P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂: V₂ = 6.0 × (2.0/3.0) × (450/300) = 6.0 × (2/3) × (3/2) = 6.0 L. The pressure increase and the temperature increase cancel exactly. 9.0 L applies only the temperature change, 4.0 L applies only the pressure change, 13.5 L multiplies by both ratios upside down for pressure, and 2.7 L inverts the temperature ratio.

questions.stem: Waves on a lake have crests 3 m apart. A swimmer counts 12 crests passing a buoy in 4 s. What is the wave speed?
questions.explain: Frequency = 12 crests ÷ 4 s = 3 Hz. Wave speed = frequency × wavelength = 3 × 3 = 9 m/s. 36 m/s multiplies the crest count by the wavelength, 12 m/s uses the count as the speed, 4 m/s divides the count by the wavelength, and 1 m/s divides the frequency by the wavelength.

questions.stem: A hiker shouts toward a cliff and hears the echo 1.5 s later. If sound travels at 340 m/s, how far away is the cliff?
questions.explain: The sound travels to the cliff and back, a total of 340 × 1.5 = 510 m, so the cliff is half that, 255 m away. 510 m forgets the round trip, 127.5 m halves twice, 227 m divides 340 by 1.5, and 340 m uses one second.

questions.stem: Light travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. What is its speed in glass with an index of refraction of 1.5?
questions.explain: The index of refraction is n = c/v, so v = c/n = 3.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 1.5 = 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Light is slower in denser optical media, which is what causes refraction. 4.5 × 10⁸ multiplies by the index and would exceed the speed of light, 3.0 × 10⁸ assumes the speed never changes, 1.5 × 10⁸ subtracts 1.5 from 3.0, and 1.0 × 10⁸ divides by 3.

questions.stem: An object stands 30 cm in front of a converging lens with a focal length of 10 cm. Where does the image form?
options: 15 cm in front of the lens
questions.explain: Use the thin-lens equation 1/f = 1/dₒ + 1/dᵢ: 1/dᵢ = 1/10 − 1/30 = 3/30 − 1/30 = 2/30, so dᵢ = 15 cm. It is positive, so the image is real and forms behind the lens (inverted and smaller). 20 cm subtracts the distances (30 − 10), 7.5 cm adds the reciprocals, 30 cm assumes the image mirrors the object distance, which only happens at 2f = 20 cm, and 15 cm in front treats a real image as virtual.

questions.stem: Resistors of 2 Ω, 4 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in series across a 24 V battery. What is the voltage across the 4 Ω resistor?
questions.explain: Series resistances add: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 Ω. The current is 24 ÷ 12 = 2 A, the same through every resistor, so the voltage across the 4 Ω resistor is 2 × 4 = 8 V. Check: 4 + 8 + 12 = 24 V. 24 V assumes each resistor gets the full voltage, as in parallel, 6 V divides 24 by 4, 12 V is the voltage across the 6 Ω resistor, and 2 V is the current.

questions.stem: A 120 V household circuit is protected by a 15 A breaker. What is the greatest number of 500 W heaters that can run on it at once without tripping the breaker?
questions.explain: The circuit can deliver P = VI = 120 × 15 = 1,800 W. Each heater draws 500 W, and 1,800 ÷ 500 = 3.6, so only 3 can run; a fourth would need 2,000 W (16.7 A). 4 rounds 3.6 up, 30 divides 15 A by 0.5 kW, 8 divides the voltage by the current (120 ÷ 15), and 3.6 forgets that only whole heaters can run.

questions.stem: A copper wire is replaced by one of the same metal that is twice as long and has half the cross-sectional area. Its resistance is
questions.explain: Resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area (R = ρL/A). Doubling the length doubles R, and halving the area doubles it again: 2 × 2 = 4. The same assumes the two changes cancel, twice as large counts only one change, one-fourth inverts both, and eight times treats the area as a diameter that is squared.

questions.stem: Two small charged spheres repel each other with force F. If both charges are doubled and the distance between them is tripled, the new force is
questions.explain: Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂/r². Doubling both charges multiplies the force by 2 × 2 = 4, and tripling the distance divides it by 3² = 9, so the new force is 4F/9. 4F/3 forgets to square the distance, 2F/3 doubles only one charge and doesn't square, 4F ignores the distance, and F/9 ignores the charges.

questions.stem: A transformer's primary coil has 200 turns and its secondary coil has 1,000 turns. With 120 V AC on the primary, what are the secondary voltage and the secondary current compared with the primary current (ignoring losses)?
options: 600 V; the secondary current is smaller
600 V; the secondary current is larger
24 V; the secondary current is larger
24 V; the secondary current is smaller
600 V; the two currents are equal
questions.explain: Voltage scales with the turns ratio: 120 × (1,000/200) = 600 V. Power in equals power out (VI is the same on both sides), so stepping the voltage up by 5 steps the current down by 5. 600 V with a larger current would create energy from nothing, 24 V inverts the turns ratio, and equal currents ignore the conservation of power.

questions.stem: How many moles are in 49 g of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄? (Atomic masses: H = 1, S = 32, O = 16.)
questions.explain: The molar mass of H₂SO₄ is 2(1) + 32 + 4(16) = 98 g/mol, so 49 g ÷ 98 g/mol = 0.5 mol. 2 mol divides the molar mass by the sample mass, 1 mol uses a molar mass of 49 (one O instead of four, with H counted once), 0.25 mol halves again, and 0.75 mol uses 65 g/mol (only one H and two O).

questions.stem: Hydrogen burns by the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. How many grams of water form when 8 g of H₂ reacts with excess oxygen? (H = 1, O = 16.)
questions.explain: 8 g of H₂ (molar mass 2 g/mol) is 4 mol. The equation gives 2 mol H₂O for every 2 mol H₂, so 4 mol of water forms: 4 × 18 = 72 g. 36 g halves the moles using the coefficient of O₂, 144 g doubles them, 9 g treats 8 g of H₂ as 0.5 mol, and 18 g is the mass of just one mole of water.

questions.stem: For the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, a container holds 6 mol of H₂ and 2 mol of O₂. When the reaction is complete, how many moles of water have formed?
questions.explain: 2 mol of O₂ can react with only 4 mol of H₂, so O₂ is the limiting reactant and 2 mol of H₂ is left over. Each mole of O₂ makes 2 mol of water, so 2 × 2 = 4 mol of H₂O. 6 mol assumes all the hydrogen reacts, 8 mol adds the reactants, 2 mol copies the moles of O₂, and 3 mol divides the hydrogen's 6 mol by its coefficient and stops there.

questions.stem: 20 g of sodium hydroxide (NaOH, molar mass 40 g/mol) is dissolved in water to make 250 mL of solution. What is the molarity?
questions.explain: Moles of NaOH = 20 ÷ 40 = 0.5 mol. Molarity = moles ÷ liters = 0.5 ÷ 0.250 = 2.0 M. 0.5 M forgets to divide by the volume, 0.08 M divides the grams by the milliliters, 0.125 M divides the moles by 4 instead of by 0.25 L, and 80 M divides the grams by the liters without converting to moles.

questions.stem: 50 mL of 6.0 M hydrochloric acid is diluted with water to a total volume of 300 mL. What is the new concentration?
questions.explain: The moles of acid don't change: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂, so 6.0 × 50 = M₂ × 300 and M₂ = 1.0 M. 36 M multiplies instead of dividing, 0.5 M uses 600 mL, 1.2 M divides by 250 mL (300 − 50), and 0.86 M treats the 300 mL as water added to the 50 mL (350 mL in all).

questions.stem: When iron rusts, iron metal (Fe) becomes iron(III) ions (Fe³⁺) in iron oxide. In this process, iron
questions.explain: Oxidation is loss of electrons (OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain). Going from Fe (charge 0) to Fe³⁺ means each atom loses 3 electrons, so iron is oxidized, while oxygen gains those electrons and is reduced. Gaining electrons would make the charge more negative, not +3. Pairing loss with reduction mixes up the definitions, and rust involves a transfer of electrons, not equal sharing.

questions.stem: Raising the temperature usually speeds up a chemical reaction. The main reason is that
options: more collisions have at least the activation energy
the activation energy of the reaction decreases
the concentration of the reactants increases
the products become more stable than the reactants
questions.explain: At higher temperature the molecules move faster, so they collide more often and, more importantly, a much larger fraction of the collisions have enough energy to get over the activation-energy barrier. The activation energy itself is unchanged (lowering it is what a catalyst does). Temperature doesn't change how exothermic a reaction is, doesn't change the reactants' concentration in a closed solution, and doesn't change the relative stability of products and reactants.

questions.stem: Which statement about a catalyst is correct?
options: It lowers the activation energy and is not used up
It raises the activation energy so the reaction goes faster
It supplies extra energy so more products form
It shifts the reaction to make more products at equilibrium
It is used up as the reaction proceeds and must be replaced
questions.explain: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed and the reaction speeds up. It comes out of the reaction unchanged, so it is not consumed. Raising the activation energy would slow the reaction, a catalyst adds no energy and doesn't change the overall energy change, it speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally so the equilibrium amounts don't change, and it is not used up.

questions.stem: Which element has chemical properties most similar to sodium (Na)?
questions.explain: Elements in the same group (column) have the same number of valence electrons and behave alike. Sodium and potassium are both alkali metals in Group 1, with one valence electron that they readily lose. Magnesium is next to sodium in the same period but has two valence electrons, neon is an unreactive noble gas, and chlorine and sulfur are nonmetals that tend to gain electrons.

questions.stem: An instant cold pack gets cold when the chemicals inside are mixed. Which statement describes this process?
options: It is endothermic: it absorbs heat from its surroundings
It is exothermic: it releases cold into its surroundings
It is exothermic: it absorbs heat from its surroundings
It is endothermic: it releases heat into its surroundings
It involves no energy change, only a physical change
questions.explain: An endothermic process takes in energy. The cold pack draws heat from whatever it touches, which is why your skin feels cold. Cold is not a substance that can be released, exothermic processes give off heat rather than absorbing it, endothermic processes don't release heat, and the temperature drop shows that energy is changing.

questions.stem: A comet follows a long elliptical orbit around the Sun. Where in its orbit does it move fastest?
options: At its closest approach to the Sun (perihelion)
At its farthest point from the Sun (aphelion)
At the same speed everywhere in its orbit
Midway between its closest and farthest points
Wherever it crosses the plane of Earth's orbit
questions.explain: Kepler's second law says a line from the Sun to an orbiting body sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Near the Sun the line is short, so the body must move faster to sweep the same area; far away it moves slowest. This is conservation of angular momentum. Aphelion is where it is slowest, only a circular orbit has constant speed, and the midpoint and plane crossing are not where the speed peaks.

questions.stem: A lunar eclipse can occur only during which phase of the Moon?
questions.explain: A lunar eclipse happens when Earth is directly between the Sun and the Moon, so Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. In that line-up the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun, with its whole sunlit face toward us: a full moon. A new moon is when the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, which is when a solar eclipse can happen. At the quarter and crescent phases the three bodies are not lined up.

questions.stem: In the lower atmosphere, air temperature falls by about 6.5°C for every 1,000 m of altitude. If it is 15°C at sea level, about what is the temperature at 3,000 m?
questions.explain: The drop is 3 × 6.5 = 19.5°C, so the temperature is 15 − 19.5 = −4.5°C. −19.5°C is the size of the drop, not the temperature, 34.5°C adds the drop, 8.5°C applies only one 1,000 m step, and 2.0°C applies two steps.

questions.stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, how do surface winds move around a low-pressure center?
questions.explain: Air flows toward low pressure, but the Coriolis effect deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. That sets up a counterclockwise spin around a low, with surface friction letting air spiral inward and then rise. Clockwise and outward describes a Northern Hemisphere high, clockwise and inward describes a Southern Hemisphere low, counterclockwise and outward mixes the two, and air doesn't flow straight in because of the Coriolis deflection.

questions.stem: Clouds form when rising air
options: cools to its dew point, so water vapor condenses
warms until its water vapor evaporates
reaches the freezing point of water
loses all of its water vapor to the ground
is compressed by the higher pressure aloft
questions.explain: Rising air expands because pressure decreases with height, and expansion cools it. When it cools to its dew point, the air is saturated and water vapor condenses on tiny particles into cloud droplets. Warming would keep the water as vapor, many clouds form well above freezing, the vapor isn't lost to the ground, and pressure is lower aloft, not higher.

questions.stem: Using the frictionless pulley system shown to lift the 900 N load, how much effort F is needed, and how much rope must be pulled to raise the load 2 m?
questions.explain: Three rope segments support the load, so the mechanical advantage is 3: F = 900 ÷ 3 = 300 N. Each of the three segments must shorten by 2 m, so 3 × 2 = 6 m of rope is pulled. Work in equals work out: 300 × 6 = 900 × 2 = 1,800 J. 300 N with 2 m of rope would create energy from nothing, 900 N ignores the pulleys, 450 N counts two ropes, and 2,700 N multiplies by the advantage instead of dividing.

questions.stem: Gear A turns counterclockwise at 60 rpm. What are the speed and direction of gear C?
questions.explain: In a simple gear train the idler (B) doesn't change the overall ratio: C's speed = 60 × (40 ÷ 10) = 240 rpm. Meshing gears turn in opposite directions, so A counterclockwise turns B clockwise, which turns C counterclockwise. 240 rpm clockwise gets the direction wrong, 15 rpm inverts the tooth ratio, and 120 rpm clockwise stops at gear B (60 × 40/20).

questions.stem: The bar shown is hinged at the left end. What upward effort F, applied as shown, holds the 60 N load at the end of the bar steady? (Ignore the bar's weight.)
questions.explain: This is a third-class lever: the effort is between the fulcrum and the load. Balance the torques about the hinge: F × 0.5 = 60 × 2, so F = 120 ÷ 0.5 = 240 N. A third-class lever always needs more effort than the load, but it moves the load farther and faster. 15 N swaps the distances, 60 N ignores them, 120 N is the load's torque in N·m, and 300 N measures the load's arm as 2.5 m.

questions.stem: In the circuit shown, what is the voltage across R3?
questions.explain: R2 and R3 in parallel give (3 × 6) ÷ (3 + 6) = 2 Ω. In series with R1 (2 Ω) the total is 4 Ω, so the battery supplies 12 ÷ 4 = 3 A. R1 drops 3 × 2 = 6 V, leaving 12 − 6 = 6 V across the parallel pair, so 6 V across R3 (which carries 1 A). 12 V gives R3 the full battery voltage, 6.5 V treats all three resistors as series (12 × 6/11), 4 V splits the voltage equally among three resistors, and 1 A is R3's current, not its voltage.

questions.stem: An airplane is in a steady, unaccelerated climb at constant airspeed. Which statement about the four forces is correct?
options: Thrust exceeds drag, because part of the weight acts rearward along the flight path.
Lift exceeds weight, and that excess lift is what makes the airplane keep climbing.
Thrust equals drag and lift equals weight, exactly as in level flight.
Lift exceeds weight and thrust equals drag, so the climb continues.
The forces are unbalanced, so the airplane must be accelerating upward.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 5) explains that in a steady climb the forces are in equilibrium along the flight path, but a component of weight now acts rearward, so thrust must equal drag plus that component and lift is actually slightly less than weight. The idea that extra lift causes a climb is the classic misconception. Thrust equal to drag describes level flight, and a steady climb at constant speed is by definition not accelerating.

questions.stem: In level flight, as airspeed is reduced from cruise toward the stall, induced drag
options: increases, because a higher angle of attack is needed for the same lift.
decreases, because it varies with the square of the airspeed.
stays the same, because the amount of lift being produced does not change.
increases, because skin friction on the wing grows at low speed.
decreases, because the wingtip vortices weaken at high angles of attack.
questions.explain: Induced drag is a by-product of lift and is greatest at low airspeed and high angle of attack, when wingtip vortices and downwash are strongest (PHAK Ch. 5). Drag that rises with the square of airspeed is parasite drag, not induced drag. Skin friction is a form of parasite drag, and the vortices strengthen rather than weaken at high angles of attack.

questions.stem: At the airspeed that gives the maximum lift-to-drag ratio (L/D max), which is true?
options: Induced and parasite drag are equal, so total drag is at its lowest.
Induced drag is at its minimum and parasite drag is zero.
Total drag is at its maximum, giving the steepest climb.
The wing is at its critical angle of attack, so lift is greatest.
Parasite drag is at its minimum, so total drag is at its lowest value.
questions.explain: On the total drag curve, induced drag falls and parasite drag rises with speed; where the two curves cross, total drag is lowest and the lift-to-drag ratio is greatest (PHAK Ch. 5). Parasite drag is never zero in flight, and parasite drag alone is lowest at low speed, not at L/D max. The critical angle of attack produces maximum lift but very high drag, so it is far from L/D max.

questions.stem: An airplane is forced into the air in ground effect below its recommended takeoff speed. What is the main danger as it climbs out of ground effect?
options: Induced drag increases, and the airplane may settle back to the runway.
Ground effect raises the critical angle of attack, so it stalls at once.
Parasite drag falls sharply, so the airplane accelerates out of control.
Induced drag decreases with height, causing a sudden steep climb.
The required thrust drops suddenly once it is more than a wingspan up.
questions.explain: Ground effect, within about one wingspan of the surface, reduces downwash and wingtip vortices and therefore reduces induced drag (PHAK Ch. 5). When the airplane climbs out of it, induced drag and required thrust rise, so an airplane lifted off too slowly may not be able to climb and can settle back down. Ground effect does not change the critical angle of attack, and climbing out increases rather than decreases induced drag and required thrust.

questions.stem: The fixed angle between the wing's chord line and the airplane's longitudinal axis is the
questions.explain: The angle of incidence is set when the wing is mounted and is measured between the chord line and the longitudinal axis (PHAK Ch. 5). Angle of attack is measured between the chord line and the relative wind, so it changes in flight. Dihedral is the upward angle of the wings from the lateral axis, pitch attitude is the nose position relative to the horizon, and sweepback is the rearward angle of the wing in plan view.

questions.stem: An airplane is sinking steadily while its pitch attitude stays level, with the nose on the horizon. Compared with level flight at the same attitude, its angle of attack is
options: greater, since the relative wind now meets the wing from below.
zero, because the nose is on the horizon.
smaller, because the descent reduces the airflow over the wing.
unchanged, because it equals the fixed angle of incidence.
negative, because the airplane is losing altitude.
questions.explain: Relative wind is parallel and opposite to the flight path, and angle of attack is measured from the chord line to the relative wind, not to the horizon (PHAK Ch. 5). If the path tilts down while the attitude stays the same, the relative wind arrives from below and the angle of attack increases. Pitch attitude and angle of attack are different things. The angle of incidence is fixed and is not the angle of attack, and a descent does not make the angle of attack negative.

questions.stem: An airplane stalls at 50 knots with its wings level. In a level, coordinated 60 degree bank turn, its stall speed is about
questions.explain: A level 60 degree bank produces a load factor of 2 G, and stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor (PHAK Ch. 5): 50 x 1.41 is about 71 knots. Doubling to 100 knots uses the load factor instead of its square root. 59 knots is the figure for a 45 degree bank, 50 knots ignores load factor, and 35 knots divides instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: Which statement about an aerodynamic stall is correct?
options: It happens whenever the critical angle of attack is exceeded, at any airspeed.
It happens only when airspeed drops below the published power-off stall speed.
It happens only when the airplane is in a nose-high attitude.
It is caused by the engine losing power at low airspeed.
It happens when the angle of incidence exceeds about 18 degrees.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 5) and the Airplane Flying Handbook stress that a wing stalls when it exceeds its critical angle of attack, which can happen at any airspeed, in any attitude and at any power setting, for example in a steep turn or an abrupt pull-up. Published stall speeds apply only to stated conditions such as 1 G and a given weight. Power loss is not the cause, and the angle of incidence is fixed and does not change in flight.

questions.stem: After the throttle is closed, what is the general spin recovery sequence given in the Airplane Flying Handbook?
options: Ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, then brisk forward elevator.
Full aileron opposite the rotation, then full back elevator.
Full rudder with the rotation, then forward elevator to unstall the wing.
Brisk forward elevator first, then aileron against the rotation.
Ailerons neutral, full back elevator, then rudder opposite the rotation.
questions.explain: The Airplane Flying Handbook gives the general sequence: power idle, ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, then positive forward elevator to break the stall, neutralizing the rudder once rotation stops (often remembered as PARE). Using aileron against the spin can make it worse. Rudder with the rotation feeds the spin, and back elevator keeps the wing stalled, so the order and direction of the inputs both matter.

questions.stem: Compared with a forward CG, loading an airplane with its CG near the aft limit generally makes it
options: less stable in pitch, with a lower stall speed and harder spin recovery.
more stable in pitch, with a higher stall speed and a slower cruise.
less stable in pitch, with a higher stall speed and an easier spin recovery.
more stable in pitch, with a lower stall speed and an easier stall recovery.
unchanged in stability, but more nose-heavy when landing.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 5 and Ch. 10) explains that an aft CG needs less tail down-force, so the airplane stalls at a lower speed and cruises a little faster, but it is less stable longitudinally and stall and spin recovery become harder. A forward CG gives more stability, a higher stall speed and a slower cruise, which is the reverse pattern. Moving the CG always changes longitudinal stability, so it cannot be left unchanged.

questions.stem: Wing dihedral contributes mainly to
options: lateral stability about the longitudinal axis.
directional stability about the vertical axis.
longitudinal stability about the lateral axis.
lateral stability about the lateral axis.
directional stability about the longitudinal axis.
questions.explain: Dihedral, the upward angle of the wings, tends to level the wings after a disturbance in roll, and roll is about the longitudinal axis, so it gives lateral stability (PHAK Ch. 5). Directional stability is about the vertical axis and comes mainly from the vertical fin. Longitudinal stability is in pitch about the lateral axis. The two remaining options pair a correct stability name with the wrong axis.

questions.stem: A pilot rolls into a left turn using aileron only, with no rudder. The nose will initially yaw
options: right, toward the rising wing, because its lowered aileron adds drag.
left, toward the lowered wing, because the right wing produces extra lift.
right, because of the torque reaction of the propeller.
left, because the raised left aileron produces more drag.
neither way, because ailerons act only about the longitudinal axis.
questions.explain: Rolling left lowers the right aileron, so the right wing makes more lift and more induced drag and is pulled back, yawing the nose right, away from the turn. This is adverse yaw, which is corrected with coordinated rudder (PHAK Ch. 6). Propeller torque is a separate effect, the lowered aileron (not the raised one) makes the extra drag, and the yaw shows that aileron inputs do affect the vertical axis.

questions.stem: In wings-level flight, a pilot presses the right rudder pedal and holds the ailerons neutral. Besides yawing the nose right about the vertical axis, the airplane will tend to
options: roll right, because the left wing moves faster and gains lift.
roll left, because the right wing moves faster and gains lift.
pitch down, because the rudder acts about the lateral axis.
roll right, because the fin pushes the tail upward.
hold wings level, since the rudder acts only about the vertical axis.
questions.explain: Yawing right swings the left wing forward, so it moves faster through the air and makes more lift than the retreating right wing, and the airplane rolls right; dihedral adds to this once the airplane sideslips. This roll is the secondary effect of rudder. Rolling left reverses which wing advances, pitching down puts the rudder on the wrong axis, a fin pushing the tail up names a force the rudder does not produce, and holding wings level ignores the secondary effect.

questions.stem: A stabilator is
options: a one-piece horizontal tail that pivots as a whole to control pitch.
a vertical fin and rudder combined into one moving surface for yaw control.
a small hinged tab that keeps the elevator from fluttering.
a combined aileron and elevator used on delta-wing aircraft.
a fixed horizontal surface mounted ahead of the main wing.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 3 and Ch. 6) describes the stabilator as a one-piece horizontal stabilizer that pivots from a central hinge point, replacing the separate fixed stabilizer and elevator. A surface ahead of the wing is a canard, a combined aileron and elevator is an elevon, and the stabilator usually carries an antiservo tab rather than being one. The vertical tail is not involved.

questions.stem: To trim an airplane with a conventional elevator for a nose-up attitude, the elevator trim tab moves
options: down, which forces the elevator's trailing edge up.
up, carrying the elevator's trailing edge up with it.
down, which forces the elevator's trailing edge down.
up, which forces the elevator's trailing edge down.
down, which pulls the stabilizer's leading edge down.
questions.explain: A trim tab moves opposite to the control surface: when the tab deflects down, airflow pushes the elevator's trailing edge up, which holds the nose up without pilot pressure (PHAK Ch. 6). A tab that moved the same way as the elevator would not hold it in position. Tab-up with elevator-down is nose-down trim, and the fixed stabilizer does not move.

questions.stem: The antiservo tab on a stabilator moves
options: the same way as the stabilator's trailing edge, making it less sensitive.
opposite to the trailing edge, lightening the control forces for the pilot.
only when the pilot turns the trim wheel, never with the controls.
on its own as a yaw damper during turbulence.
opposite to the trailing edge, making the stabilator more sensitive.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 6) states that an antiservo tab moves in the same direction as the stabilator's trailing edge, which increases control forces and prevents the pilot from overcontrolling a very sensitive surface; it also serves as the trim tab. Moving opposite to the surface to lighten forces describes a servo or balance tab. The tab moves with every stabilator deflection, not only with trim, and it has nothing to do with yaw damping.

questions.stem: Which trailing-edge flap slides rearward on tracks before it deflects, increasing wing area as well as camber, and gives the largest increase in lift of the common types?
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 6) describes the Fowler flap as a slotted flap that first moves aft and then down, increasing both chord (wing area) and camber, which produces the greatest increase in lift. A plain flap only hinges down, a split flap hinges down from the lower surface, and a slotted flap opens a gap but does not add much area. A slat is a leading-edge device, not a trailing-edge flap.

questions.stem: What is the main aerodynamic effect of deploying spoilers?
options: They reduce lift and add drag, and on one wing they can help with roll control.
They add camber to the wing, which lowers the stall speed for landing.
They energize the boundary layer, delaying the stall to higher angles of attack.
They open a slot at the leading edge so the wing can reach higher angles of attack.
They weaken the wingtip vortices, which reduces induced drag in cruise.
questions.explain: Spoilers are panels on the upper wing surface that disrupt airflow, killing lift and increasing drag, which is useful for descents and for slowing down after landing; raised on one side, they assist the ailerons in roll (PHAK Ch. 6). Adding camber is what flaps do, and energizing the boundary layer or opening a slot describes vortex generators, slots and slats. Reducing tip vortices is the job of winglets.

questions.stem: Most modern light airplanes have a semimonocoque fuselage. In this type of structure,
options: the skin carries part of the load, reinforced by bulkheads, formers and stringers.
the stressed skin carries all of the load, so no internal bracing is needed at all.
a welded steel-tube truss carries all loads, and the skin only streamlines it.
the forward fuselage is monocoque and the tailcone is a tube-and-fabric truss.
the wings are braced by external struts rather than by internal spars alone.
questions.explain: In a semimonocoque structure, a substructure of bulkheads or formers and stringers is attached to a stressed skin, and the skin and framework share the loads (PHAK Ch. 3). A skin carrying everything with no bracing is full monocoque, a tube truss with a nonstructural covering is truss construction, and reading semi as half of the fuselage misreads the term. External wing struts describe a semicantilever wing, not the fuselage.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT part of the empennage?
questions.explain: The empennage is the tail section: the vertical stabilizer and rudder, the horizontal stabilizer and elevator, and their trim tabs (PHAK Ch. 3). Ailerons are on the outer trailing edge of the wings and control roll, so they are not part of the tail. All the other options are tail components.

questions.stem: In an airplane with a fixed-pitch propeller, the pilot suspects carburetor ice and applies full carburetor heat. If ice is present, the RPM will
options: drop at first, then rise gradually as the ice melts.
rise immediately and stay higher while heat is on.
drop and then hold steady at the lower value.
stay the same, because carburetor heat only affects mixture.
rise briefly, then fall below the starting value.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 7) explains that warm carburetor-heat air is less dense and richens the mixture, so RPM drops first; if ice was present it then melts and RPM rises gradually. A drop that simply holds steady means no ice was present. Carburetor heat clearly changes engine output, and RPM does not jump straight up, because the density effect comes first.

questions.stem: Which description fits preignition rather than detonation?
options: The mixture ignites before the normal spark, often from a hot spot.
The charge explodes instead of burning evenly after normal ignition.
Lower-grade fuel than specified causes the charge to explode in the cylinder.
Fuel vaporizes in the lines and interrupts the flow to the engine.
Ice forms in the carburetor venturi and restricts the flow of air.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 7) defines preignition as the fuel-air mixture igniting before the engine's normal ignition event, usually from a glowing deposit or hot spot. Uncontrolled explosive burning after normal ignition is detonation, and using fuel below the specified grade is a classic cause of detonation. Vapor lock and carburetor ice are different problems altogether.

questions.stem: As an airplane with a carbureted engine climbs and the pilot does not lean the mixture, the mixture becomes
options: richer, because the air thins while fuel flow stays about the same.
leaner, because the carburetor draws less fuel at altitude.
leaner, because the air becomes denser with height.
richer, because the air becomes denser with height.
unchanged, because the carburetor compensates for altitude automatically.
questions.explain: Air density falls with altitude, but a carburetor meters fuel by volume of air, so the same fuel goes into less air by weight and the mixture gets richer (PHAK Ch. 7). That is why pilots lean the mixture as they climb. Air does not get denser with height, and a basic carburetor has no automatic altitude compensation.

questions.stem: A gas turbine engine whose output drives a shaft for something other than a propeller, such as a helicopter rotor, is a
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 7) describes the turboshaft as delivering power to a shaft that drives something other than a propeller, which is how most turbine helicopters and APUs work. A turboprop drives a propeller through a reduction gear, a turbofan uses a ducted fan, and a turbojet makes all its thrust from exhaust. A ramjet has no turbine or shaft at all.

questions.stem: In a high-bypass turbofan engine, most of the thrust comes from
options: the fan air that bypasses the engine core.
the hot exhaust gas leaving the core.
a propeller driven through a reduction gearbox.
fuel burned in an afterburner behind the turbine.
the compressor air passing through the turbine.
questions.explain: In a turbofan the fan moves a large mass of air around the core; with a high bypass ratio that bypass air produces most of the thrust, which makes these engines quieter and more fuel efficient (PHAK Ch. 7; Airplane Flying Handbook, transition to jets). Core exhaust is the main source of thrust in a turbojet or low-bypass engine. A reduction-geared propeller describes a turboprop, and afterburners are not used on high-bypass airliner engines.

questions.stem: During a turbine engine start, the engine lights off normally, but RPM stays well below idle and will not accelerate. This is a
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 7) defines a hung (false) start as one where the engine starts normally but RPM stays at a low value instead of rising to normal. A hot start is one where exhaust gas temperature exceeds its limit, a compressor stall is a breakdown of airflow through the compressor, and a flameout is the fire going out in a running engine. A wet start is fuel flowing with no light-off at all.

questions.stem: Propeller blades are twisted along their length so that
options: blade angle decreases toward the tip, evening out the angle of attack.
blade angle increases toward the tip, because the tip travels fastest.
the tips stall first and give the pilot early warning of a stall.
the torque reaction of the engine is cancelled at high power.
the propeller can be feathered if the engine fails in flight.
questions.explain: Each section of the blade travels at a different speed, fastest at the tip, so the blade angle is largest near the hub and smallest at the tip to keep the angle of attack fairly uniform (PHAK Ch. 7). Reversing the twist would overload the tips. The twist does not cancel torque, provide stall warning or allow feathering, which needs a special pitch-changing hub.

questions.stem: In a single-engine airplane whose propeller turns clockwise as seen from the cockpit, why does P-factor yaw the nose left during a high-power, high angle of attack climb?
options: The descending blade on the right has a higher angle of attack and makes more thrust.
The ascending blade on the left has a higher angle of attack and makes more thrust.
The spiraling slipstream strikes the right side of the vertical fin.
The engine's torque reaction rolls the airplane to the left.
Gyroscopic precession pushes the nose left as the tail comes up.
questions.explain: P-factor (asymmetric loading) comes from the descending right-side blade meeting the air at a greater angle of attack than the ascending left-side blade, so the right side makes more thrust and yaws the nose left (PHAK Ch. 5). The ascending blade has the lower angle of attack. Slipstream, torque and precession are separate left-turning tendencies, and the slipstream actually strikes the left side of the fin.

questions.stem: In an airplane with a constant-speed propeller, the throttle controls ______ and the propeller control regulates ______.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 7) explains that with a constant-speed propeller the throttle sets power output, read on the manifold pressure gauge, while the propeller control sets the RPM that the governor holds by changing blade angle. Swapping the two is the common mistake. Fuel-air mixture is set by the mixture control, and the pilot does not select blade angle directly; the governor does.

questions.stem: Ice blocks both the pitot tube's ram-air inlet and its drain hole, while the static port stays open. As the airplane then climbs, the airspeed indicator will
options: show an increase, acting like an altimeter.
hold the value shown when the blockage formed.
show a decrease as altitude increases.
read correctly, because the static port is open.
questions.explain: With the pitot pressure trapped, the indicator compares a fixed pressure with a static pressure that falls as the airplane climbs, so the reading rises like an altimeter (PHAK Ch. 8). A drop to zero happens when only the ram inlet is blocked and the drain stays open. The reading holds steady only in level flight, and it cannot be correct because the trapped pitot pressure no longer reflects airspeed.

questions.stem: The static ports become completely blocked in cruise, and the pilot then descends. What do the altimeter and airspeed indicator show?
options: Altimeter stuck at the cruise altitude; airspeed higher than actual.
Altimeter stuck at the cruise altitude; airspeed lower than actual.
Altimeter reading lower than actual; airspeed reading correctly.
Altimeter stuck at the cruise altitude; airspeed reading correctly.
Altimeter unwinding normally; airspeed reading higher than actual.
questions.explain: With static pressure trapped, the altimeter freezes at the altitude where the blockage happened (PHAK Ch. 8). In a descent, the trapped static pressure is lower than the real outside pressure, so the gap between pitot and static pressure is larger and the airspeed reads high; in a climb it would read low. The airspeed indicator uses static pressure too, so it cannot stay accurate, and the altimeter cannot unwind without fresh static pressure.

questions.stem: In an unpressurized airplane, selecting the cabin alternate static source usually causes
options: a high altimeter and airspeed, and a brief climb on the VSI.
a slightly low altimeter and a high airspeed reading.
all three pitot-static instruments to freeze where they are.
a slightly high altimeter but a low airspeed reading.
no change, because cabin pressure equals outside pressure.
questions.explain: Air flowing past the fuselage lowers cabin pressure slightly below outside static pressure, so on the alternate source the altimeter reads a little high, the airspeed reads a little high, and the VSI shows a momentary climb (PHAK Ch. 8). Lower static pressure raises both readings, so a low reading on either is wrong. The instruments keep working, and cabin pressure is not quite equal to outside pressure.

questions.stem: A pilot flies from a warm, high-pressure area into a cold, low-pressure area, never resets the altimeter, and holds the same indicated altitude. The airplane's true altitude
options: decreases, because both changes make the altimeter read higher than true altitude.
increases, because both changes make the altimeter read lower than true altitude.
stays the same, because the temperature and pressure errors cancel out.
increases, because cold air is denser and lifts the airplane higher.
decreases from the pressure change but rises with the cold, so it barely changes.
questions.explain: Flying from high to low pressure without resetting makes the altimeter read high, and flying into colder than standard air also makes it read high (PHAK Ch. 8: high to low, or hot to cold, look out below). Both errors act in the same direction, so a pilot holding the indicated altitude is actually lower than shown. They do not cancel, and colder air lowers true altitude for a given reading rather than raising it.

questions.stem: Because the turn coordinator's gyro gimbal is canted, unlike the turn-and-slip indicator's, the turn coordinator shows
options: rate of roll as well as rate of turn.
the exact bank angle in degrees.
pitch attitude as well as rate of turn.
only rate of turn, never rate of roll.
slip and skid through the gyro instead of the ball.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 8) explains that the canted gimbal lets the turn coordinator's gyro sense both rate of roll and rate of turn, while the turn-and-slip indicator shows rate of turn only. Neither instrument shows bank angle or pitch, which come from the attitude indicator. Slip and skid are shown by the inclinometer ball, not by the gyro.

questions.stem: The heading indicator must be checked against the magnetic compass about every 15 minutes, mainly because of
options: precession caused by friction in the gyro.
acceleration error on east and west headings.
variation between true and magnetic north.
northerly turning error during banked turns.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 8) states that precession, caused mainly by friction, makes the heading indicator creep or drift, so it is reset to the compass periodically, about every 15 minutes. Deviation, acceleration error and northerly turning error are errors of the magnetic compass, not the gyro. Variation is the angle between true and magnetic north and does not cause the gyro to drift.

questions.stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, as a pilot starts a turn toward east from a heading of north, the magnetic compass will at first
options: briefly show a turn in the opposite direction.
lead the turn, showing more change than actual.
read accurately if the turn is coordinated.
lag only if the airplane is also accelerating.
swing toward south before settling on east.
questions.explain: Magnetic dip causes northerly turning error: in the Northern Hemisphere, when turning from a north heading the compass first swings the opposite way and then lags the turn (PHAK Ch. 8). Leading the turn is what happens when turning from south. Coordination does not remove the error, which comes from dip rather than acceleration, and the card does not swing toward south.

questions.stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, an airplane on a heading of east accelerates. The magnetic compass will
options: show no error, because acceleration error occurs only on north and south headings.
show no error unless the airplane is also turning.
show a turn toward north, but only in the Southern Hemisphere.
questions.explain: Acceleration error is greatest on east and west headings; in the Northern Hemisphere accelerating makes the compass show a turn toward north and decelerating shows a turn toward south, remembered as ANDS (PHAK Ch. 8). Showing south mixes up acceleration and deceleration. North and south headings are where turning error is worst, not acceleration error, and the error appears in straight flight without any turn. In the Southern Hemisphere the error is reversed.

questions.stem: Under 14 CFR 91.155, what are the basic VFR minimums in Class E airspace below 10,000 feet MSL?
options: 3 SM visibility; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds
5 SM visibility; 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 1 SM horizontally from clouds
1 SM visibility; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds
3 SM visibility; 1,000 ft below, 500 ft above and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.155 sets Class E below 10,000 ft MSL at 3 statute miles with cloud clearance of 500 below, 1,000 above and 2,000 horizontal. 3 SM and clear of clouds is Class B. 5 SM with 1,000, 1,000 and 1 SM is Class E at or above 10,000 ft MSL. 1 SM is a Class G day figure, and the last option reverses the below and above distances.

questions.stem: A VFR flight cruises at 11,500 feet MSL in Class E airspace, more than 1,200 feet above the surface. What are the minimum visibility and cloud clearance?
options: 5 SM; 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 1 SM horizontally
3 SM; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 2,000 ft horizontally
5 SM; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 2,000 ft horizontally
3 SM; 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 1 SM horizontally
1 SM; 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 1 SM horizontally
questions.explain: At or above 10,000 ft MSL in Class E (and in Class G above 1,200 ft AGL), 14 CFR 91.155 requires 5 statute miles visibility and 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 1 statute mile horizontally from clouds. The 3 SM and 500/1,000/2,000 values apply below 10,000 ft MSL. The other options mix the higher-altitude visibility with lower-altitude cloud clearances or the reverse.

questions.stem: A VFR pilot calls Approach before entering Class C airspace. The controller replies, 'Aircraft calling Approach, standby.' The pilot may
options: not enter, because two-way radio communication has not been established.
enter, because the controller has replied to the call and acknowledged it.
enter, but only below 2,500 feet AGL until called back.
enter, as long as the transponder is squawking 1200.
not enter until an explicit 'cleared into Class C' is received.
questions.explain: Class C requires two-way radio communication before entry, and the AIM (3-2-4) explains that a reply with your call sign, even 'standby', establishes it, while a reply without your call sign does not. Here the controller did not use the call sign, so the pilot must stay outside. A transponder or altitude restriction does not substitute for communication, and an explicit clearance is the Class B requirement, not Class C.

questions.stem: Unless otherwise authorized, what is the maximum indicated airspeed at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 NM of the primary airport of a Class C or Class D airspace area?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.117(b) limits aircraft to 200 knots indicated at or below 2,500 ft AGL within 4 NM of the primary airport of Class C or D airspace; 200 knots also applies beneath Class B shelves and in VFR corridors. 250 knots is the general limit below 10,000 ft MSL. The other figures are not regulatory limits.

questions.stem: The section of runway before a displaced threshold, marked with white arrows, may be used for
options: taxi, takeoff, and rollout from the opposite end, but not touchdown.
