taxiing only, never for takeoff or for the landing rollout of any aircraft.
nothing at all, like a blast pad or stopway.
touchdown, but not for taxiing or takeoff.
takeoff only in an emergency or with a waiver.
questions.explain: The AIM (2-3-3) explains that a displaced threshold shortens the runway available for landing, but the pavement behind it can be used for taxiing, for takeoff in either direction, and for the rollout of aircraft landing from the opposite end. Pavement unusable for any of these, such as a blast pad, is marked with yellow chevrons instead. Touching down there is exactly what the displacement is meant to prevent.

questions.stem: While taxiing, you see a black sign with a yellow letter B and yellow border, next to a yellow sign with a black letter A and an arrow pointing right. This tells you that
options: you are on taxiway B, and taxiway A is to the right.
you are on taxiway A, and taxiway B is to the right.
you must hold short of taxiway A until cleared.
taxiway B ends ahead, and you must turn left onto A.
runway B is ahead, and taxiway A is the exit to the right.
questions.explain: Per the AIM (2-3-9 and 2-3-10), a black sign with yellow letters and a yellow border is a location sign showing where you are, and a yellow sign with black letters and an arrow is a direction sign showing the direction to another taxiway. So you are on B and A lies to the right. Mandatory hold signs are red with white letters, and runways are shown by numbers, not letters.

questions.stem: Runway holding position markings are four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed. A pilot taxiing toward the runway must stop
options: before the solid lines, which are on the side nearest the pilot.
before the dashed lines, which are on the side nearest the pilot.
only at night or in instrument weather.
past the markings, at the runway edge line.
100 feet beyond the markings, at the end of the centerline.
questions.explain: The AIM (2-3-5) states that holding position markings have the solid lines on the hold side, facing an aircraft approaching the runway, and that the pilot must stop before them without a clearance to proceed. The dashed lines face aircraft leaving the runway. The markings apply in all conditions, and stopping past them puts the airplane inside the runway safety area.

questions.stem: An airport rotating beacon shows two quick white flashes between each green flash. This identifies
options: a civil airport below VFR minimums.
questions.explain: The AIM (2-1-9) states that military airport beacons flash alternately white and green but are told apart from civil beacons by dual-peaked (two quick) white flashes between the green flashes. A civil land airport uses a single white flash alternating with green, a water airport uses white and yellow, and a heliport uses green, yellow and white. A beacon on in daylight may mean below-VFR weather, but that is not shown by a different flash pattern.

questions.stem: On final approach, the PAPI shows three white lights and one red light. The airplane is
questions.explain: According to the AIM (2-1-2), the four-light PAPI shows two white and two red on the glide path; three white and one red is slightly high, and four white is well high. One white and three red is slightly low, and four red is well low. More white lights always mean higher.

questions.stem: An aircraft in flight without a radio receives a flashing green light signal from the tower. This means
options: return for landing; a steady green will follow.
give way to other aircraft and continue circling.
questions.explain: The light gun signal table in the AIM (4-3-13) and 14 CFR 91.125 gives flashing green in flight as 'return for landing (to be followed by steady green at the proper time)'. Steady green in flight is cleared to land. Flashing red means airport unsafe, do not land, steady red means give way and continue circling, and alternating red and green means exercise extreme caution.

questions.stem: An aircraft on the ground receives a flashing white light signal from the tower. This means
options: return to starting point on airport.
taxi clear of the runway that is in use.
questions.explain: In the AIM (4-3-13) light gun table, flashing white applies only on the ground and means return to starting point on the airport. Flashing red on the ground means taxi clear of the runway in use, flashing green means cleared to taxi, steady red means stop, and steady green means cleared for takeoff.

questions.stem: An airship and an airplane that is towing a glider are converging at about the same altitude, with the airship to the airplane's right. Under 14 CFR 91.113, which has the right-of-way?
options: The airplane, because a towing aircraft has priority over other engine-driven aircraft.
The airship, because under the category rules an airship has right-of-way over an airplane.
The airship, because it is to the airplane's right.
Neither; both must alter course to the right.
The airplane, because airplanes are more maneuverable than airships.
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.113(d) normally gives an airship the right-of-way over an airplane, but it adds that an aircraft towing or refueling other aircraft has the right-of-way over all other engine-driven aircraft, and an airship is engine-driven. The to-the-right rule applies only to aircraft of the same category, and both turning right is the head-on rule. Maneuverability is the reason less maneuverable aircraft usually get priority, which would favor the airship, not the airplane.

questions.stem: Two airplanes are approaching an airport to land at the same time. Under 14 CFR 91.113, which has the right-of-way?
options: The lower one, but it may not cut in front of or overtake the other.
The one at the higher altitude, because it has the better view of traffic.
The faster one, because it will reach the runway first.
The one on the other's right, as with converging aircraft.
The one that announced its position first on the radio.
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.113(g) gives the right-of-way to the aircraft at the lower altitude when two are approaching to land, but forbids it from using that rule to cut in front of or overtake another aircraft on final. Height, speed and radio calls do not decide priority. The to-the-right rule is for converging aircraft in flight, not for landing.

questions.stem: Compared with a fast-moving cold front, an approaching warm front typically brings
options: widespread stratiform cloud, steady precipitation and poor visibility.
a narrow line of cumulonimbus with heavy showers and strong gusty winds.
rapidly rising pressure followed by quickly clearing skies.
cumuliform clouds with showers but good visibility outside them.
a sharp temperature drop and wind shift with very little cloud.
questions.explain: A warm front has a gentle slope, so warm air rides slowly up over the cold air, producing widespread stratiform cloud, steady rain or drizzle, and low ceilings, poor visibility and fog (PHAK Ch. 12). A narrow band of thunderstorms, a sharp wind shift, rapidly rising pressure and good visibility behind showers are all features of a cold front.

questions.stem: Freezing rain falling at the surface tells a pilot that
options: warmer, above-freezing air lies above, a temperature inversion.
the temperature is below freezing at every altitude down to the surface.
the air aloft is colder than the air at the surface.
a cold front has already passed the area.
only rime ice is likely to form on the airframe.
questions.explain: Freezing rain forms when rain falls from a warmer, above-freezing layer into below-freezing air near the surface, so its presence shows warmer air aloft, an inversion (PHAK Ch. 12). If it were below freezing at every level the precipitation would fall as snow. Freezing rain produces large drops that form clear ice, which is more dangerous than rime, and it is usually tied to warm-front conditions.

questions.stem: Moist air from over warm water blows steadily onto colder land along a coast, and fog forms and spreads inland. This is
questions.explain: Advection fog forms when moist air is moved by wind over a colder surface and cooled to its dew point; it is common along coasts and, unlike radiation fog, needs wind (PHAK Ch. 12). Radiation fog forms on clear, calm nights over land. Upslope fog needs air pushed up rising terrain, steam fog forms when cold air moves over warm water, and ice fog needs extremely cold temperatures.

questions.stem: With the same altimeter setting at each, which airport conditions produce the highest density altitude?
options: Elevation 5,000 ft, temperature 30 degrees C, humid air
Elevation 5,000 ft, temperature 30 degrees C, dry air
Elevation 5,000 ft, temperature 0 degrees C, humid air
Sea level, temperature 30 degrees C, humid air
Elevation 5,000 ft, temperature 0 degrees C, dry air
questions.explain: Density altitude rises with higher elevation, higher temperature and higher humidity, because each makes the air less dense: high, hot and humid is the worst case (PHAK Ch. 4 and Ch. 11). Dry air at the same elevation and temperature is slightly denser, colder air is denser, and a sea-level field is far lower even when hot. Only the first option combines all three factors.

questions.stem: An airplane's true heading is 220 degrees, and the magnetic variation is 12 degrees east. What is the magnetic heading?
questions.explain: To convert true to magnetic, subtract easterly variation and add westerly variation (PHAK Ch. 16: east is least, west is best): 220 - 12 = 208 degrees. Adding to get 232 applies the rule for west variation. 220 ignores variation, 196 subtracts it twice, and 212 is an arithmetic slip.

questions.stem: How far, and in which direction, is 36 degrees N, 080 degrees W from 35 degrees N, 080 degrees W?
options: It depends on latitude, because meridians converge
questions.explain: Both points are on the same meridian (080 degrees W) and differ by one degree of latitude; each degree of latitude is 60 minutes, and one minute of latitude is about one nautical mile, so the distance is about 60 NM due north (PHAK Ch. 16). 60 NM is about 69 statute miles, and 1 NM is one minute, not one degree. Converging meridians change the length of a degree of longitude, not latitude.

questions.stem: A VFR flight will cruise more than 3,000 feet AGL on a true course of 175 degrees, where variation is 12 degrees west. Under 14 CFR 91.159, which cruising altitude is appropriate?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.159 bases VFR cruising altitudes on magnetic course: 0 to 179 degrees uses odd thousands plus 500, and 180 to 359 degrees uses even thousands plus 500. The magnetic course is 175 + 12 (west is added) = 187 degrees, so an even thousand plus 500, such as 6,500 ft, is correct. 5,500 and 7,500 come from using the true course, and 6,000 and 7,000 lack the 500-foot VFR offset.

questions.stem: In a helicopter, raising the collective pitch control
options: increases the pitch of all main rotor blades by the same amount.
tilts the rotor disk in the direction the pilot wants to travel.
changes the pitch angle of the tail rotor blades to control yaw.
changes each blade's pitch at a different point in its rotation.
raises rotor RPM directly without changing blade pitch.
questions.explain: The Helicopter Flying Handbook (Ch. 3) explains that the collective changes the pitch of all main rotor blades together, increasing total rotor thrust and requiring more power. Tilting the disk by changing each blade's pitch around its rotation is the cyclic. Tail rotor pitch is set by the antitorque pedals, and RPM is managed by the throttle and governor, not by the collective alone.

questions.stem: In a hover, a single-rotor helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise as seen from above tends to drift
options: to the right, in the direction of the tail rotor's thrust.
to the left, opposite the direction of the tail rotor's thrust.
to the left, from the main rotor's torque.
questions.explain: The Helicopter Flying Handbook (Ch. 2) calls this translating tendency: the tail rotor's sideways thrust, which counters main rotor torque, also pushes the whole helicopter to the right on a counterclockwise rotor, so designers tilt the mast or rig the cyclic slightly left. Drift goes with the tail rotor thrust, not against it. Torque makes the fuselage yaw rather than drift, and coning and the advancing blade do not cause sideways drift.

questions.stem: In forward flight, a helicopter's dissymmetry of lift is mainly compensated by
options: blade flapping: the advancing blade flaps up, which reduces its angle of attack.
blade flapping: the advancing blade flaps down, which increases its angle of attack.
extra tail rotor thrust, which balances the lift across the disk.
the pilot raising the collective to add lift on the retreating side.
coning, which bends both blades upward by the same amount.
questions.explain: The advancing blade meets faster air than the retreating blade; the Helicopter Flying Handbook (Ch. 2) explains that it flaps up, lowering its angle of attack, while the retreating blade flaps down, raising its angle of attack, so lift evens out (cyclic feathering also helps). Flapping down on the advancing side would make the imbalance worse. The tail rotor controls yaw, collective changes lift on both sides equally, and coning is symmetrical, so it cannot correct a side-to-side imbalance.

questions.stem: Based on the turn coordinator shown, what is the aircraft doing?
options: A coordinated standard-rate turn to the right
A coordinated standard-rate turn to the left
A 30° right bank in a level climb
A skidding turn to the right
questions.explain: The miniature aircraft's right wing sits on the R index mark, which is a standard-rate turn (3° per second, 360° in 2 minutes) to the right, and the ball is centred, so the turn is coordinated. The turn coordinator shows rate and direction of turn, not bank angle or pitch ('no pitch information'), and a skid would push the ball outside the turn (to the left).

questions.stem: The turn coordinator shows a left turn with the ball displaced to the left. Which describes the turn and the correction?
options: A slipping turn; add left rudder
A skidding turn; add right rudder
A slipping turn; add right rudder
A skidding turn; add left rudder
A coordinated turn; no correction needed
questions.explain: The ball has fallen to the inside of the turn, so the aircraft is slipping: too much bank for the rate of turn, or too little rudder. 'Step on the ball': press the rudder on the side the ball has moved to, here left rudder. A ball thrown to the outside (right, in a left turn) would mean a skid.

questions.stem: Based on the attitude indicator shown, what is the aircraft's attitude?
options: Banked 30° left, nose above the horizon
Banked 30° right, nose above the horizon
Banked 30° left, nose below the horizon
Banked 45° left, nose above the horizon
Banked 30° right, nose below the horizon
questions.explain: The bank pointer sits on the 30° mark and the horizon has dropped on the right and risen on the left, so the aircraft is banked left; the horizon tilts the opposite way to the bank, which is the classic trap. The miniature aircraft sits above the horizon line, on the 10° pitch mark, so the nose is up. 45° is marked by the small triangle, not reached here.

questions.stem: What altitude does the altimeter shown indicate?
questions.explain: Read the three pointers: the thin 10,000-ft pointer with the triangle is just past 0 (under 10,000 ft), the short wide 1,000-ft hand is between 7 and 8 (7,000 ft), and the long 100-ft hand is at 3.5 (350 ft): 7,350 ft. 3,750 swaps the two main hands, 17,350 misreads the 10,000-ft pointer, and 8,350 rounds the thousands hand up.

questions.stem: The airspeed needle is in the yellow arc, as shown. What does this range mean?
options: Caution range: fly here only in smooth air
Never exceed: structural failure is likely
questions.explain: The yellow arc runs from VNO (maximum structural cruising speed) to VNE (the red line): flight there is allowed only in smooth air, with caution. The green arc is the normal operating range, the white arc is the flap operating range, and the red line marks VNE, the never-exceed speed.

questions.stem: Referencing the primary flight display shown, what is the aircraft's height above ground level (AGL) if the terrain below is about 4,700 feet MSL?
questions.explain: The altitude tape's boxed readout shows the aircraft at 11,600 ft MSL. Height above ground = altitude MSL − terrain elevation = 11,600 − 4,700 = 6,900 ft AGL. 4,300 ft uses the cyan selected altitude (9,000 ft) instead of the actual altitude, 11,600 ft is the MSL reading itself, 16,300 ft adds instead of subtracting, and 4,700 ft is the terrain.

questions.stem: You are holding short at the sign shown and will turn RIGHT onto the runway for an intersection takeoff. Which runway are you departing on?
options: Neither: this sign marks a taxiway
It cannot be determined from this sign
Runway 23, because the higher number is always on the right
questions.explain: On a runway holding position sign, the number on the left is the runway whose threshold lies to your left. '5-23' means the Runway 5 threshold is to the left and the Runway 23 threshold to the right. Turning right takes you away from the Runway 5 threshold, in the direction of 050°, so you depart on Runway 5. Red signs with white numbers are runway holding signs, not taxiway signs.

questions.stem: You see the signs shown while taxiing. What do they tell you?
options: You are on taxiway B; taxiway A is to the right
You are on taxiway A; taxiway B is to the right
Taxiway B is ahead; you are on taxiway A
Hold short of runway B, then turn right onto A
Taxiway A is closed; continue on taxiway B
questions.explain: A black sign with a yellow letter and yellow border is a location sign: it names the taxiway you are on (B). A yellow sign with a black letter and an arrow is a direction sign: it shows the taxiway branching off and which way it goes (A, to the right). Runway holding signs are red, and closures are marked with a yellow X.

questions.stem: Based on the PAPI lights shown beside the runway, what is the aircraft's position relative to the glide path?
questions.explain: A four-light PAPI shows two white and two red when the aircraft is on the glide path. Three red and one white means slightly below; four red means well below; three white and one red slightly above; four white well above. The lights nearest the runway turn red first as you sink low.

questions.stem: A pilot who has lost two-way radio communication should set the transponder to which code?
questions.explain: 7600 signals a radio (communications) failure. 7700 is a general emergency, 7500 unlawful interference (hijack), 1200 the standard VFR code in the US, and 2000 is squawked when entering US airspace from an area where no code was assigned.

questions.stem: An aircraft takes on 1,500 US gallons of Jet-A. About how much weight does this add?
questions.explain: Jet-A weighs about 6.7 lb per US gallon: 1,500 × 6.7 = 10,050 lb. 9,000 lb uses avgas's 6.0 lb/gal, 12,450 lb uses water's 8.3 lb/gal, and 8,250 lb and 11,250 lb use 5.5 and 7.5 lb/gal.

questions.stem: The parasite drag created where the wing joins the fuselage, as the airflows around the two parts meet and mix, is called
questions.explain: Interference drag comes from intersecting airflows at junctions such as wing roots and struts; fairings reduce it. Form drag comes from an object's shape, skin friction drag from air rubbing along the surface, induced drag is a by-product of producing lift, and wave drag comes from shock waves near the speed of sound.

questions.stem: Which airspeed is indicated airspeed corrected for instrument and installation (position) error?
questions.explain: IAS corrected for instrument and position error is CAS. CAS corrected for compressibility is EAS; correcting for altitude and nonstandard temperature (air density) gives TAS, the speed through the air; groundspeed is TAS adjusted for wind; Mach is TAS as a fraction of the local speed of sound.

questions.stem: Under the standard weather flight categories, which conditions are classed as IFR?
options: Ceiling 500 to below 1,000 feet and/or visibility 1 to below 3 statute miles
Ceiling 1,000 to 3,000 feet and/or visibility 3 to 5 statute miles
Ceiling below 500 feet and/or visibility below 1 statute mile
Ceiling below 1,500 feet and visibility below 5 statute miles
Ceiling above 3,000 feet and visibility above 5 statute miles
questions.explain: IFR is a ceiling of 500 to below 1,000 ft and/or visibility of 1 to below 3 SM. Ceiling 1,000–3,000 ft and/or 3–5 SM is marginal VFR (MVFR); below 500 ft and/or below 1 SM is low IFR (LIFR); above 3,000 ft and above 5 SM is VFR.

questions.stem: While taxiing, you receive a steady red light signal from the control tower. This means
options: Taxi clear of the runway in use
Return to the starting point on the airport
questions.explain: On the ground, steady red means stop. Flashing red means taxi clear of the runway in use, flashing white means return to the starting point, steady green means cleared for takeoff, and alternating red and green means exercise extreme caution.

questions.stem: Before entering Class B airspace, a VFR pilot must
options: receive an explicit ATC clearance to enter
only establish two-way radio communication with ATC
questions.explain: Class B requires an ATC clearance ('cleared into the Class B airspace'), plus an operating Mode C/ADS-B transponder. Two-way radio contact alone is enough for Class C and D, but not B. VFR flight in Class B needs no IFR plan or instrument rating, and 1200 is just the VFR code.

questions.stem: What are the VFR visibility and cloud-clearance minimums in Class B airspace?
options: 3 statute miles; 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontally
5 statute miles; 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 1 statute mile horizontally
3 statute miles; 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 3,000 feet horizontally
questions.explain: Because ATC separates all traffic in Class B, the VFR minimum is 3 SM visibility and clear of clouds. 3 SM with 500 below/1,000 above/2,000 horizontal is Class C, D and E below 10,000 ft MSL; 5 SM with 1,000/1,000/1 SM is Class E at or above 10,000 ft MSL; 1 SM clear of clouds is Class G by day at low altitude.

questions.stem: The attitude indicator and heading indicator hold their reference because of which gyroscopic property?
questions.explain: A spinning gyro resists changes to the orientation of its spin axis (rigidity in space), so the attitude and heading indicators stay fixed while the aircraft moves around them. Precession, the gyro's response to a force applied 90° ahead in rotation, is what drives the turn coordinator. Magnetic dip affects the compass, not gyros.

questions.stem: An airport's rotating beacon alternates white and green flashes. What type of airport is it?
options: An airport that is closed to traffic
questions.explain: White and green alternating is a lighted civil land airport. A military airport shows a dual-peaked (two quick) white flash between greens, a water airport white and yellow, and a heliport green, yellow and white.

questions.stem: An aircraft weighs 2,000 lb with its center of gravity 40 inches aft of the datum. A 100 lb bag is loaded 80 inches aft of the datum. Where is the new CG?
questions.explain: Total moment = 2,000 × 40 + 100 × 80 = 80,000 + 8,000 = 88,000 lb-in; total weight = 2,100 lb; CG = 88,000 ÷ 2,100 = 41.9 in. 60.0 averages the two arms, 44.0 divides by the old weight, 38.1 forgets the bag's moment, and 40.0 assumes the CG doesn't move.

questions.stem: At standard rate, how long does a 270° turn take?
questions.explain: A standard-rate turn is 3° per second, 360° in 2 minutes (the '2 MIN' on the turn coordinator). 270 ÷ 3 = 90 seconds. 120 seconds is a full 360° turn, 60 seconds is 180°, and 45 seconds would need double standard rate.

questions.stem: In the USAF designation KC-135, what does the 'K' indicate?
options: The aircraft is modified for aerial refueling (tanker)
The aircraft is a cargo transport
The aircraft first served in the Korean War
The aircraft is fitted for electronic warfare
The aircraft is a special operations variant
questions.explain: In the US military designation system the letter before the basic mission letter is a modified mission: K = tanker. C, the basic mission, is cargo/transport, so a KC-135 is a transport airframe modified for aerial refueling. Electronic warfare is E, and special operations is M (as in MC-130).

questions.stem: Which was the USAF's first operational stealth aircraft, used in combat over Panama in 1989 and in the 1991 Gulf War?
questions.explain: The F-117A became operational in 1983 and first saw combat in Panama (1989), then struck Baghdad in Desert Storm (1991). The B-2A entered service in 1997 and the F-22A in 2005; the SR-71 was a fast high-altitude reconnaissance aircraft and the B-1B a variable-sweep bomber, not stealth designs of that kind.

questions.stem: An airplane is in a steady, power-reduced descent at a constant airspeed. Which statement about the forces along the flight path is correct?
options: Drag exceeds thrust, and a forward component of weight makes up the difference.
Thrust equals drag, and lift is less than weight, which is what makes it descend.
Weight exceeds lift by the same amount that thrust exceeds drag.
Drag exceeds thrust, so the airplane is decelerating along the flight path.
Lift equals weight and thrust equals drag, exactly as in level flight.
questions.explain: In a steady descent the forces are balanced along the flight path, but part of the weight now acts forward along that path, so drag can exceed thrust without the airplane slowing down (PHAK Ch. 5). Lift is slightly less than weight because some weight is carried along the path, but the reduced lift is not what drives the descent. If drag exceeded thrust with no forward weight component the airplane would decelerate, which contradicts the constant airspeed.

questions.stem: In a level, coordinated turn, what force actually turns the airplane?
options: The horizontal component of lift, produced by banking the wings.
The rudder, which yaws the nose around toward the new heading.
Centrifugal force, which pulls the airplane toward the inside of the turn.
The vertical component of lift, which increases as the bank steepens.
Thrust, which is redirected sideways when the airplane is banked.
questions.explain: Banking tilts the lift vector, and its horizontal component pulls the airplane toward the center of the turn (PHAK Ch. 5). The rudder only keeps the turn coordinated; it does not create the turning force. Centrifugal force acts toward the outside of the turn and is balanced by the horizontal lift component, while the vertical component must equal weight to keep the turn level.

questions.stem: At the same angle of attack and air density, an airplane accelerates from 100 to 150 knots true airspeed. The lift produced by the wing becomes about
questions.explain: In the lift equation, L = CL x 1/2 x density x V squared x S, so with CL, density and wing area unchanged, lift varies with the square of airspeed: (150/100) squared = 2.25. Taking the speed ratio directly gives 1.5, and its square root gives 1.22. Cubing the ratio gives 3.38, and 0.44 is the inverse of the correct answer.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how a wing produces lift?
options: Air speeds up over the curved upper surface, lowering its pressure, while the wing turns the airflow downward and is pushed up in reaction.
Air over the longer upper surface must rejoin the lower air at the trailing edge at the same time, so it speeds up to make lift.
Only Newton's third law matters, because air striking the lower surface creates all the lift and pressure plays no part.
Higher pressure builds on the upper surface and pushes the wing up, because the air there is compressed by the camber.
The fuselage and horizontal tail produce most of the lift, while the wings mainly provide lateral stability.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 4) uses both explanations together: Bernoulli's principle, where faster flow over the upper surface means lower pressure, and Newton's third law, where the wing deflects air downward and the air pushes the wing up. They describe the same flow, and the wings are the airplane's main lift-producing surfaces. The equal-transit-time idea is a well-known myth, since air over the top actually reaches the trailing edge first, and the pressure is lower, not higher, on the upper surface.

questions.stem: A wing's chord line is pitched 8 degrees above the horizon while the airplane climbs along a flight path 3 degrees above the horizon. What is the wing's angle of attack?
options: 5 degrees, the angle between the chord line and the relative wind.
11 degrees, the sum of the pitch and the climb angle.
8 degrees, because angle of attack equals the pitch of the chord line.
3 degrees, because angle of attack equals the flight path angle.
0 degrees, because the climb is steady and unaccelerated.
questions.explain: The relative wind is parallel and opposite to the flight path, so it arrives 3 degrees above the horizon; the angle between it and the chord line is 8 minus 3 = 5 degrees. Adding the angles gives 11, which treats the relative wind as coming from below the horizon. Pitch attitude and flight path angle are each only part of the picture, which is why angle of attack and pitch are not the same thing.

questions.stem: In straight-and-level, unaccelerated flight, which statement about the four forces is correct?
options: Lift equals and opposes weight, and thrust equals and opposes drag.
Lift equals and opposes drag, and thrust equals and opposes weight.
Lift exceeds weight slightly, and thrust equals and opposes drag.
Lift equals and opposes weight, and thrust exceeds drag to hold airspeed.
Thrust equals the sum of lift and drag, and weight equals lift.
questions.explain: In unaccelerated level flight the forces are in equilibrium: lift acts upward against weight and thrust acts forward against drag, and each pair is equal (PHAK Ch. 5). Pairing lift with drag or thrust with weight mixes up the directions in which the forces act. If lift exceeded weight the airplane would accelerate upward, and if thrust exceeded drag it would speed up, so neither describes steady flight.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly classifies the types of drag?
options: Form, skin friction and interference drag are parasite drag; induced drag exists only because the wing produces lift.
Induced drag is a form of parasite drag, caused by rivets and surface roughness.
Skin friction and induced drag both come from lift, while form drag is parasite drag.
Interference drag is induced drag, because it forms where the wing joins the fuselage.
Parasite drag is produced only when the wing is generating lift, and disappears in a zero-lift dive.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 5) divides total drag into parasite drag, made up of form, interference and skin friction drag, which come from moving any shape through the air, and induced drag, which is a by-product of producing lift. In a zero-lift condition induced drag disappears but parasite drag remains. Surface roughness causes skin friction, and the wing-fuselage junction causes interference drag, both of which are parasite drag.

questions.stem: The critical Mach number of an airfoil is the
options: free-stream Mach number at which airflow somewhere on the airfoil first reaches Mach 1.
Mach number at which the entire airplane first flies faster than sound.
free-stream Mach number at which shock waves first form ahead of the leading edge.
Mach number at which induced drag reaches its maximum value.
highest Mach number the airplane is certificated to fly.
questions.explain: Air speeds up over the curved upper surface, so local flow reaches Mach 1 while the airplane is still subsonic; the free-stream Mach number at which this first happens is the critical Mach number, and beyond it shock waves and wave drag build rapidly. The airplane itself is not supersonic at that point. A bow shock ahead of the leading edge appears only in supersonic flight, and the certificated limit is the maximum operating Mach number, MMO.

questions.stem: In level flight at constant weight, an airplane doubles its airspeed. Compared with before, induced drag and parasite drag become about
options: one quarter as great, and four times as great.
one half as great, and twice as great.
four times as great, and one quarter as great.
four times as great, and four times as great.
one quarter as great, and twice as great.
questions.explain: Parasite drag rises with the square of airspeed, so doubling speed makes it about four times as great. Induced drag varies inversely with the square of airspeed in level flight, because the required angle of attack falls, so it drops to about one quarter. Swapping the two relationships is the usual trap, and a factor of two applies neither.

questions.stem: An airplane's maximum lift-to-drag ratio is 12:1. After an engine failure at 5,000 feet AGL in still air, flown at the L/D max airspeed, about how far can it glide?
questions.explain: A 12:1 glide ratio gives 12 feet forward for every foot of altitude lost: 5,000 x 12 = 60,000 feet, and 60,000 / 6,076 is about 9.9 nautical miles (about 11.4 statute miles). Twelve nautical miles reads the ratio as nautical miles per thousand feet. Flying faster or slower than the L/D max speed increases total drag and shortens the glide.

questions.stem: An airplane stalls at 60 knots with its wings level. In a level, coordinated 70 degree bank turn, its stall speed is about
questions.explain: A level 70 degree bank needs a load factor of 1 / cos 70, about 2.92 G, and stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor: 60 x 1.71 is about 103 knots. Multiplying by the load factor itself gives 175 knots. 85 knots is the 60 degree bank figure, 73 knots uses the 45 to 50 degree range, and 60 knots ignores load factor.

questions.stem: A normal-category airplane, limited to +3.8 G, enters a level, coordinated 75 degree bank turn. What is the load factor, and is it within the limit?
options: About 3.9 G, which exceeds the +3.8 G limit.
About 3.7 G, which is just within the +3.8 G limit.
About 3.9 G, which is within the +4.4 G normal-category limit.
About 2.0 G, which is well within the +3.8 G limit.
About 1.0 G, because a level turn does not add load.
questions.explain: Load factor in a level turn is 1 / cos of the bank angle: 1 / cos 75 = 3.86 G, which is above the +3.8 G normal-category limit (PHAK Ch. 5). 3.7 G comes from using the tangent instead of the secant. +4.4 G is the utility-category limit, 2.0 G is the 60 degree bank value, and a level turn always raises the load factor above 1 G.

questions.stem: An airplane's design maneuvering speed (VA) is 105 knots at its maximum gross weight of 2,400 lb. At 1,950 lb, VA is about
questions.explain: VA decreases with the square root of weight: 105 x the square root of (1,950 / 2,400) is about 95 knots. A lighter airplane accelerates more for a given lift force, so it reaches its limit load at a lower speed and needs a lower VA. 116 knots inverts the ratio, 85 knots scales by weight without the square root, and 105 knots ignores the weight change.

questions.stem: An airplane stalls at 55 knots in wings-level, 1 G flight. If the pilot abruptly pulls to 4 G, at what airspeed can the wing stall?
questions.explain: Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor: the square root of 4 is 2, so 55 x 2 = 110 knots. Multiplying by the load factor itself gives 220 knots. 78 knots is the 2 G figure and 95 knots the 3 G figure, while 55 knots applies only at 1 G; this is the accelerated stall that can happen well above the published stall speed.

questions.stem: In a fully developed spin to the left, which statement is correct?
options: Both wings are stalled, and the left, descending wing is stalled more deeply.
Only the left wing is stalled, while the right wing is still producing lift.
Both wings are stalled, and the right, rising wing is stalled more deeply.
Neither wing is stalled; the rotation comes from rudder alone.
Both wings are stalled equally, so there is no rolling moment.
questions.explain: A spin is an aggravated stall with autorotation: both wings are stalled, but the descending wing meets the relative wind at a higher angle of attack, so it is more deeply stalled and produces less lift and more drag (PHAK Ch. 5). That imbalance keeps the airplane rolling and yawing toward the low wing. If one wing were still flying normally it would be an incipient spiral or roll, not a developed spin.

questions.stem: Compared with the same airplane loaded with its CG near the aft limit, loading it near the forward CG limit makes its stall speed
options: higher, because the tail must push down harder, adding to the load on the wing.
lower, because the airplane becomes more stable and less likely to stall.
the same, because stall speed depends only on gross weight.
higher, because the wing's critical angle of attack is reduced.
lower, because the tail's down-force adds lift to the wing.
questions.explain: With a forward CG, the horizontal tail must produce more downward force to hold the nose up, and the wing must carry that extra down-load as well as the weight, so stall speed rises (PHAK Ch. 10). Greater stability does not lower the stall speed. The critical angle of attack does not change with CG, and tail down-force adds to the wing's load rather than to its lift.

questions.stem: Many wings have washout, twisted so the tips meet the air at a lower angle of attack than the roots. The purpose is to
options: make the root stall first, so the ailerons stay effective near the stall.
make the tips stall first, so the nose drops quickly at the stall.
reduce parasite drag at cruise by making the tips thinner.
increase the wing's critical angle of attack at the root.
reduce the tendency of the airplane to yaw in a slip.
questions.explain: Washout lowers the angle of attack at the tips, so the root reaches its critical angle first and the stall progresses outward, leaving the outboard ailerons in unstalled air for roll control (PHAK Ch. 5). A tip-first stall is what designers try to avoid, because it can cause a sudden wing drop. Washout does not change the critical angle of attack, which is a property of the airfoil.

questions.stem: After a gust pitches an airplane's nose up, it immediately starts back toward its trimmed attitude, but each overshoot is larger than the last. Its longitudinal stability is
options: positive static stability with negative dynamic stability.
negative static stability with positive dynamic stability.
positive static stability with positive dynamic stability.
neutral static stability with negative dynamic stability.
negative static stability with neutral dynamic stability.
questions.explain: Static stability is the initial tendency after a disturbance: returning toward equilibrium is positive static stability (PHAK Ch. 5). Dynamic stability describes the motion over time, and oscillations that grow are negative dynamic stability. Positive dynamic stability would make the oscillations die out, and negative static stability would make the nose keep moving away from trim from the start.

questions.stem: Stability about the vertical axis, the tendency to weathervane back into the relative wind after a yaw, comes mainly from
options: the vertical stabilizer and side area located behind the CG.
the wing dihedral, which raises the lower wing.
the horizontal stabilizer and its tail-down force.
a forward CG position within the approved range.
the rudder, which the pilot deflects against the yaw.
questions.explain: Directional stability works like a weathervane: the vertical fin and fuselage side area aft of the CG are pushed back into line with the relative wind when the airplane yaws (PHAK Ch. 5). Dihedral provides lateral stability about the longitudinal axis, and the horizontal tail and CG mainly affect longitudinal stability. The rudder is a control the pilot moves, not a source of inherent stability.

questions.stem: An airplane has strong directional stability but weak lateral (dihedral) stability. It tends to suffer from
options: spiral instability, slowly steepening into a spiral after a disturbance.
Dutch roll, a coupled yawing and rolling oscillation.
phugoid oscillations in pitch and airspeed.
adverse yaw whenever the ailerons are used.
a tendency to snap into a spin at cruise speed.
questions.explain: When directional stability is strong relative to lateral stability, a yaw that follows a bank makes the outer wing faster, so the bank steepens and the airplane winds into a spiral (PHAK Ch. 5). Dutch roll is the opposite case, with strong lateral stability compared with directional stability. Phugoid motion is a longitudinal oscillation, and adverse yaw comes from aileron drag, not from the balance of stability.

questions.stem: The rudder is a movable surface hinged to the
options: vertical stabilizer, and with the elevator, stabilizers and trim tabs it forms part of the empennage.
horizontal stabilizer, and with the elevator it forms part of the empennage.
vertical stabilizer, but it is grouped with the wings rather than the empennage.
wing's trailing edge, inboard of the ailerons, and moves in the opposite direction.
vertical stabilizer, and with the ailerons and flaps it forms part of the empennage.
questions.explain: The empennage, or tail section, includes the vertical stabilizer with its rudder and the horizontal stabilizer with its elevator, plus any trim tabs (PHAK Ch. 3). The rudder is hinged to the rear of the vertical stabilizer and yaws the airplane about the vertical axis. The elevator, not the rudder, is hinged to the horizontal stabilizer, and ailerons and flaps are wing surfaces.

questions.stem: An airplane is trimmed for level cruise. The pilot adds power and accelerates to a higher airspeed while holding altitude. Without retrimming, the pilot must hold
options: forward elevator pressure, and should trim nose-down to relieve it.
back elevator pressure, and should trim nose-up to relieve it.
forward elevator pressure, and should trim nose-up to relieve it.
no elevator pressure, because trim holds an attitude, not a speed.
back elevator pressure, and should trim nose-down to relieve it.
questions.explain: Trim sets the airplane to fly at a particular angle of attack and so a particular airspeed; at the higher speed the tail produces more down-force and the nose wants to rise, so the pilot must push forward to hold altitude. Trimming nose-down removes that pressure. Trim holds an airspeed rather than an attitude, which is why a speed change always needs new trim.

questions.stem: Leading-edge slots and slats increase a wing's maximum lift mainly by
options: ducting high-energy air over the upper surface, raising the critical angle of attack.
increasing the wing's camber and area, lowering the critical angle of attack.
spoiling lift near the tips so the root stalls first.
reducing the angle of attack at the leading edge at all airspeeds.
increasing airspeed over the lower surface to raise pressure there.
questions.explain: A slot or extended slat lets high-pressure air from below the wing flow through a gap onto the upper surface, re-energizing the boundary layer and delaying separation, so the wing can reach a higher angle of attack before stalling (PHAK Ch. 6). Trailing-edge flaps increase camber and sometimes area, and generally lower the critical angle of attack. Stall strips, not slots, are used to make the root stall first.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a device and its main effect is correct?
options: Wing flaps: increase both lift and drag, allowing a steeper approach at a lower airspeed.
Spoilers: increase both lift and drag, allowing a steeper approach at a lower airspeed.
Winglets: increase both lift and drag so the airplane can land in a shorter distance.
Vortex generators: create larger wingtip vortices to reduce parasite drag in cruise.
Wing flaps: reduce induced drag in cruise by weakening the wingtip vortices.
questions.explain: Extending flaps increases camber, so the wing makes more lift at a given airspeed and much more drag, which lowers the stall speed and steepens the approach without a speed increase (PHAK Ch. 6). Spoilers do the opposite to lift: they destroy it and add drag. Winglets reduce induced drag by weakening the tip vortices, and vortex generators make small vortices that energize the boundary layer and delay flow separation.

questions.stem: On an airplane that uses roll spoilers, the pilot raises the spoiler on the right wing only. The airplane will
options: roll right, and the added drag yaws the nose right, toward the turn.
roll left, because the right wing's extra drag pulls it back.
roll right, while adverse yaw swings the nose left.
pitch down, with no rolling motion, because only lift is reduced.
roll left, and the reduced drag yaws the nose right.
questions.explain: A raised spoiler destroys lift and adds drag on its own wing, so that wing drops and the airplane rolls right; the extra drag on the same wing also yaws the nose right, toward the turn (PHAK Ch. 6). This is why spoilers used for roll do not produce adverse yaw the way a down-going aileron does. Raising a spoiler on one wing only does not give a pure pitch change.

questions.stem: In a tailwheel airplane whose propeller turns clockwise as seen from the cockpit, the pilot pushes forward to raise the tail during the takeoff roll. Gyroscopic precession makes the nose
options: yaw left, because the force on the top of the disc acts 90 degrees later on the right side.
yaw right, because the force on the top of the disc acts on the left side.
pitch up, because precession resists the change in attitude.
yaw left, because the spiraling slipstream strikes the tail harder.
roll right, opposite to the engine's torque reaction.
questions.explain: Raising the tail tilts the propeller disc as if a forward force were applied to its top; precession makes the force appear 90 degrees later in the direction of rotation, at the right side of the disc, so the nose yaws left (PHAK Ch. 5). Getting the 90 degree shift in the wrong direction gives a right yaw. The slipstream also yaws the nose left, but that is a separate tendency, and precession produces yaw here, not a pitch-up.

questions.stem: In a single-engine airplane whose propeller turns clockwise as seen from the cockpit, the spiraling slipstream yaws the nose left because it
options: wraps around the fuselage and strikes the left side of the vertical stabilizer.
strikes the right side of the vertical stabilizer.
pushes the left wing down, rolling the airplane to the left.
makes the descending blade take a bigger bite of air.
acts on the spinning propeller 90 degrees ahead of the force.
questions.explain: The propeller's slipstream rotates in the same direction as the propeller, corkscrewing around the fuselage and hitting the left side of the vertical fin, which pushes the tail right and the nose left (PHAK Ch. 5). A bigger bite by the descending blade is P-factor, and a force acting 90 degrees ahead is gyroscopic precession. Rolling to the left is the torque reaction, not slipstream.

questions.stem: Compared with a cruise propeller on the same airplane, a fixed-pitch climb propeller has
options: a lower blade angle, giving higher RPM and better takeoff and climb but less efficient cruise.
a higher blade angle, giving higher RPM and better takeoff and climb performance.
a lower blade angle, giving lower RPM and better high-speed cruise efficiency.
a higher blade angle, giving lower RPM and better takeoff and climb performance.
the same blade angle, with longer blades that turn more slowly.
questions.explain: A climb propeller has a lower pitch, so it meets less resistance, lets the engine reach higher RPM and develop more power at low airspeed, which helps takeoff and climb (PHAK Ch. 7). The trade-off is poorer efficiency at cruise, where a higher-pitch cruise propeller does better. A higher blade angle loads the engine more and lowers RPM at low speed, which is the cruise propeller's characteristic.

questions.stem: In a four-stroke reciprocating engine, during which strokes are both the intake and exhaust valves closed?
questions.explain: The cycle runs intake, compression, power, exhaust (PHAK Ch. 7). The intake valve is open on the intake stroke and the exhaust valve is open on the exhaust stroke, but both stay closed during compression and power so the charge can be compressed and the burning gases can push the piston down. Any answer that includes the intake or exhaust stroke has a valve open during it.

questions.stem: In a carbureted airplane, which conditions give the greatest risk of carburetor ice?
options: Outside air 60 degrees F (16 degrees C), relative humidity 90 percent, descending at reduced power.
Outside air 15 degrees F (-9 degrees C), relative humidity 30 percent, cruising at high power.
Outside air 95 degrees F (35 degrees C), relative humidity 15 percent, climbing at full power.
Outside air 40 degrees F (4 degrees C), relative humidity 20 percent, descending at reduced power.
Outside air 30 degrees F (-1 degree C), relative humidity 25 percent, cruising at high power.
questions.explain: Fuel vaporization and the venturi's pressure drop can cool the intake air far below the outside temperature, so carburetor ice is most likely between about 20 and 70 degrees F (-7 to 21 degrees C) with high humidity or visible moisture, and especially at low power, where the partly closed throttle adds a further restriction (PHAK Ch. 7). Ice is still possible at warmer temperatures, even 70 to 80 degrees F or higher, when the air is very humid. Dry air carries little moisture to freeze, so the low-humidity options are low risk even when the temperature is near freezing.

questions.stem: During a long, full-power climb on a hot day, the pilot suspects detonation. Which action is appropriate?
options: Enrich the mixture, reduce power, and lower the nose to increase airspeed and cooling.
Lean the mixture to raise power and clear the detonation.
Raise the nose to slow down and reduce the load on the engine.
Apply full carburetor heat to raise the intake temperature.
Keep full power and close the cowl flaps to stabilize temperatures.
questions.explain: Detonation is an explosive, uncontrolled burning of the charge, usually caused by high cylinder temperatures, a lean mixture or too low a fuel grade (PHAK Ch. 7). A richer mixture, less power and more cooling airflow from a lower pitch attitude and open cowl flaps all reduce cylinder temperature. Leaning, slowing down, adding carburetor heat or closing the cowl flaps all raise the temperatures that cause it.

questions.stem: Which engine type does the PHAK describe as most efficient at speeds of about 250 to 400 mph and altitudes of about 18,000 to 30,000 feet?
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 7) notes that turboprops are most efficient at speeds between about 250 and 400 mph and altitudes between about 18,000 and 30,000 feet, and they also perform well at the low speeds needed for takeoff and landing. Turbofans are most efficient at higher speeds, roughly 400 to 600 mph, and turbojets at still higher speeds and altitudes. A turboshaft drives a rotor or other equipment rather than producing thrust for airplane cruise.

questions.stem: Modern airliners cruising at about Mach 0.8 almost all use high-bypass turbofan engines rather than turbojets, turboprops or pistons, mainly because a turbofan
options: moves a large mass of air at a modest speed increase, giving better fuel efficiency and less noise at that speed.
moves a small mass of air at a very high speed, which is most efficient at Mach 0.8.
uses a propeller, which stays efficient at speeds above about Mach 0.8.
burns avgas, which is cheaper and more widely available than jet fuel.
drives its fan with a reciprocating engine, combining piston economy with jet thrust.
questions.explain: A turbofan's large fan accelerates a big mass of bypass air only moderately, which is more propulsively efficient and quieter than a turbojet's small, very fast jet at airliner cruise speeds (PHAK Ch. 7). A turbojet is most efficient at higher speeds, and propellers lose efficiency well below Mach 0.8, which limits turboprops to slower aircraft. Piston engines lack the power-to-weight ratio for this role, and turbofans burn jet fuel, not avgas.

questions.stem: A fuel sample drained from an airplane's tank is green. Which fuel grade does this indicate?
options: Jet A, the kerosene-based turbine fuel.
Automotive gasoline approved under an STC.
questions.explain: Aviation gasoline is dyed by grade: 80 is red, 100 is green and 100LL is blue (PHAK Ch. 7). Jet A is clear or straw-coloured and smells of kerosene, which is why checking colour and smell guards against misfueling. Green fuel is therefore grade 100, not the low-lead blue fuel most piston airplanes now use.

questions.stem: Under the current GAMA definition, an airplane's basic empty weight includes
options: unusable fuel, full engine oil and full hydraulic fluid, but not usable fuel, crew or payload.
usable fuel, unusable fuel and full engine oil, but not crew or payload.
unusable fuel and the required crew, but not engine oil or payload.
only the airframe, engine and fixed equipment, with no fluids at all.
unusable fuel, full engine oil, the pilot and the baggage.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 10) defines basic empty weight as the standard empty weight plus optional equipment, including unusable fuel, full operating fluids such as hydraulic fluid, and full engine oil. Usable fuel, crew, passengers and baggage are added later to reach gross weight, which therefore includes the pilots and falls during flight as fuel burns. Older definitions counted only undrainable oil, but no definition includes usable fuel or occupants.

questions.stem: An airplane has these loads (weight, arm): empty airplane 1,600 lb at 38.0 in; front seats 340 lb at 37.0 in; rear seat 160 lb at 73.0 in; 40 gal of 100LL at 48.0 in; baggage 60 lb at 95.0 in. Where is the loaded CG?
options: About 42.6 inches aft of the datum.
About 58.2 inches aft of the datum.
About 42.0 inches aft of the datum.
About 41.3 inches aft of the datum.
About 44.8 inches aft of the datum.
questions.explain: The fuel weighs 40 x 6 = 240 lb, so the total weight is 2,400 lb; the moments are 60,800 + 12,580 + 11,680 + 11,520 + 5,700 = 102,280 lb-in, and 102,280 / 2,400 = 42.6 inches. 58.2 is the plain average of the five arms. 42.0 leaves out the fuel and 41.3 leaves out the baggage, which shows why every item must be included.

questions.stem: An airplane weighs 5,000 lb with its CG at 82.0 inches, but the aft limit is 80.0 inches. How much baggage must be moved from the aft compartment (arm 150 in) to the forward compartment (arm 30 in) to bring the CG to the limit?
questions.explain: For a weight shift, weight moved = total weight x CG change / distance moved: 5,000 x 2.0 / (150 - 30) = 10,000 / 120, about 83 lb. 67 lb divides by the aft arm, 150, and 333 lb divides by the forward arm, 30, instead of by the distance the bags travel. The total weight does not change when weight is only shifted, so it stays 5,000 lb in the formula.

questions.stem: An airplane weighs 3,200 lb with its CG at 45.0 inches. A 200 lb passenger seated at 90.0 inches gets out. What is the new CG?
questions.explain: The original moment is 3,200 x 45.0 = 144,000 lb-in; removing 200 x 90.0 = 18,000 lb-in leaves 126,000 lb-in, and 126,000 / 3,000 lb = 42.0 inches. 39.4 inches divides by the old weight instead of the new one. 47.6 inches adds the passenger instead of removing them, and the CG must move forward because weight left from aft of the CG.

questions.stem: An airplane's maximum takeoff weight is 2,550 lb and its basic empty weight is 1,520 lb. The pilot and two passengers weigh 170, 180 and 200 lb, with 50 lb of baggage. What is the most 100LL fuel, in whole gallons, that can be loaded?
questions.explain: Occupants and baggage total 600 lb, so 2,550 - 1,520 - 600 = 430 lb is left for fuel, and 430 / 6 lb per gallon = 71.7 gallons. Rounding up to 72 gallons (432 lb) would put the airplane 2 lb over its maximum takeoff weight. 64 gallons uses Jet A's 6.7 lb per gallon, 80 gallons forgets the baggage, and 105 gallons leaves out the heaviest passenger.

questions.stem: An airplane takes off at 2,400 lb with its CG at 42.0 inches. During the flight it burns 45 gallons of 100LL from tanks at 48.0 inches. Where is the CG at landing?
questions.explain: The fuel burned weighs 45 x 6 = 270 lb with a moment of 270 x 48.0 = 12,960 lb-in; the landing moment is 100,800 - 12,960 = 87,840 lb-in, and 87,840 / 2,130 lb is about 41.2 inches. Because the tanks are aft of the CG, burning fuel moves the CG forward, so 42.8 inches has the shift in the wrong direction. 36.6 inches divides by the takeoff weight, and 42.6 inches adds the fuel instead of removing it.

questions.stem: A helicopter's main rotor tips turn at 400 knots, and it flies forward at 100 knots. What airspeeds do the advancing and retreating blade tips meet?
options: 400 knots on both, because rotor RPM is constant.
questions.explain: Forward speed adds to the rotational speed on the advancing side and subtracts from it on the retreating side: 400 + 100 = 500 knots and 400 - 100 = 300 knots. This difference is the cause of dissymmetry of lift, which blade flapping and cyclic feathering compensate for (Helicopter Flying Handbook). Constant RPM keeps the rotational part the same, but the forward speed still changes the relative wind on each side.

questions.stem: A helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise as seen from above is flown fast in turbulence at high gross weight. It develops a low-frequency vibration. If retreating blade stall follows, the helicopter will
options: pitch nose-up and roll to the left.
pitch nose-down and roll to the right.
pitch nose-up and roll to the right.
yaw sharply right with no pitch or roll.
pitch nose-down and roll to the left.
questions.explain: With counterclockwise rotation, the blades advance on the right and retreat on the left, and at high forward speed the retreating blade can exceed its critical angle of attack (Helicopter Flying Handbook). Because of gyroscopic precession and the loss of lift on that side, the classic signs are low-frequency vibration, the nose pitching up and a roll toward the retreating side, which here is the left. High speed, high weight, high density altitude, turbulence and steep turns all make it more likely.

questions.stem: As a helicopter accelerates from a hover through about 16 to 24 knots, it gains effective translational lift because the rotor
options: moves into undisturbed air, reducing induced flow, so it makes more lift for the same power.
begins to autorotate, so the engine needs less power.
flaps its advancing blade down, increasing its angle of attack.
leaves ground effect, so the downwash is no longer restricted.
turns faster, because the governor increases RPM with airspeed.
questions.explain: Translational lift comes from the rotor flying out of its own downwash and tip vortices into clean air; with less induced flow the blades meet the air at a more effective angle of attack, so they produce more lift for the same power (Helicopter Flying Handbook). Leaving ground effect actually costs lift, and the advancing blade flaps up, not down. Rotor RPM is held nearly constant, and the rotor is still engine-driven.

questions.stem: In a steady vertical autorotation, which part of each main rotor blade produces the force that keeps the rotor turning?
options: The driving region, roughly 25 to 70 percent of the radius from the hub.
The driven region near the tips, which produces most of the lift.
The stall region near the hub, where the blade is above its critical angle.
The whole blade equally, because the upward airflow is uniform.
Only the tail rotor, which is driven by the freewheeling unit.
questions.explain: The Helicopter Flying Handbook divides the blade into three regions in autorotation: the driven region near the tips, the driving region from about 25 to 70 percent of the radius, and the stall region near the hub. In the driving region the total aerodynamic force tilts slightly forward of the axis of rotation, which accelerates the rotor. The driven region slows the rotor, the stall region adds drag, and the tail rotor is driven by the main rotor transmission rather than driving anything.

questions.stem: A helicopter is descending almost vertically at about 400 feet per minute, below effective translational lift airspeed and using partial power, when it begins to settle with power (vortex ring state). Which is the recommended recovery?
options: Apply forward cyclic to gain airspeed, and lower the collective if altitude permits.
Raise the collective to full power to stop the descent.
Apply aft cyclic to raise the nose and slow the descent.
Hold the collective steady and apply full left pedal.
Close the throttle and enter a vertical autorotation.
questions.explain: Vortex ring state needs a near-vertical descent of at least about 300 feet per minute, airspeed below effective translational lift and 20 to 100 percent of available power (Helicopter Flying Handbook). Forward cyclic moves the rotor out of its own recirculating vortices, and lowering the collective reduces the vortex strength. Raising the collective is the instinctive trap: it strengthens the vortices and increases the sink rate.

questions.stem: A helicopter with a fully articulated rotor touches down hard on one wheel and starts a rapidly increasing rocking oscillation. Rotor RPM is in the normal operating range. What should the pilot do?
options: Lift off to a hover immediately, then land again once the rotor is back in balance.
Close the throttle and lower the collective fully, holding the helicopter on the ground.
Apply cyclic opposite the rocking to damp the oscillation.
Hold the controls steady and wait for the landing gear dampers to stop it.
Apply full pedal to yaw the helicopter out of the oscillation.
questions.explain: This is ground resonance: a hard one-wheel or one-skid contact throws the blades out of phase, and the rotor's off-centre mass couples with the bouncing landing gear (Helicopter Flying Handbook). If rotor RPM is normal, lifting off breaks the contact with the ground and lets the blades realign. Closing the throttle and lowering the collective is the action only when RPM is too low to lift off, and cyclic or pedal inputs on the ground usually make it worse.

questions.stem: In a hover, the pilot of a helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise as seen from above raises the collective. To hold the heading, the pilot must
options: add left pedal, increasing tail-rotor pitch to counter the added torque that yaws the nose right.
add right pedal, decreasing tail-rotor pitch to counter the added torque that yaws the nose left.
add left pedal, decreasing tail-rotor pitch to counter the added torque that yaws the nose right.
make no pedal input, because the tail rotor's thrust rises with collective automatically.
add right pedal, increasing tail-rotor pitch to counter the added torque that yaws the nose right.
questions.explain: Raising the collective increases main rotor pitch and engine power, so torque reaction turns the fuselage clockwise as seen from above, yawing the nose right on a counterclockwise rotor (Helicopter Flying Handbook). Left pedal increases tail-rotor blade pitch and thrust to stop that yaw. Lowering the collective does the reverse and needs right pedal.

questions.stem: During an autorotation in a helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise as seen from above, the tail rotor
options: keeps turning, driven through the transmission, and right pedal is needed because engine torque is gone.
stops turning, because the freewheeling unit disconnects it with the engine.
keeps turning, driven through the transmission, and extra left pedal is needed for the torque.
stops providing thrust, so heading is held with the cyclic alone.
turns only from the airflow over it, like a windmilling propeller.
questions.explain: The freewheeling unit disconnects the engine from the main rotor, but the tail rotor is driven from the main rotor transmission, so it keeps turning and still gives yaw control (Helicopter Flying Handbook). With no engine torque to counter, the nose tends to yaw left as the collective is lowered, and the pilot applies right pedal. Left pedal is needed for power increases, not for autorotation.

questions.stem: Which set lists the three major flight controls of a single-rotor helicopter, as the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook names them?
options: The cyclic, the collective and the anti-torque pedals.
The cyclic, the collective and the throttle.
The collective, the throttle and the governor.
The cyclic, the anti-torque pedals and the governor.
The cyclic, the collective, the throttle and the governor.
questions.explain: The Helicopter Flying Handbook lists the cyclic, which tilts the rotor disc, the collective, which changes the pitch of all main rotor blades together, and the anti-torque pedals, which control tail-rotor pitch and yaw, as the flight controls. The throttle controls engine power to hold rotor RPM, often through a correlator and governor that adjust it automatically. They manage the engine rather than fly the helicopter, so including them is the trap.

questions.stem: Compared with a conventional tail, a T-tail places the horizontal stabilizer on top of the vertical fin. A known disadvantage of this design is that the horizontal tail
options: can be blanked by the stalled wing's wake at high angles of attack, risking a deep stall.
sits in the propeller slipstream, which makes elevator forces too heavy in cruise.
adds dihedral effect, which makes the airplane spirally unstable.
is too close to the CG to give any pitch control at all.
increases interference drag at the wing root at cruise speeds.
questions.explain: Mounting the horizontal tail high keeps it out of the propwash and the wing's downwash in normal flight, but at very high angles of attack the turbulent wake of a stalled wing can engulf it, reducing elevator effectiveness and making recovery difficult, which is called a deep stall. Being clear of the slipstream is an effect of the T-tail, not a drawback in cruise. The design does not move the tail closer to the CG or add wing-root interference drag.

questions.stem: Is the turn shown on the turn coordinator coordinated?
options: No; it is a skidding right turn, so ease off right rudder, adding left rudder, to center the ball
No; it is a slipping right turn, so add right rudder to center the ball
No; it is a skidding left turn, so add right rudder to center the ball
No; it is a slipping right turn, so reduce the bank angle to center the ball
Yes; the wing is on the index mark, so it is a coordinated standard-rate turn
questions.explain: The miniature aircraft's wing is on the R index, so the airplane is turning right at standard rate, but the ball has been thrown to the outside of the turn, to the left, which is a skid: too much rudder for the bank, so the rate of turn is too great. 'Step on the ball' means pressing the pedal on the side the ball has moved to, here left rudder, or easing off the right rudder. The wing position shows only rate and direction; only a centred ball shows a coordinated turn, and a slip would put the ball on the inside, to the right.

questions.stem: An airplane is heading 090 degrees and holds the turn shown on the turn coordinator for 45 seconds. Its heading will then be about
questions.explain: The wing is on the L index, which is a standard-rate turn of 3 degrees per second to the left, and the centred ball shows it is coordinated. In 45 seconds the airplane turns 135 degrees left: 090 - 135 = -045, which is 315 degrees. 225 degrees is a 135 degree turn to the right, 045 degrees uses half standard rate, and 270 degrees is a 180 degree turn.

questions.stem: Which statement explains the turn shown on the turn coordinator?
options: It is a slipping right turn: the horizontal component of lift exceeds centrifugal force.
It is a skidding right turn: centrifugal force exceeds the horizontal component of lift.
It is a slipping right turn: centrifugal force exceeds the horizontal component of lift.
It is a skidding left turn: the horizontal component of lift exceeds centrifugal force.
It is a coordinated right turn at half standard rate, with balanced forces.
questions.explain: The wing is about halfway to the R index, so the airplane is turning right at about half standard rate, and the ball has fallen to the inside of the turn, to the right, which is a slip. In a slip the bank is too steep for the rate of turn, so the horizontal component of lift is greater than centrifugal force (PHAK Ch. 8); right rudder will center the ball. In a skid the ball moves outside the turn because centrifugal force is the larger force.

questions.stem: A 3,000 lb airplane holds the bank shown on the attitude indicator in a level, coordinated turn. About how much total lift must its wings produce?
questions.explain: The bank pointer is on the 60 degree mark, and a level 60 degree bank needs a load factor of 1 / cos 60 = 2 G, so the wings must lift 3,000 x 2 = 6,000 lb (PHAK Ch. 5). 4,240 lb is the 45 degree bank value and 3,460 lb the 30 degree value. 5,200 lb uses the tangent of 60 degrees instead of the secant, and 3,000 lb ignores the added load of the turn.

questions.stem: An airplane stalls at 58 knots with its wings level. It holds the bank shown on the attitude indicator in a level, coordinated turn. Its stall speed is about
questions.explain: The bank pointer sits on the 45 degree mark, with the horizon raised on the left side, a left bank; a level 45 degree bank gives a load factor of about 1.41 G, and stall speed rises with its square root, about 1.19: 58 x 1.19 is about 69 knots. 82 knots multiplies by the load factor itself, and 62 knots is the 30 degree bank figure. 116 knots doubles the stall speed, which happens only at 4 G.

questions.stem: The static ports ice over during a climb, and the pilot keeps climbing at the same pitch attitude. What do the vertical speed indicator and airspeed indicator show?
options: The VSI shows zero, and the airspeed reads lower than actual.
The VSI shows zero, and the airspeed reads higher than actual.
The VSI keeps showing the climb, and the airspeed reads correctly.
The VSI shows a descent, and the airspeed reads lower than actual.
The VSI shows zero, and the airspeed reads correctly.
questions.explain: With static pressure trapped, the VSI sees no pressure change and sits at zero, and the altimeter freezes (PHAK Ch. 8). As the airplane climbs, the trapped static pressure is higher than the real outside pressure, so the pitot-minus-static difference shrinks and the airspeed reads low. It reads high only when descending with a blocked static source, and it cannot read correctly because it uses static pressure too.

questions.stem: In a typical light airplane, the suction gauge drops to zero in flight. Which instruments should the pilot now treat as unreliable?
options: The attitude indicator and the heading indicator
The turn coordinator and the attitude indicator
The heading indicator and the magnetic compass
The airspeed indicator and the altimeter
questions.explain: In most light airplanes the attitude and heading indicators are vacuum-driven, while the turn coordinator is electrically driven as a backup (PHAK Ch. 8). A vacuum failure therefore leaves the turn coordinator and magnetic compass working. The airspeed indicator and altimeter are pitot-static instruments and do not depend on the vacuum system.

questions.stem: Precession in a spinning gyro is best described as
options: a tilting of the rotor in which a force acts 90° ahead in the direction of rotation.
the rotor's resistance to any force trying to change its plane of rotation.
a tilting of the rotor in which a force acts 90° behind the point where it is applied.
a tilting of the rotor in which a force acts 180° from the point where it is applied.
the gradual slowing of the rotor caused by bearing friction over time.
questions.explain: When a force is applied to the rim of a spinning rotor, the resulting movement takes effect 90° ahead of the point of application, in the direction of rotation (PHAK Ch. 8). Resistance to a change in the plane of rotation is rigidity in space, the other gyro property. Friction causes unwanted precession, or drift, but precession itself is not simply the rotor slowing down.

questions.stem: In conventional vacuum-driven instruments, in which planes do the gyro rotors of the attitude indicator and the heading indicator spin?
options: Attitude indicator: horizontal plane; heading indicator: vertical plane
Attitude indicator: vertical plane; heading indicator: horizontal plane
Both rotors spin in the horizontal plane
Both rotors spin in the vertical plane
Attitude indicator: horizontal plane; heading indicator: canted 30°
questions.explain: The attitude indicator's rotor spins in a horizontal plane, so rigidity holds it level with the natural horizon as the airplane pitches and banks, while the heading indicator's rotor spins in a vertical plane with the compass card attached (PHAK Ch. 8). Swapping the two is the common error. A canted gimbal belongs to the turn coordinator, not the heading indicator.

questions.stem: At 30°N, a pilot uses only the magnetic compass to make a left turn from east to north. Using the rule of thumb that the lead equals the latitude, the pilot should roll out when the compass reads about
questions.explain: Turning error makes the compass lag on turns toward north in the Northern Hemisphere, so the pilot must roll out early, undershooting north by about the latitude (UNOS: undershoot north, overshoot south). In a left turn the compass reading is decreasing toward 360°, so rolling out 30° early means rolling out at 030°. 330° overshoots north, which is the technique for turns to south, and 360° ignores the lag altogether.

questions.stem: Northerly turning error and acceleration error in the magnetic compass are both caused mainly by
options: magnetic dip, the downward pull of the earth's field on the compass magnets.
deviation, the pull of magnetic fields from the airplane's own equipment.
variation, the angle between true north and magnetic north.
precession of the compass card caused by friction in its pivot.
the compass fluid swirling, which happens only in turbulence.
questions.explain: Away from the magnetic equator, the earth's field lines slope down toward the poles, and this dip makes the compass magnets tilt; when the airplane banks or accelerates, the card is pulled off its true reading, giving turning and acceleration errors (PHAK Ch. 8). Deviation and variation are fixed offsets that do not depend on turning or accelerating. Precession is a gyro effect, and fluid swirl only adds oscillation, not the predictable lead and lag.

questions.stem: An airplane is flying a heading of north. On the magnetic compass card, where will the 3 (030°) appear?
options: Just to the left of the lubber line
Just to the right of the lubber line
At the bottom of the card, opposite the N
It is hidden until the airplane turns east
questions.explain: The pilot reads the compass card from behind, so its numbers run the opposite way to a heading indicator: heading north, 030° appears to the left of the lubber line and 330° to the right. That is why turning toward a number shown on the left requires a right turn. Expecting 030° on the right is the heading-indicator habit that causes wrong-way turns on the compass.

questions.stem: With no wind, the true course is 068° and the variation is 8° E. The compass correction card shows 'For 060 steer 063.' What compass heading should be flown?
questions.explain: Easterly variation is subtracted, so the magnetic heading is 068 - 8 = 060°, and the correction card then says to steer 063° to make good 060° magnetic. 057° applies the deviation in the wrong direction. 079° and 073° add the easterly variation instead of subtracting it, and 071° applies the deviation to the true course without converting to magnetic first.

questions.stem: A pilot cruises at 140 knots indicated at 8,000 feet. Using the rule of thumb that true airspeed is about 2% higher than indicated for every 1,000 feet of altitude, what is the approximate true airspeed?
questions.explain: The rule of thumb adds 2% per 1,000 ft: 8 x 2% = 16%, and 140 x 1.16 = about 162 knots. 151 knots uses only 1% per 1,000 ft, and 118 knots subtracts the correction, as if thinner air made TAS lower. 140 knots ignores the correction, and TAS always exceeds IAS at altitude because the air is less dense.

questions.stem: Below the tropopause in a standard atmosphere, a jet climbs while holding a constant Mach number. Its true airspeed
options: decreases, because the speed of sound falls as the air gets colder.
increases, because the air gets thinner with altitude.
stays the same, because Mach number is fixed.
decreases, because the speed of sound falls as air pressure drops.
increases, because the speed of sound rises with altitude.
questions.explain: Mach number is true airspeed divided by the local speed of sound, and the speed of sound depends only on air temperature. Below the tropopause the temperature falls with height, so the speed of sound falls and TAS at a constant Mach decreases. Pressure on its own does not change the speed of sound, and TAS increasing with altitude is true for a constant indicated airspeed, not a constant Mach.

questions.stem: As an airplane climbs toward its absolute ceiling, what happens to VX and VY?
options: VX increases and VY decreases until they are equal.
VX decreases and VY increases until they are equal.
Both increase, keeping the same gap between them.
Both decrease, keeping the same gap between them.
Neither changes, because both are fixed indicated airspeeds.
questions.explain: The best-angle speed (VX) slowly increases with altitude and the best-rate speed (VY) slowly decreases, and the two meet at the absolute ceiling, where the airplane can no longer climb (PHAK Ch. 11). Reversing the trends is the common mix-up. They are not fixed values, which is why some POHs list VX and VY for different altitudes.

questions.stem: What is the difference between VLO and VLE?
options: VLO is the most for extending or retracting the gear; VLE is the most with the gear down.
VLE is the most for extending or retracting the gear; VLO is the most with the gear down.
VLO is the top of the white arc; VLE is the bottom of the white arc.
VLO is the gear speed for takeoff; VLE is the gear speed for landing.
VLO and VLE are always the same speed, given two names.
questions.explain: VLO is the maximum landing gear operating speed, the fastest the gear may be moving in transit, and VLE is the maximum landing gear extended speed, the fastest the airplane may fly with the gear already down and locked. VLE is often higher than VLO because a gear in transit, with doors open, is more vulnerable. Swapping them is the main trap, and the white arc marks flap speeds, not gear speeds.

questions.stem: Which of these speeds is NOT shown by a colour marking on a light airplane's airspeed indicator?
