options: Stall speed in the landing configuration (VS0)
questions.explain: VA is not marked on the airspeed indicator because it changes with weight; it is found in the POH and sometimes on a placard (PHAK Ch. 8). VNE is the red line, VNO is the top of the green arc, VFE is the top of the white arc, and VS0 is the bottom of the white arc.

questions.stem: Pressure altitude and true altitude are the same when
options: the altimeter is set to the local altimeter setting.
the airplane is flying above 18,000 feet MSL.
the outside air temperature is standard, whatever the pressure.
the airplane is directly over a field at sea level.
questions.explain: Pressure altitude is measured from the standard datum plane of 29.92 inHg, so it equals true altitude only when the atmosphere is standard, with sea-level pressure of 29.92 inHg and a standard temperature lapse (PHAK Ch. 8). The local setting makes indicated altitude close to true altitude, not pressure altitude. Standard temperature alone is not enough if the pressure is nonstandard, and flying above 18,000 feet only means 29.92 is set.

questions.stem: An airport's elevation is 3,200 feet, and the altimeter setting is 29.62 inHg. What is the pressure altitude?
questions.explain: Pressure altitude = field elevation + (29.92 - altimeter setting) x 1,000 ft = 3,200 + (0.30 x 1,000) = 3,500 ft. When the setting is below standard, pressure altitude is higher than field elevation, so subtracting to get 2,900 ft is the main trap. 3,200 ft ignores the correction, and 3,230 ft uses 100 ft per inch instead of about 1,000 ft per inch.

questions.stem: The pressure altitude at an airport is 3,500 feet and the temperature is 25 °C. Using about 120 feet of density altitude for each degree above standard, what is the approximate density altitude?
questions.explain: Standard temperature at 3,500 ft is 15 - (2 x 3.5) = 8 °C, so the air is 17 °C warmer than standard, and 3,500 + (17 x 120) = about 5,540 ft. 4,700 ft compares 25 °C with the sea-level standard of 15 °C, forgetting the lapse rate. 3,500 ft ignores temperature, and 1,500 ft subtracts the correction, although warmer than standard air always raises density altitude.

questions.stem: A pilot departs with the altimeter set to 30.12 inHg and flies into an area where the setting is 29.82 inHg without resetting it. The altimeter shows 5,500 feet. What is the approximate true altitude?
questions.explain: The setting dropped by 0.30 inHg, and each 0.01 inHg is about 10 ft, so the altimeter reads about 300 ft too high and the airplane is near 5,500 - 300 = 5,200 ft (high to low, look out below). 5,800 ft applies the error in the wrong direction, 5,500 ft ignores it, and 5,470 ft uses 100 ft per inch instead of about 1,000 ft. 4,900 ft doubles the error.

questions.stem: The true course is 075°, the wind correction angle is 8° right, the variation is 10° W and the deviation for this heading is -2°. What compass heading should be flown?
questions.explain: Work from true course to compass heading: TC 075 + 8 (right WCA) = TH 083; + 10 (west variation is added) = MH 093; - 2 (deviation) = CH 091. 095° adds the deviation instead of subtracting it, and 071° subtracts the westerly variation. 083° leaves out the wind correction, and 075° applies the wind correction in the wrong direction.

questions.stem: The true course is 090°, the true airspeed is 120 knots and the wind is from 360° at 20 knots. Using the rule that the wind correction angle is about the crosswind divided by the TAS, times 60, what true heading should be flown?
questions.explain: The wind blows straight across the course from the left, so the crosswind is the full 20 knots, and WCA = (20 / 120) x 60 = 10°. The pilot crabs into the wind, to the left, so the true heading is 090 - 10 = 080°. 100° turns away from the wind, 090° ignores it, 070° doubles the correction and 085° halves it.

questions.stem: A leg is 189 nautical miles long, and the expected groundspeed is 135 knots. How long will the leg take?
questions.explain: Time = distance / groundspeed = 189 / 135 = 1.4 hours, and 0.4 hour is 0.4 x 60 = 24 minutes, giving 1 hour 24 minutes. 1 hour 40 minutes reads the decimal 1.4 hours as if it were 1 hour 40 minutes. The other options are arithmetic slips of 10 or 20 minutes.

questions.stem: A day VFR flight will take 2 hours 15 minutes at a cruise fuel burn of 9.5 gallons per hour. Including the minimum day VFR reserve in 14 CFR 91.151, how much usable fuel is needed?
questions.explain: Day VFR requires enough fuel to reach the destination plus 30 minutes at normal cruise, so the total is 2.75 hours x 9.5 gph = about 26.1 gallons. 21.4 gallons has no reserve, and 28.5 gallons uses the 45-minute night VFR reserve. 25.2 gallons treats 2 hours 15 minutes as 2.15 hours, and 30.9 gallons uses a one-hour reserve.

questions.stem: Two points lie on the 60° N parallel, 1° of longitude apart. About how far apart are they?
questions.explain: Meridians converge toward the poles, so a degree of longitude is about 60 NM multiplied by the cosine of the latitude: 60 x cos 60° = 30 NM. 60 NM is correct only at the equator, or for a degree of latitude anywhere. 52 NM uses the cosine of 30° instead, 15 NM halves the answer again, and 69 is the statute-mile value for a degree of latitude.

questions.stem: An airplane flies due north along a meridian from 34° 30' N to 35° 15' N at a groundspeed of 90 knots. About how long does this take?
questions.explain: The change in latitude is 45 minutes of arc, and one minute of latitude is about one nautical mile, so the distance is 45 NM, and 45 / 90 = 0.5 hour = 30 minutes. 50 minutes treats the change as 75 NM by reading 0.75° as 75. 26 and 35 minutes come from wrongly converting between statute and nautical miles, and 45 minutes assumes one mile per minute.

questions.stem: An airplane is on the 090° radial of a VOR. To fly directly to the station, the pilot should set the OBS to
questions.explain: Radials are magnetic bearings outbound FROM the station, so the 090° radial lies east of the VOR, and the course to the station is the reciprocal, 270°, which gives a TO indication with the needle centered. Setting 090° with TO gives reverse sensing, and 090° with FROM is the course for flying outbound, away from the station. 180° would not take the airplane to the station from the east.

questions.stem: The OBS is set to 030°, the CDI needle is centered and the ambiguity indicator shows FROM. Where is the airplane, whatever its heading?
options: On the 030° radial, northeast of the station
On the 210° radial, southwest of the station
On the 030° radial, southwest of the station
On the 120° radial, southeast of the station
questions.explain: A centered needle with FROM means the airplane is on the radial set in the OBS, here the 030° radial, which runs northeast from the station. With TO showing, a centered needle on 030° would place it on the 210° radial, southwest of the station. The VOR display is not heading-sensitive, so it shows position, not which way the airplane is pointing.

questions.stem: A pilot finds the airplane's position by computing heading, groundspeed and elapsed time from a known starting point, using the true airspeed and forecast wind. This method is called
questions.explain: Dead reckoning works out position from heading, groundspeed and time flown, based on calculations from TAS and wind (PHAK Ch. 16). Pilotage, also called contact navigation, means navigating by visible landmarks. Radio navigation and RNAV rely on ground or satellite signals rather than calculation alone.

questions.stem: Which statement about the tropopause is correct?
options: It caps the troposphere and lies higher over the equator than over the poles.
It caps the troposphere and lies higher over the poles than over the equator.
It marks where temperature starts falling sharply with increasing height.
It is the top of the stratosphere, where most weather occurs.
It lies at a fixed 36,000 feet everywhere on the earth.
questions.explain: The tropopause is the boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere; above it the temperature stops falling and stays roughly constant, and it is higher over the equator than over the poles (PHAK Ch. 12). Temperature falls with height below the tropopause, not above it. Most weather occurs in the troposphere, and the tropopause height changes with latitude and season.

questions.stem: In the standard atmosphere, what is the temperature at 12,000 feet?
questions.explain: The standard atmosphere starts at 15 °C at sea level and cools about 2 °C per 1,000 feet, so at 12,000 ft it is 15 - 24 = -9 °C. +3 °C uses only 1 °C per 1,000 ft, -24 °C is the total drop without starting from 15 °C, and -21 °C uses 3 °C per 1,000 ft. +9 °C reverses the sign.

questions.stem: A strong temperature inversion lies just above the ground. What conditions are most likely beneath it?
options: Smooth, stable air with poor visibility from trapped haze or smoke
Unstable air with good visibility and building cumulus clouds
Strong convective turbulence and showery precipitation
Temperature falling with height faster than the standard rate
Rising air that carries haze and smoke away from the surface
questions.explain: In an inversion, temperature increases with height, so the air is very stable: vertical motion is suppressed and haze, smoke and pollutants are trapped near the ground, giving smooth air but poor visibility, often with fog or low cloud (PHAK Ch. 12). Cumulus, convective turbulence and showers are signs of unstable air. A lapse rate steeper than standard is the opposite of an inversion.

questions.stem: At an airport with an elevation of 1,500 feet, the temperature is 22 °C and the dewpoint is 14 °C. About where are the bases of any convective clouds?
questions.explain: Unsaturated air cools toward its dewpoint at a converging rate of about 2.5 °C per 1,000 ft, so a spread of 8 °C gives a base about 8 / 2.5 x 1,000 = 3,200 ft AGL, and adding the 1,500 ft elevation gives about 4,700 ft MSL (PHAK Ch. 12). 3,200 ft MSL forgets that the result is above ground level. 5,500 ft MSL uses 2 °C per 1,000 ft, the standard lapse rate, and 3,300 ft MSL uses the Fahrenheit rate of 4.4 with Celsius values.

questions.stem: Which conditions are most likely to produce radiation fog?
options: A clear, nearly calm night over low land, with a small temperature-dewpoint spread
An overcast night with a steady 15-knot wind blowing in from the sea
Cold, dry air moving across a much warmer lake
Moist, stable air pushed by wind up gradually rising terrain
A clear, windy night with a large temperature-dewpoint spread
questions.explain: Radiation fog forms when the ground cools rapidly under clear skies at night and chills the moist air above it to its dewpoint; it needs calm or light wind and a small spread, and it is most common in low-lying areas (PHAK Ch. 12). Sea air moved by wind over colder land makes advection fog, cold air over warm water makes steam fog, and air pushed up a slope makes upslope fog. A large spread and strong wind prevent radiation fog.

questions.stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, as a cold front passes a station, the surface wind and pressure usually
options: shift from southwest to northwest, and the pressure starts to rise.
shift from northwest to southwest, and the pressure starts to fall.
shift from southwest to northwest, and the pressure keeps falling.
stay from the southwest, and the pressure starts to rise.
shift from northeast to southeast, and the pressure starts to rise.
questions.explain: Ahead of a cold front, winds in the Northern Hemisphere are usually from the south or southwest and pressure falls; as the front passes, the wind veers to the west or northwest, the temperature drops, and the pressure rises sharply. The reversed shift with falling pressure describes the warm sector approaching, not frontal passage. A wind shift is one of the most reliable signs that a front has passed.

questions.stem: A thunderstorm cell is considered to have entered its mature stage when
options: precipitation begins falling from the cloud base, showing that downdrafts have formed.
the cloud first grows into towering cumulus with strong updrafts.
downdrafts take over the whole cell and the updrafts die out.
the top spreads into an anvil and the rain becomes light.
the cloud first reaches the height of the freezing level.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Ch. 12) states that precipitation starting to fall from the cloud base signals that a downdraft has developed and the cell has entered the mature stage, when updrafts and downdrafts exist side by side and the storm is most intense. Towering cumulus with only updrafts is the cumulus stage. Downdrafts dominating the whole cell, with an anvil top and weakening rain, mark the dissipating stage.

questions.stem: Glossy, transparent ice that flows back over the wing before it freezes is formed mainly by
options: large supercooled droplets, as in cumuliform cloud or freezing rain.
small supercooled droplets that freeze the instant they strike.
water vapor that turns straight to ice on a cold surface.
ice crystals in high cirrus cloud.
small droplets in stratiform cloud at very low temperatures.
questions.explain: Clear ice forms when large supercooled drops strike the airframe and spread back before freezing, giving a heavy, smooth glaze that is hard to remove; it is common in cumuliform cloud and freezing rain (PHAK Ch. 12). Small droplets that freeze on impact trap air and form rough, milky rime ice, typical of stratiform cloud. Vapor freezing directly on a surface is frost, and ice crystals do not usually stick.

questions.stem: On final approach, an airplane flies into a microburst. What does the pilot usually notice first?
options: A rising headwind that increases airspeed and pushes the airplane above the glide path
A sudden tailwind that reduces airspeed and drops the airplane below the glide path
A strong downdraft before any change in the horizontal wind
A strong updraft that reduces airspeed while the airplane climbs
A gusty crosswind that drifts the airplane off the runway centerline
questions.explain: The outflow from a microburst spreads out in all directions, so an airplane flying into it first meets an increasing headwind that raises airspeed and lift, then the downdraft, then a strong tailwind that drains airspeed (AIM Ch. 7). The danger is that a pilot who reduces power for the first effect is then caught low and slow by the downdraft and tailwind. The tailwind and downdraft come later, not first.

questions.stem: METAR KXYZ 121853Z 24015G25KT 3SM -RA BR BKN008 OVC015 12/10 A2990. What flight category does this report describe?
options: IFR, because the ceiling is 800 feet
MVFR, because the visibility is 3 statute miles
MVFR, because the ceiling is 1,500 feet overcast
LIFR, because the visibility is below 5 statute miles
VFR, because the broken layer is not a ceiling
questions.explain: The ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer, here BKN008, 800 ft, which falls in the IFR range of 500 to below 1,000 ft. Visibility of 3 SM is only MVFR, but the category is set by whichever element is worse, so the report is IFR. OVC015 is above the lower broken layer, LIFR needs a ceiling below 500 ft or visibility below 1 SM, and a broken layer does count as a ceiling.

questions.stem: In a METAR, the wind group 31012G22KT means the wind is
options: from 310° true at 12 knots, gusting to 22 knots.
from 310° magnetic at 12 knots, gusting to 22 knots.
blowing toward 310° true at 12 knots, gusting to 22 knots.
from 310° true, varying between 12 and 22 knots in direction.
from 310° true at 22 knots, with gusts of 12 knots above that.
questions.explain: A METAR gives the direction the wind is blowing from, in degrees true, then the speed, with G for the peak gust: 310° true at 12 knots, gusting 22 (PHAK Ch. 13). Winds from the tower and ATIS are given in magnetic degrees, which is the common trap. Variable direction is shown with a V between two directions, such as 280V340, and the number after G is the gust speed itself, not an amount added.

questions.stem: A METAR reports 1/4SM FG VV002. What is the ceiling?
options: 200 feet, the vertical visibility into an indefinite ceiling
None, because no broken or overcast layer is reported
2,000 feet, the vertical visibility into an indefinite ceiling
20 feet, the vertical visibility into an indefinite ceiling
200 feet, the depth of a fog layer with clear sky above
questions.explain: VV002 reports vertical visibility of 200 ft into an obscuration, here fog, and vertical visibility counts as an indefinite ceiling, so the ceiling is 200 ft and the conditions are LIFR (AIM Ch. 7). Heights in METAR sky groups are in hundreds of feet, so 002 is 200 ft, not 2,000 or 20. It is not a ceiling-free report, and it says nothing about clear sky above the fog.

questions.stem: A TAF includes TEMPO 1520/1524 2SM TSRA BKN015CB. This means that between 2000Z and 2400Z on the 15th,
options: short spells of 2 SM in thunderstorms and rain, with a 1,500-foot cumulonimbus ceiling, are expected.
conditions will change permanently to 2 SM in thunderstorms and rain, with a 1,500-foot ceiling.
there is a 20% chance of 2 SM in thunderstorms and rain, with a 1,500-foot ceiling.
short spells of 2 SM in thunderstorms and rain, with a 150-foot cumulonimbus ceiling, are expected.
short spells of 2 SM in thunderstorms and rain are expected, between 2000 and 2400 local time.
questions.explain: TEMPO means temporary changes, each expected to last less than an hour and in total less than half of the stated period, here 2000Z to 2400Z on the 15th (AIM Ch. 7). A lasting change is shown by FM or BECMG, and a probability is shown by PROB30 or PROB40, not TEMPO. BKN015 is 1,500 ft, because heights are in hundreds of feet, and TAF times are UTC, not local.

questions.stem: The altimeter shown is set to the local altimeter setting on short final. What altitude does it indicate?
questions.explain: The thin 10,000-ft pointer is just past 0 and the short, wide 1,000-ft hand has not yet reached 1, so the airplane is below 1,000 ft; the long 100-ft hand points between 8 and 9, at 850 ft. 8,500 ft reads the long hand as thousands, 1,850 ft treats the short hand as past 1, and 10,850 ft treats the 10,000-ft pointer as past 1.

questions.stem: Based on the airspeed indicator shown, what is the maximum flap extended speed (VFE)?
questions.explain: VFE is the top of the white arc, which on this indicator ends at 100 knots. 50 knots is the bottom of the white arc (VS0, the stall speed with flaps down) and 60 knots is the bottom of the green arc (VS1, the clean stall speed). 140 knots is the top of the green arc (VNO), and 170 knots is the red line (VNE).

questions.stem: Referencing the primary flight display shown, if the pilot holds the vertical speed shown, about how long will it take to reach the selected altitude?
questions.explain: The boxed readout shows the actual altitude, 7,400 ft, and the cyan value shows the selected altitude, 5,000 ft, so the airplane must descend 2,400 ft. At 800 fpm that takes 2,400 / 800 = 3 minutes. 9 minutes 15 seconds divides the whole 7,400 ft by 800, 6 minutes 15 seconds divides the selected altitude by 800, and 2 minutes 24 seconds misreads 2,400 / 1,000.

questions.stem: An airplane's nose is pointed at 080°, but GPS shows it is moving over the ground along 088°. Which statement is correct?
options: Its heading is 080° and its track is 088°, so the wind is drifting it right.
Its heading is 088° and its track is 080°, so the wind is drifting it left.
Its heading is 080° and its track is 088°, so the wind is drifting it left.
Its course is 080° and its heading is 088°, so the wind is drifting it right.
Its heading and track are both 084°, the average of the two values.
questions.explain: Heading is the direction the nose points, and track is the airplane's actual path over the ground, so here the heading is 080° and the track is 088°. A track to the right of the heading means the wind is drifting the airplane right, so the wind is coming from the left. Course is the intended path planned on the chart, not the direction the nose points, and the two values are never averaged.

questions.stem: A pilot sees an indicated airspeed of 120 knots and a GPS groundspeed of 135 knots. What is the wind component along the flight path?
options: It cannot be determined without the true airspeed.
No wind; the 15-knot difference is instrument error
questions.explain: Wind is the difference between true airspeed and groundspeed, not indicated airspeed and groundspeed. At altitude TAS can be well above IAS, so a groundspeed higher than IAS could come from a tailwind, from no wind at all, or even from a headwind if TAS is above 135 knots. Comparing IAS with groundspeed is the trap; the pilot needs the TAS first.

questions.stem: A route leg measures 46 statute miles. Air navigation distances are normally given in nautical miles. About how long is the leg in nautical miles?
questions.explain: A nautical mile is about 6,076 ft, roughly 1.15 statute miles, so 46 / 1.15 = 40 NM; air navigation uses nautical miles and knots, while METAR visibility in the US is given in statute miles. 53 NM multiplies by 1.15 instead of dividing, which makes the nautical figure larger, but nautical miles are the longer unit. 29 NM treats the statute miles as kilometres.

questions.stem: What is TACAN?
options: A military UHF navigation aid that gives both bearing and distance from the station
A civil VHF navigation aid that gives bearing only, like a VOR
A military VHF navigation aid that gives distance only, like DME
A ground radar that shows controllers each aircraft's altitude
A satellite system that has replaced DME in military aircraft
questions.explain: TACAN (tactical air navigation) is the military UHF system that gives both azimuth (bearing) and slant-range distance in one unit (AIM Ch. 1). A civil VOR gives bearing only on VHF, and DME adds distance. At a VORTAC, civil aircraft use the VOR for bearing and the TACAN's distance function as their DME, while military aircraft can use the TACAN for both.

questions.stem: How does temperature generally change with height in the stratosphere?
options: It stays nearly constant at first, then increases with height.
It keeps falling about 2 °C per 1,000 feet, as in the troposphere.
It falls faster than in the troposphere, because the air is thinner.
It rises in the day and falls at night with most of the weather.
It reaches its lowest value at the top of the stratosphere.
questions.explain: Above the tropopause, temperature stops falling; in the lower stratosphere it stays roughly constant, and higher up it increases with height, because ozone absorbs ultraviolet energy from the sun. The standard lapse of about 2 °C per 1,000 ft applies to the troposphere, where nearly all weather and moisture are found. The top of the stratosphere is warmer than its base, not colder.

questions.stem: Which cloud type produces thunderstorms and is most likely to contain severe turbulence, hail and lightning?
questions.explain: Cumulonimbus is the thunderstorm cloud, built by strong updrafts and downdrafts, and it can contain severe or extreme turbulence, hail, lightning, icing and wind shear (PHAK Ch. 12). Nimbostratus gives steady rain from stable air with little turbulence. Altocumulus, cirrocumulus and stratocumulus are not thunderstorm clouds, although they can show some light turbulence.

questions.stem: A strong surface wind blows across hangars, trees and rough ground near an airport. The bumpy air it creates at low level is
questions.explain: Mechanical turbulence forms when wind flows over and around obstructions such as buildings, trees and rough terrain, breaking up into eddies near the surface. Convective turbulence comes from uneven heating of the ground and rising thermals, and clear air turbulence is found at high altitude near the jet stream. Wake turbulence comes from aircraft wingtip vortices, and frontal turbulence from lifting along a front.

questions.stem: Which group contains only gyroscopic instruments?
options: Attitude indicator, heading indicator and turn coordinator
Attitude indicator, altimeter and turn coordinator
Heading indicator, magnetic compass and turn coordinator
Airspeed indicator, vertical speed indicator and altimeter
Attitude indicator, heading indicator and vertical speed indicator
questions.explain: The attitude indicator, heading indicator and turn coordinator all work on gyroscopic principles (PHAK Ch. 8). The altimeter and vertical speed indicator are static-system instruments, and the airspeed indicator uses both pitot and static pressure. The magnetic compass is a magnetic instrument with no gyro, which is why the heading indicator is set to it.

questions.stem: Climbing in the flight levels with 29.92 set, the pilot sees the altimeter shown. What does it indicate?
questions.explain: The thin pointer with the triangle is between 2 and 3, so the airplane is above 20,000 ft; the short, wide hand is between 3 and 4 (3,000 ft) and the long hand is on 4 (400 ft), giving 23,400 ft. 3,400 ft ignores the 10,000-ft pointer, and 13,400 ft reads it as only past 1. 24,300 ft swaps the two main hands, and 32,400 ft swaps the 10,000-ft and 1,000-ft readings.

questions.stem: Excluding throttle and rudder, what control inputs will return the aircraft shown on the primary flight display to straight-and-level flight?
options: Roll right and push forward to lower the nose
Roll left and push forward to lower the nose
Roll right and pull back to raise the nose
Roll left and pull back to raise the nose
Push forward only; the wings will level by themselves
questions.explain: The horizon has tilted with its left side up and the bank pointer is on the 30° mark, so the aircraft is in a left bank; the horizon has also dropped below the miniature aircraft, so the nose is about 10° up. Rolling right levels the wings and easing the yoke forward lowers the nose to the horizon. Reading the tilted horizon as a right bank is the main trap, and the wings will not reliably level by themselves.

questions.stem: The primary flight display shown is in level cruise, and the GPS groundspeed is 131 knots. What is the approximate wind component along the flight path?
questions.explain: Wind along the path is the difference between true airspeed and groundspeed: the TAS box shows 151 knots and the groundspeed is 131 knots, so the airplane is losing 20 knots to a headwind. A 3-knot tailwind compares groundspeed with the boxed indicated airspeed of 128 knots, which is the trap. 23 knots is the gap between IAS and TAS, which comes from altitude, not wind.

questions.stem: What does the vertical speed indicator shown read?
questions.explain: The needle is below the zero mark at 9 o'clock, on the DOWN side, three small ticks past the 1 (1,000 fpm) mark, and each small tick is 100 fpm, so the reading is a 1,300 fpm descent. Reading it as a climb ignores which side of zero the needle is on. 1,200 and 1,400 fpm miscount the ticks, and 130 fpm ignores that the scale is in thousands of feet per minute.

questions.stem: What heading does the heading indicator shown display?
questions.explain: Read the card under the lubber line at the top: it sits on the short 5° tick halfway between 24 (240°) and the 10° tick at 250°, so the heading is 245°. 240° and 250° read the nearest longer tick instead of the short one, and 255° counts one tick too far. 065° is the reciprocal, read from the bottom of the card.

questions.stem: A flight will cruise at FL210 over the 48 contiguous states. Under 14 CFR 91.135, how must it be conducted?
options: Under IFR, with an ATC clearance to enter and operate in Class A airspace
Under VFR, if the pilot keeps 5 SM visibility and 1,000 ft vertically from clouds
Under VFR, once two-way radio contact is set up and Mode C is squawking
Under VFR or IFR, as long as the aircraft has ADS-B Out on 978 MHz UAT
Under VFR, but only with an explicit clearance like the one used in Class B
questions.explain: Class A runs from 18,000 ft MSL up to and including FL600, and 14 CFR 91.135 requires every flight in it to operate under IFR with an ATC clearance, so VFR is not permitted at all. The 5 SM and 1,000 ft values are VFR minimums for Class E at or above 10,000 ft MSL, which do not apply in Class A. A Mode C transponder is required, but ADS-B Out in Class A must be 1090ES, not UAT. A VFR clearance to enter is a Class B idea.

questions.stem: Which description fits a typical Class C airspace area?
options: A 5 NM surface area and a shelf out to 10 NM from 1,200 ft, both up to 4,000 ft above the airport
A 5 NM surface area and a shelf out to 10 NM from 1,200 ft, both up to 2,500 ft above the airport
A 10 NM surface area and a shelf out to 20 NM from 1,200 ft, both up to 4,000 ft above the airport
A 5 NM surface area and a shelf out to 20 NM from 700 ft, both up to 10,000 ft MSL
A 4 NM surface area and a shelf out to 30 NM from 1,200 ft, both up to 4,000 ft above the airport
questions.explain: The AIM (3-2-4) describes Class C as a 5 NM radius core from the surface to 4,000 ft above the airport elevation, with a 10 NM shelf from 1,200 ft up to the same ceiling. The 20 NM ring is the outer area, which is not Class C airspace. 2,500 ft above the airport is the usual Class D ceiling, and 10,000 ft MSL with a 30 NM ring describes Class B and its Mode C veil.

questions.stem: On a sectional chart, an airport lies inside a faded magenta band (vignette). Outside any other controlled airspace, inside that band Class E airspace begins at
questions.explain: A faded magenta vignette marks where the floor of Class E drops to 700 ft AGL around an airport with an instrument approach. A dashed magenta line marks Class E down to the surface, and a faded blue vignette marks a 1,200 ft AGL floor. Where nothing is charted, Class E generally begins at 14,500 ft MSL, and 18,000 ft MSL is the floor of Class A.

questions.stem: At night, a VFR airplane flies in Class G airspace at 900 feet AGL, well below 10,000 feet MSL, and is not in an airport traffic pattern. What does 14 CFR 91.155 require?
options: 3 SM visibility; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds
1 SM visibility; clear of clouds, the same as by day
1 SM visibility; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds
3 SM visibility; clear of clouds at all times
5 SM visibility; 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 1 SM horizontally from clouds
questions.explain: In Class G at or below 1,200 ft AGL, the day minimum is 1 SM and clear of clouds, but at night it rises to 3 SM with 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 2,000 ft horizontally. The only night exception is an airplane in the traffic pattern within half a mile of the runway, which may use 1 SM and clear of clouds. 1 SM with 500, 1,000 and 2,000 is the Class G day minimum above 1,200 ft AGL, and 5 SM with 1,000, 1,000 and 1 SM applies at or above 10,000 ft MSL.

questions.stem: Under 14 CFR 91.157, what is the minimum weather for a special VFR clearance within a Class D surface area during the day?
options: 1 SM flight visibility, remaining clear of clouds.
3 SM flight visibility, remaining clear of clouds.
1 SM flight visibility, 500 ft below and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds.
A 1,000 ft ceiling and 3 SM ground visibility.
1 SM visibility, plus an instrument rating and an IFR-equipped aircraft.
questions.explain: Special VFR needs an ATC clearance, 1 SM flight visibility and staying clear of clouds, with 1 SM ground visibility for takeoff or landing where it is reported. An instrument rating and an IFR-equipped aircraft are required only for special VFR at night, between sunset and sunrise. A 1,000 ft ceiling and 3 SM is the basic VFR minimum in a surface area, which is exactly what special VFR lets a pilot operate below.

questions.stem: A VFR flight in Class E airspace climbs from 9,500 feet MSL to 11,500 feet MSL. How do the cloud clearances required by 14 CFR 91.155 change?
options: Below clouds rises from 500 ft to 1,000 ft and horizontal from 2,000 ft to 1 SM; above stays 1,000 ft
Below clouds rises from 500 ft to 1,000 ft; the above and horizontal distances stay the same
Above clouds rises from 1,000 ft to 2,000 ft; the below and horizontal distances stay the same
Horizontal rises from 2,000 ft to 1 SM; the below and above distances stay the same
Nothing changes, because Class E cloud clearances change only at 18,000 ft MSL
questions.explain: Below 10,000 ft MSL, Class E requires 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 2,000 ft horizontally, and at or above 10,000 ft MSL it requires 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 1 SM horizontally. So two distances grow while the 1,000 ft above clouds stays the same, and visibility also rises from 3 SM to 5 SM. 18,000 ft MSL is where Class A begins, not where the Class E values change.

questions.stem: A VFR pilot wants to cross an active military operations area (MOA). Which statement is correct?
options: VFR flight may enter without a clearance, but the pilot should use extreme caution and get traffic advisories.
Flight is not allowed at any time, as with a prohibited area.
Entry requires permission from the using agency, as for a restricted area.
VFR entry requires an ATC clearance and a Mode C transponder, as for Class B.
VFR flight may enter, because only IFR traffic is kept out while the MOA is active.
questions.explain: The AIM (3-4-5) says MOAs separate certain nonhazardous military training from IFR traffic, and VFR pilots may fly through without a clearance but should use extreme caution and contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories. IFR traffic may be cleared through only if IFR separation can be provided. Permission from the using agency is the rule for a restricted area, which contains invisible hazards such as artillery, and a prohibited area such as P-56 is closed to flight altogether.

questions.stem: Under the standing FAA NOTAM for major sporting events in stadiums seating 30,000 or more, the TFR generally covers
options: a 3 NM radius up to 3,000 ft AGL, from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the event.
a 30 NM radius up to 18,000 ft MSL, for the whole day of the event.
a 1 NM radius up to 1,000 ft AGL, only while the game is in play.
a 3 NM radius up to 3,000 ft AGL, from 3 hours before to 3 hours after the event.
a 5 NM radius up to 2,500 ft AGL, only while broadcast aircraft are overhead.
questions.explain: The sporting-event TFR, issued as an FDC NOTAM, covers 3 NM around the stadium up to and including 3,000 ft AGL, from one hour before the scheduled start until one hour after the event ends. A 30 NM ring is the size used for VIP (presidential) TFRs, not stadiums. TFRs of every kind are published as NOTAMs, so pilots must check NOTAMs before each flight.

questions.stem: Ground control says, 'N123AB, runway 27, taxi via Alpha, hold short of runway 18.' What should the pilot reply?
options: Read back the runway assignment and 'hold short of runway 18' with the call sign.
Say 'Roger' with the call sign, since only clearances onto a runway need a readback.
Say 'Wilco' only, because a hold short instruction needs no readback.
Click the microphone twice to acknowledge the instruction.
Read back only 'runway 27, via Alpha' with the call sign.
questions.explain: The AIM (4-3-18) requires pilots to read back all runway hold short instructions, along with the runway assignment, and to include the call sign. 'Roger' means only that the transmission was received, and 'Wilco' means 'will comply', but neither is a readback. Leaving out the hold short point drops the most safety-critical part of the instruction.

questions.stem: The tower says, 'N123AB, runway 27, line up and wait.' The pilot should
options: taxi onto runway 27, line up, and stay there until cleared for takeoff.
hold short of runway 27 until cleared for takeoff.
take off when ready, since the runway is now assigned to the flight.
line up on runway 27 and take off as soon as the landing traffic is clear.
taxi to the run-up area for runway 27 and wait for a release.
questions.explain: The AIM (4-3-10) defines 'line up and wait' as an instruction to taxi onto the departure runway and wait in position; it is not a takeoff clearance. The pilot must hear 'cleared for takeoff' before starting the roll, whatever traffic does. Holding short is a separate instruction, and the run-up area plays no part in it.

questions.stem: Outside Class A, B and C airspace and Mode C veils, an operating transponder with altitude reporting is required in the 48 contiguous states
options: at and above 10,000 ft MSL, except at and below 2,500 ft AGL.
at and above 10,000 ft MSL, with no exception for flight close to the surface.
at and above 12,500 ft MSL, except at and below 2,500 ft AGL.
at and above 14,500 ft MSL, except at and below 1,200 ft AGL.
at and above 18,000 ft MSL only, where Class A begins.
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.215 requires Mode C in Class A, B and C, within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL, above Class C up to 10,000 ft MSL, and at and above 10,000 ft MSL except at and below 2,500 ft AGL. The 2,500 ft AGL exception covers high terrain. Mode C sends pressure altitude, while Mode A sends only the four-digit code. 12,500 ft MSL is the crew oxygen threshold, not a transponder altitude.

questions.stem: Which list correctly matches transponder codes to their meanings?
questions.explain: In the United States, 1200 is the VFR code, 7500 means unlawful interference (hijack), 7600 means lost communications and 7700 means emergency, as listed in the AIM (4-1-20 and 6-2-2). The common memory aid is 'seventy-five, taken alive; seventy-six, radio fix; seventy-seven, going to heaven.' 7000 is the VFR code used in much of Europe, not the US. Pilots should avoid passing through 7500, 7600 and 7700 when changing codes.

questions.stem: An aircraft with ADS-B In on the 978 MHz UAT link can display NEXRAD images, METARs and TFRs. Which service sends these?
questions.explain: Flight Information Service-Broadcast (FIS-B) uplinks weather and aeronautical data such as NEXRAD, METARs, TAFs, NOTAMs and TFRs free of charge, and only on 978 MHz UAT. TIS-B broadcasts radar-derived traffic, and ADS-R rebroadcasts ADS-B reports between the 1090 and 978 links. Mode S is a transponder mode, and ATIS is a recorded voice broadcast of airport information.

questions.stem: An airplane with a radio failure is circling in the traffic pattern and receives a steady red light from the tower. This means
options: give way to other aircraft and continue circling.
questions.explain: Under 14 CFR 91.125 and the AIM (4-3-13), steady red to an aircraft in flight means give way to other aircraft and continue circling. Flashing red in flight means airport unsafe, do not land, and 'stop' is the meaning of steady red on the ground. Flashing green in flight means return for landing, and alternating red and green means exercise extreme caution.

questions.stem: To an aircraft on the ground, what do a steady red and a flashing red light from the tower mean?
options: Steady red: stop; flashing red: taxi clear of the runway in use
Steady red: taxi clear of the runway in use; flashing red: stop
Steady red: stop; flashing red: return to the starting point on the airport
Steady red: give way and hold position; flashing red: airport unsafe
Steady red: stop; flashing red: exercise extreme caution
questions.explain: The light gun table in the AIM (4-3-13) gives steady red on the ground as stop and flashing red on the ground as taxi clear of the runway in use. Return to the starting point is flashing white, and exercise extreme caution is alternating red and green. 'Airport unsafe' is the meaning of flashing red only to an aircraft in flight.

questions.stem: To an aircraft on the ground, what do a steady green and a flashing green light from the tower mean?
options: Steady green: cleared for takeoff; flashing green: cleared to taxi
Steady green: cleared to taxi; flashing green: cleared for takeoff
Steady green: cleared to land; flashing green: return for landing
Steady green: cleared to taxi; flashing green: return to the starting point
Steady green: cleared to cross the runway; flashing green: exercise caution
questions.explain: On the ground, steady green means cleared for takeoff and flashing green means cleared to taxi (AIM 4-3-13). Cleared to land and return for landing are the in-flight meanings of the same two signals. Return to the starting point is flashing white, and caution is alternating red and green, so the swapped and mixed options are the usual traps.

questions.stem: A pilot is flying on an IFR clearance in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) in controlled airspace. Which statement about separation is correct?
options: ATC separates the flight from other IFR traffic, but the pilot in command keeps final authority and must see and avoid when weather permits.
ATC separates the flight from all traffic, including VFR aircraft, so the pilot has no see-and-avoid duty.
The pilot alone is responsible for separation, and ATC gives traffic advisories only on request.
ATC becomes the final authority for the flight's operation until it leaves the clouds.
ATC separates IFR traffic only in Class A airspace, so elsewhere the pilot must self-separate.
questions.explain: In controlled airspace ATC provides separation between IFR aircraft, which is why an IFR clearance is needed to fly in IMC there. 14 CFR 91.3 still makes the pilot in command the final authority for the flight, and 91.113(b) requires every pilot to see and avoid other aircraft whenever conditions permit, even under IFR. ATC does not separate IFR from VFR traffic in Class E, so VFR aircraft can be present when breaking out of cloud.

questions.stem: A runway's centerline is aligned with a magnetic heading of 044 degrees. How are its two ends numbered?
questions.explain: A runway number is its magnetic direction rounded to the nearest 10 degrees with the last zero dropped, so 044 becomes 04, shown as 4. The opposite end is 044 + 180 = 224, which rounds to 220, or 22. 5 and 23 round up instead of to the nearest ten, and 4 and 24 add 200 instead of 180. Runway numbers are always magnetic, never true.

questions.stem: Which pavement marking shows the ILS critical area holding position on a taxiway?
options: Two solid yellow lines across the taxiway joined by pairs of short yellow lines, like a ladder
Two solid and two dashed yellow lines across the taxiway
A single dashed yellow line across the taxiway
A white bar across the runway with white arrows leading up to it
Yellow chevrons pointing toward the runway threshold
questions.explain: The AIM (2-3-5) describes the ILS critical area holding position marking as two yellow solid lines spaced two feet apart, connected by pairs of solid lines at intervals, forming a ladder across the taxiway. Two solid and two dashed lines mark a runway holding position, and a single dashed line marks a taxiway/taxiway holding position. White arrows with a bar show a displaced threshold, and yellow chevrons mark an unusable blast pad or stopway.

questions.stem: At night, a pilot wants an airport's pilot-controlled runway lights at their highest intensity. On the published frequency, the pilot should key the microphone
options: once and hold it down for 5 seconds.
questions.explain: The AIM (2-1-8) gives 7 clicks within 5 seconds for the highest intensity, 5 clicks for medium and 3 clicks for the lowest. Keying 7 times first is recommended to be sure the system activates, then the pilot can step down. 15 minutes is how long the lights stay on after activation, not the keying window.

questions.stem: On an instrument runway, the runway edge lights change from white to yellow
options: on the last 2,000 ft or half the runway length, whichever is less.
on the last 1,000 ft, alternating with red.
on the first 2,000 ft, to mark the touchdown zone.
on the last 3,000 ft, to warn of the runway end.
only when the runway surface is wet or contaminated.
questions.explain: The AIM (2-1-4) states that on instrument runways yellow replaces white on the last 2,000 ft or half the runway length, whichever is less, forming a caution zone for landings. The runway end lights show red toward the runway. Alternating red and white with a 3,000 ft and 1,000 ft pattern is the runway centerline lighting code, not the edge lights.

questions.stem: Looking down the runway toward the far end, the runway centerline lights appear
options: white, then alternating red and white from 3,000 to 1,000 ft remaining, then red for the last 1,000 ft.
white, then yellow for the last 2,000 ft, then red at the runway end.
green, then red for the last 1,000 ft remaining.
white, then alternating red and white for the last 1,000 ft remaining.
alternating green and yellow, then red for the last 1,000 ft remaining.
questions.explain: The AIM (2-1-5) says runway centerline lights are white until the last 3,000 ft, alternate red and white from 3,000 to 1,000 ft remaining, and are all red for the last 1,000 ft. Yellow for the last 2,000 ft describes the edge lights on an instrument runway. Alternating green and yellow is used on taxiway centerline lead-off lights, which mark the path off the runway.

questions.stem: A wind tetrahedron swings freely with the wind. To land into the wind, a pilot should land
options: toward where the small end points, because the small end points into the wind.
toward where the large end points, because the large end points into the wind.
away from where the small end points, because the small end points downwind.
toward where the small end points, but only if the segmented circle shows left traffic.
in either direction, because a tetrahedron shows only wind speed, not direction.
questions.explain: The PHAK (Chapter 14) explains that the small end of a tetrahedron points into the wind, so landing into the wind means landing toward that end. A wind sock works the other way round: the wind blows into its large open end and the small end points downwind, which is where the trap comes from. Traffic pattern direction comes from the segmented circle's indicators, separately from wind direction.

questions.stem: At an airport without an operating control tower, the AIM recommends that an arriving airplane enter the traffic pattern
options: at a 45 degree angle to the downwind leg, abeam the middle of the runway, at pattern altitude.
on a straight-in final from at least 5 miles out, at pattern altitude.
at a 45 degree angle to the base leg, while descending to pattern altitude.
by crossing midfield at pattern altitude and turning directly onto base.
on the upwind leg at 500 ft AGL, making right turns unless told otherwise.
questions.explain: The AIM (4-3-3) recommends entering at a 45 degree angle to the downwind leg, abeam the midpoint of the runway, already at pattern altitude, which is usually about 1,000 ft AGL. The standard pattern uses left turns (14 CFR 91.126) unless markings or published procedures say otherwise, with the legs flown as upwind, crosswind, downwind, base and final. Straight-in and base entries are not the recommended method, and descending into the pattern is discouraged.

questions.stem: Which list correctly matches airport sign colors to sign types?
options: Black on yellow: direction or destination; yellow on black: location; white on red: mandatory
Black on yellow: location; yellow on black: direction or destination; white on red: mandatory
Black on yellow: direction or destination; yellow on black: location; red on white: mandatory
White on black: direction or destination; yellow on black: location; white on red: information
Black on yellow: mandatory; yellow on black: location; white on red: direction or destination
questions.explain: The AIM (2-3-8 to 2-3-12) gives mandatory instruction signs (holding positions, no entry) white letters on a red background, location signs yellow letters on a black background with a yellow border, and direction and destination signs black letters on a yellow background. The first trap swaps location and direction. Runway distance remaining signs are white numbers on black, but they are not direction signs.

questions.stem: At night, you see another aircraft ahead at about your altitude showing a steady green light and a flashing red light. It is generally
options: crossing from your left to your right.
crossing from your right to your left.
turning toward you from your right.
questions.explain: Position lights are red on the left wingtip, green on the right wingtip and white on the tail, and the flashing red is the anti-collision beacon. Seeing only green means you are looking at the aircraft's right side, so it is moving toward your right. Red alone would mean it is crossing to your left, white alone that it is flying away, and red and green together that it is coming head-on.

questions.stem: Which list gives the usual colors of an airplane's exterior lights?
options: Position lights red left, green right, white tail; beacon red; strobes and landing lights white
Position lights green left, red right, white tail; beacon red; strobes and landing lights white
Position lights red left, green right, red tail; beacon white; strobes white, landing lights amber
Position lights red left, green right, white tail; beacon green; strobes red, landing lights white
Position lights red left, green right, white tail; beacon white; strobes red, landing lights white
questions.explain: Position (navigation) lights are red on the left wingtip, green on the right and white facing aft. The rotating beacon is red, the wingtip strobes are white, and landing and taxi lights are white. The first trap reverses the wingtip colors, and green is used for airport and runway threshold lighting, not for an aircraft beacon.

questions.stem: While taxiing at night among other aircraft, why does the AIM advise pilots to switch off the white strobe lights?
options: Their intense flashes can dazzle and blind other pilots and ground crews, especially in the dark.
They drain the battery faster than the beacon while the engine is at idle.
Regulations forbid any anti-collision light from being on until the takeoff roll.
They interfere with the tower's light gun signals to aircraft on the ground.
They cannot be seen from the ground, so they serve no purpose until airborne.
questions.explain: The AIM (4-3-23) says strobes should be turned off on the ground when they would adversely affect other pilots, because their very bright flashes can temporarily blind people nearby, especially at night. 14 CFR 91.209 requires anti-collision lights to be on when the aircraft is equipped with them, but lets the pilot turn them off in the interest of safety. The red beacon usually stays on to warn ground crews that engines are running, and strobes go on when entering the runway.

questions.stem: A VFR flight will cruise more than 3,000 ft AGL on a magnetic course of 178 degrees. To correct for wind, the magnetic heading is 186 degrees. Which altitude complies with 14 CFR 91.159?
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.159 bases VFR cruising altitudes on magnetic course, not heading. A magnetic course of 0 to 179 degrees uses odd thousands plus 500 ft (such as 3,500, 5,500 or 7,500), and 180 to 359 degrees uses even thousands plus 500 ft. Using the 186 degree heading gives an even-plus-500 altitude such as 4,500 or 6,500, and whole thousands like 5,000 or 6,000 are IFR altitudes.

questions.stem: Under 14 CFR 91.151, an airplane flying VFR at night must carry enough fuel to reach the first point of intended landing and then fly, at normal cruising speed, for at least
options: 45 minutes, plus enough fuel to reach an alternate airport.
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.151 sets the VFR reserve at 30 minutes by day and 45 minutes at night for airplanes, and 20 minutes for rotorcraft. Carrying fuel to an alternate as well is the IFR rule in 91.167, not a VFR requirement. 60 minutes is not a regulatory figure.

questions.stem: An airplane is filed IFR to a destination whose forecast requires an alternate. Under 14 CFR 91.167, it must carry fuel to
options: fly to the destination, then to the alternate, then 45 minutes at normal cruising speed.
fly to the destination, then 45 minutes at normal cruising speed, with no alternate fuel.
fly to the destination, then to the alternate, then 30 minutes at normal cruising speed.
fly to the destination and then to the alternate, with no further reserve.
fly to the destination, then 30 minutes of holding, then to the alternate.
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.167 requires an IFR airplane to carry enough fuel to complete the flight to the first airport of intended landing, fly from there to the alternate, and then fly 45 minutes at normal cruising speed (30 minutes for helicopters). An alternate is needed unless, from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA, the forecast is at least a 2,000 ft ceiling and 3 SM visibility. A 30 minute reserve is the VFR day figure.

questions.stem: Except when needed for takeoff or landing, how low may an airplane fly over a congested area of a city under 14 CFR 91.119?
options: No lower than 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft horizontally
No lower than 500 ft above the surface
No lower than 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 1,000 ft horizontally
No lower than 2,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 1,000 ft horizontally
No closer than 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.119(b) sets the congested-area minimum at 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 ft of the aircraft. 500 ft above the surface applies over other than congested areas, and 500 ft from any person, vessel, vehicle or structure applies over open water or sparsely populated areas. Everywhere, the pilot must also stay high enough to make an emergency landing without undue hazard to people or property.

questions.stem: An airplane is cleared into Class B airspace and flies at 6,000 ft MSL inside it, 15 NM from the primary airport. Unless otherwise authorized, its maximum indicated airspeed is
options: 250 knots, the general limit below 10,000 ft MSL.
200 knots, because it is inside Class B airspace.
200 knots, because it is within 20 NM of the primary airport.
230 knots, the Class B speed limit.
no fixed limit, because ATC assigns all speeds in Class B.
questions.explain: 14 CFR 91.117(a) limits aircraft below 10,000 ft MSL to 250 knots indicated, and that limit applies inside Class B. The 200 knot limit in 91.117(c) applies in the airspace beneath a Class B shelf and in VFR corridors through it, and 91.117(b) sets 200 knots near the primary airport of Class C or D, not Class B. 230 knots is a holding pattern speed, not a Class B rule.

questions.stem: The US Air Force became a separate military service on 18 September 1947 under which law?
questions.explain: President Truman signed the National Security Act on 26 July 1947, and the Department of the Air Force and the USAF came into being on 18 September 1947, with Stuart Symington as the first Secretary of the Air Force and General Carl Spaatz as the first Chief of Staff. The Air Corps Act of 1926 created the Army Air Corps inside the Army. Goldwater-Nichols reorganized joint command in 1986, and the Key West Agreement of 1948 came after the USAF already existed.

questions.stem: Henry H. 'Hap' Arnold, who commanded the Army Air Forces in World War II, is the only person to have held
options: five-star rank in two services, as General of the Army and General of the Air Force.
the post of first Chief of Staff of the newly independent US Air Force.
the post of first Secretary of the Air Force under the 1947 law.
command of the Tuskegee Airmen's 332nd Fighter Group in Italy.
the record as the first pilot to fly faster than the speed of sound.
questions.explain: Arnold learned to fly at the Wright brothers' school in 1911, became General of the Army in December 1944, and was named General of the Air Force in 1949, the only five-star rank in USAF history. The first USAF Chief of Staff was Carl Spaatz, and the first Secretary of the Air Force was Stuart Symington. Benjamin O. Davis Jr. commanded the 332nd, and Chuck Yeager made the first supersonic flight.

questions.stem: The Tuskegee Airmen, the first Black military aviators in the US armed forces, flew bomber escort missions over Europe from Italy, most famously as the
questions.explain: The Tuskegee Airmen trained at Tuskegee, Alabama; the 99th Fighter Squadron deployed first and later joined the 332nd Fighter Group under Benjamin O. Davis Jr., whose fighters had red-painted tails. Davis later became the first Black general in the US Air Force. The 509th Composite Group dropped the atomic bombs, the Eighth Air Force flew bombers from England, the 1st Air Commando Group served in Burma, and the Flying Tigers fought in China.

questions.stem: The 1948 to 1949 Berlin Airlift, Operation Vittles, was flown to
options: supply West Berlin by air after the Soviet Union blocked its road, rail and canal routes.
evacuate the people of West Berlin ahead of an expected Soviet invasion.
drop supplies to Allied troops cut off during the early Korean War.
fly occupation troops home from Germany after World War II ended.
supply East Berlin after the Berlin Wall divided the city.
questions.explain: When the Soviet Union blockaded West Berlin's surface routes in June 1948, US and British aircraft, mainly C-47s and C-54s, flew in about 2.3 million tons of food, coal and supplies until the blockade was lifted in 1949. It was the first major test of the newly independent USAF. It was a supply operation, not an evacuation; the Korean War began in 1950, and the Berlin Wall was not built until 1961.

questions.stem: During the Korean War, USAF F-86 Sabres fought Soviet-built MiG-15s in the first large-scale jet-versus-jet air battles. The area of northwest Korea where most of this fighting took place became known as
questions.explain: MiG Alley was the region of northwest North Korea near the Yalu River, where F-86 Sabres met MiG-15s flying from bases across the border in China. Thud Ridge was a ridgeline near Hanoi named by F-105 pilots in Vietnam, and the Ho Chi Minh Trail was a supply route in that war. The Slot was in the Solomon Islands in World War II, and the Hump was the World War II airlift over the Himalayas into China.

questions.stem: On 14 October 1947, Captain Charles 'Chuck' Yeager became the first pilot to exceed the speed of sound in level flight, flying the
questions.explain: Yeager's rocket-powered Bell X-1 was dropped from a B-29 over Muroc (later Edwards AFB) and reached about Mach 1.06, breaking the sound barrier in level flight. The X-15 was a later hypersonic rocket plane of the 1960s, and the Skyrocket was the first aircraft to reach Mach 2, in 1953. The X-2 explored speeds above Mach 3 in the mid-1950s, and the F-104 was an operational fighter that came years later.

questions.stem: Which USAF bomber, in service since the 1950s and powered by eight jet engines, flew the December 1972 Linebacker II campaign against Hanoi and Haiphong?
questions.explain: The B-52, with eight engines in four pods, flew Linebacker II, the 11-day bombing campaign of December 1972 that helped bring North Vietnam back to the peace talks. The B-47 had six engines and left bomber service in the 1960s, and the delta-winged B-58 retired in 1970. The variable-sweep B-1B entered service in the 1980s and the B-2 stealth bomber in the 1990s, both long after Vietnam.

questions.stem: In the designations YF-22 and XB-70, what do the 'Y' and 'X' prefixes mean?
options: Y is a prototype built for test and evaluation; X is experimental.
Y is experimental; X is a prototype built for test and evaluation.
Y is a modified mission for cargo; X is a special test aircraft.
Y is a trainer version; X is an export version.
Y is a two-seat version; X is an unmanned version.
questions.explain: In the US military designation system, status prefixes come before the mission letters: X means experimental (still being developed) and Y means a prototype built in small numbers for test and evaluation. The YF-22 prototype won the Advanced Tactical Fighter competition, and the XB-70 Valkyrie was an experimental Mach 3 bomber. Trainer is the mission letter T, cargo is C, and unmanned aircraft use Q.

questions.stem: In the designation MQ-9 Reaper, the letters M and Q show that it is a
options: maritime patrol aircraft with an anti-submarine role.
multi-mission version of a cargo aircraft.
medical evacuation version of a target drone.
modified trainer used for quick reaction alert.
questions.explain: In the designation system, M is the multi-mission modified mission letter and Q marks an unmanned aircraft, so the MQ-9 is a remotely piloted aircraft that flies both ISR and strike missions with weapons such as Hellfire missiles. Its reconnaissance-only relative, the RQ-4 Global Hawk, uses R for reconnaissance. Patrol is P, anti-submarine is S, cargo is C, and trainer is T.

questions.stem: The F-35 comes in A, B and C models that differ mainly in how they take off and land. The F-35A flown by the USAF is the
options: short takeoff and vertical landing (STOVL) model.
carrier model with a larger wing and a tailhook.
two-seat training model with dual controls.
unmanned model controlled from a lead aircraft.
questions.explain: The F-35A is the conventional takeoff and landing model and the only one with an internal cannon. The F-35B is the STOVL model with a lift fan, used by the Marine Corps, and the F-35C is the carrier model with a larger wing and a tailhook, used by the Navy. There is no two-seat or unmanned F-35.

questions.stem: The F-22 Raptor is an air dominance fighter. Which feature lets it sustain supersonic flight without using afterburner?
options: A lift fan behind the cockpit
questions.explain: Supercruise is the ability to fly supersonic in military (non-afterburning) power, which the F-22's engines give it. The F-22 also has thrust-vectoring nozzles, but they improve maneuverability, not sustained speed. Variable-sweep wings belong to the B-1B, and the lift fan to the F-35B.

questions.stem: The KC-46A Pegasus tanker is based on which airliner, and which aircraft is it replacing in part?
options: The Boeing 767; the older KC-135 Stratotanker
The Boeing 767; the C-17 Globemaster III
The Airbus A330; the KC-135 Stratotanker
questions.explain: The KC-46A is built on the Boeing 767 and is replacing part of the KC-135 fleet, which first flew in the 1950s on an airframe related to the Boeing 707. The KC-10 was based on the DC-10, and the A330 is the basis of other nations' tankers, not the KC-46. The C-17 is an airlifter and the E-3 an airborne warning and control aircraft, so neither is a tanker the KC-46 replaces.

questions.stem: The E-3 Sentry, recognized by the large rotating radar dome above its fuselage, performs which mission?
options: Airborne command post for nuclear forces
questions.explain: The E-3 Sentry, built on a Boeing 707 airframe, uses its rotodome radar for all-weather surveillance and to command and control the air battle, the AWACS mission. Ground surveillance was the E-8C JSTARS mission, electronic attack is flown by the EC-130H Compass Call, and signals intelligence by the RC-135. Airborne command posts such as the E-4B do a different job.

questions.stem: The A-10 Thunderbolt II, built around its 30 mm GAU-8/A Avenger cannon, was designed mainly for
options: close air support of ground troops, including attacks on armored vehicles.
suppression of enemy air defenses with radar-homing missiles.
questions.explain: The A-10 is a close air support aircraft with a titanium armor 'bathtub' around the pilot and a large 30 mm cannon, and it attacked Iraqi armor and artillery in Desert Storm in 1991. Air superiority is the F-22's and F-15C's job, strategic bombing belongs to the B-1B, B-2 and B-52, and suppression of enemy air defenses is a mission flown by F-16s. The A-10 has no reconnaissance role.

questions.stem: How does the F-15E Strike Eagle differ from the F-15C Eagle?
options: It is a two-seat dual-role fighter with a weapon systems officer, for ground attack and air combat.
It is a single-seat air superiority fighter with no air-to-ground role.
It is a two-seat trainer version with no combat role.
It is a stealth version that carries its weapons in internal bays.
It is a carrier-capable version flown by the US Navy.
questions.explain: The F-15E Strike Eagle carries a pilot and a weapon systems officer and is a dual-role fighter for deep strike as well as air-to-air combat. The single-seat F-15C was built for air superiority. The F-15E is not a stealth aircraft, carrying weapons on external stations, and no F-15 model operates from carriers.

questions.stem: In USAF pilot training, which aircraft is the twin-engine supersonic jet trainer, and which is the single-engine turboprop primary trainer?
questions.explain: Student pilots begin primary training in the single-engine turboprop T-6 Texan II, and the twin-engine supersonic T-38 Talon is used for advanced training on the fighter and bomber track. The T-1 Jayhawk is a twin-engine subsonic business-jet trainer for the airlift and tanker track. The T-37 Tweet was a twin-jet primary trainer that the T-6 replaced, and the T-45 Goshawk is a Navy jet trainer.

questions.stem: You reach the signs shown while taxiing toward an instrument runway. What do they tell you?
options: You are on taxiway B; hold here when ATC says to protect the ILS critical area.
You are on taxiway B; you must always stop here, even without an ATC instruction.
You are on taxiway ILS, and taxiway B is the next taxiway ahead.
You are leaving the ILS critical area, and taxiway B is ahead.
You are on taxiway B; the ILS approach to the runway ahead is out of service.
questions.explain: The black sign with a yellow letter and border is a location sign, so you are on taxiway B, and the red sign with white 'ILS' is the ILS critical area holding position sign. The AIM (2-3-8) says pilots must hold there when ATC instructs them to protect the ILS signal, usually in poor weather. The sign seen when leaving the critical area is a yellow boundary sign, not a red one, and the sign gives no information about whether the ILS is working.

questions.stem: You are holding short at the signs shown and will turn LEFT onto the runway for an intersection takeoff. Which runway and heading will you depart on?
options: Either runway; a holding sign does not show which way the thresholds lie
questions.explain: On a runway holding position sign the numbers are arranged to match the thresholds, so in '9-27' the Runway 9 threshold is to the left and the Runway 27 threshold is to the right (AIM 2-3-8). Turning left sends you toward the Runway 9 end, which means you are rolling west on Runway 27, heading about 270 degrees. The yellow on black 'A' is a location sign showing you are on taxiway A. The mixed options pair a runway with the opposite heading.

questions.stem: Based on the sign array shown, which taxiway are you on?
options: Taxiway B and D, where they meet
It cannot be determined from these signs
questions.explain: The panel with a yellow letter on a black background and a yellow border is the location sign, so you are on taxiway B. The yellow panels with black letters and arrows are direction signs: D lies to the left, and F branches off ahead and to the right. Because the array includes a location sign, your position can be determined, which is why the 'cannot be determined' option is a trap.

questions.stem: Ground control tells you to taxi via Charlie. Based on the signs shown, to reach taxiway C you should
options: turn left at this intersection onto the taxiway that angles forward to the left.
turn right at this intersection onto the taxiway that leads off to the right.
make a sharp left turn back onto the taxiway that angles behind you.
continue straight ahead, because C is the taxiway you are already on.
stop, since you cannot tell which taxiway you are on from these signs.
questions.explain: The black and yellow 'G' panel is the location sign, so you are on taxiway G, not C. The yellow direction panel for C has an arrow pointing up and to the left, which means taxiway C leaves this intersection forward and to the left. The arrow to the right belongs to taxiway K, and an arrow pointing down and to the left would show a taxiway angling back behind you.

questions.stem: During a visual approach, the PAPI looks as shown. What is the airplane's position, and what should the pilot do?
options: Well below the glide path; correct upward until two white and two red lights show.
Slightly below the glide path; a small reduction in descent rate is enough.
Well above the glide path; increase the rate of descent.
On the glide path; hold the present descent rate.
Slightly above the glide path; reduce power slightly.
questions.explain: All four PAPI lights are red, which the AIM (2-1-2) defines as well below the glide path, where obstacle clearance may not be assured. The pilot should stop the descent or climb until the PAPI shows two white and two red, the on-glide-path picture. Three red and one white would be slightly below, and more white lights always mean higher.

questions.stem: Based on the PAPI lights shown beside the runway, the airplane is
questions.explain: All four PAPI lights are white, which means the airplane is well above the glide path. Three white and one red would be slightly above, two of each is on the glide path, and more red lights mean lower. The pilot should increase the descent carefully until two white and two red show, rather than diving steeply at the runway.
